Uniform Title: *Agnikāryapaddhati* Manuscript:

Manuscript No. 781, Research Library, Jammu and Kashmir Government, Śrīnagar Description: A brief liturgical manual concerning the fire sacrifice (*agnikārya*) from Kashmir. It contains highly interesting incidental information regarding the deities worshipped in Kashmir. Some of these belong to the mainstream Kaula Tantra of the early period, such as Siddhalakṣmī, who was the tutelary goddess of the Malla kings of Nepal.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: February 5, 2012.
Country of publication: India.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady, the Illustrious Great Queen.

Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas. Oṃ, I bow to that Bhairavāgama which they declare to be the seed of the Veda-tree, which possesses complete and infinite branches, and the very fruit thereof.
Now, the detailed manual for the fire-ritual (agnikārya) is written.
Therein, first, one should worship Pustakavāgīśvarī in the book.
Seated upon a lotus, she is brilliant white, three-eyed, and holds a trident, a rosary, a lotus, and a sword.
With four hands, I bow to Sarasvatī, who flows along as she is carried away, bestowing spiritual perfection.
To Śrī Pustakavāgīśvarī, [I offer] food for self-anointing; the fragrance, salutation.
Argha: *namaḥ*. Flower: *namaḥ*. Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech; *namaḥ* to Sarasvatī.
Oṃ hsauḥ aṃ āṃ, and so forth, ending with laṃ haṃ kṣaḥ; hsauḥ, salutation to Sarasvatī.
Therein, first is the worship of Gaṇapati for the purpose of pacifying obstacles.
Outside the maṇḍala, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus on one's right and having placed fruit and other offerings upon the pericarp, [one performs] the worship there.

Gaṇeśvara holds a rosary and a goad, and with his four arms he bears a vessel of sweets (*laḍupātra*) and a noose; he has two tusks and rides upon a lion. "Come, come, O Lord Gaṇapati! Accept this worship!"—thus is the invocation.
Oṃ gūṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ, obeisance to the Remover of Obstacles. *harasvatama* *lava e hma rakṣamalavaya-ūṃ*, grant me wealth, grant it twice!
Svāhā. 32.
Now, the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa) is as follows:

Having bathed there and performed his daily obligatory rites, with his body adorned with ornaments such as the twelve-finger-high *uṣṇīṣa* and other finery, wearing a ring on his finger, with his hair restrained, seated upon a *svastika* or similar seat with his head facing east and his hair and body-hair directed upward,
his limbs smeared with fragrant perfumes, well-pleased, well-purified, well-incensed, and having taken excellent betel and being anointed with sandalwood and agallochum;
His body was adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and armlets; there—
I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! O Bhavodbhava, arise in every existence, arise, and favor me in every birth.
With this mantra, his limbs were smeared with fragrant perfumes, he was well-incensed with incense by means of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, and he took his betel.
Protect me, O Amṛteśvarabhairava! 3!
With this mantra, he was adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and armlets.
Having gone to the ground on his knees and prostrated, he worshipped Śambhu; thus the detailed account is set forth.
Having constructed a pedestal for the water-pot measuring thirty-six finger-breadths.

There, one should place two jars at a distance of twelve finger-breadths to one's left; and having constructed the mandala of the secondary enclosure consisting of the weapons of the world-protectors to one's right.
There, having prepared the *argha* vessel for the weapon (*astra*) in the southwest (*nairṛtya*), one should sprinkle all the ritual substances (*dravya*) with it:
*oṃ phaṭ, may there be purification of all ritual substances and offerings, phaṭ svāhā*. Again, one should consecrate the flowers and other items with their respective mantras.
Āṃ dhūmra 2 jīva 2 saḥ 2, O life-force of all species of flowers, come here, svāhā!
Thus is the mantra for the flower.
Oṃ, homage to Kālāgnirudra, who is fragrant with the incense of the world and who carries all perfumes; [this is for] the incense.
Salutations to the lamp, whose form is the light of the world; salutations to the lamp.
O Gandhamādinī, bring back the fragrance; svāhā to the sandalwood!
Hrīṃ svāhā, [offering] to Kuṅkuma.
Oṃ lāṃ, obeisance to the Earth, the power of Dharitrī; [this is] for the arghya.
Oṃ vlīṃ, homage to Varuṇa, the royal sage; [this is] in the water.
Thus ends the consecration of the substance.

One should worship the gentle messenger (Dūtī), who has four arms, possesses a beautiful voice, and proclaims the sound of mantra; she holds a rosary, a book, a garland, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the messenger Śuddhavidyā, who consists of mantra alone.
Thus, one should worship the messenger (dūtī) through the Śāmbhava pervasion:
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the messenger of Śiva.
Thus, one should cause the messenger (dūtī) of the Śākta pervasion to sound [the instrument].
Let us know Amṛteśa; let us meditate upon Vyomadeha; may that Netra inspire us. || 3 ||
Let us know that Great Lord; let us meditate upon Him whose speech is pure; may that Śiva inspire us. || 3 ||
Let us know Him of many forms; let us meditate upon Him with hollow eyes; may that Ghorasiva impel us. 3.
At the forefront of the circle of planets.
Homage to the halo of light. Homage to the bull.

Salutation to Bhyaṅgeśa. Salutation to the Mothers of the Quarters (Diṅmātṛs). Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa. Kuṃ, salutation to Kumāra. Śrīṃ, salutation to Śrī. Saṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. Oṃ, salutation to Viśvakarman.
Then follows the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma). The invocation is performed above the circle of the planets.
One should meditate upon the Lord face-to-face, using a handful of flowers as the measure.
"O All-pervading One, together with your retinue, welcome!"—thus one should utter.
Welcome, welcome to Śiva and his retinue! O sir!
Then, above the mandala of the planets.
One should worship Amṛteśvara, Amṛtalakṣmī, and the Niṣkala [form] in the center; outside of that, one should worship the Sūryas and the Bhairavas with their respective mantras.

p. 2b) Oṃ kṣamaraya-ūṃ, homage to Kapāleśa Bhairava. Oṃ hrūṃ, homage to Śikhivāhana Bhairava. Oṃ kṣuṃ, homage to Krodharāja Bhairava. Oṃ jhrūṃ, homage to Vikarāla Bhairava. Oṃ hvūṃ, homage to Manmatha Bhairava. Oṃ...
Hryūṃ, obeisance to Meghanādabhairava. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Somarājabhairava. Oṃ ṭhūṃ, obeisance to Vidyārājabhairava.
Outside of that are the planetary deities (grahas).
In the beginning and in the middle, the Sun.
Oṃ rūṃ, salutation to Agni. Oṃ hāṃ jhrīṃ saḥ, salutation to Vīreśvara Bhairava. Oṃ hrāṃ jhrīṃ saḥ, salutation to Vīralakṣmī.
Then, in order starting from the east.
Oṃ vlūṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ srūṃ, homage to the Moon. [In the] East.
Oṃ, obeisance to Kuṃkumāra. Oṃ rahara-ūṃ, obeisance to Aṅgāraka. [In the southeast.]
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Viṣṇu. Oṃ srūṃ, homage to Budha. [To the right.]
Oṃ lūṃ, homage to Indra. Oṃ rṣūṃ, homage to Jīva. In the west.
Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ! Speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech; salutation to Sarasvatī.
Oṃ, homage to the supreme Asura! [In the] north.
Oṃ āṃ vrāṃ vraṃ, homage to Brahmā. Oṃ kṣmryūṃ, homage to Śanaiścara. [In the] southwest.
Oṃ gaṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa. Oṃ yūṃ, salutations to Gahava. In the northwest.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, to Rudra; salutation! Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Ketu; in the northwest.
Īśa is on the left side outside the sacrifice, in the form of a wing.

Oṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Oṃ, obeisance to Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda. Outside the sacrificial area, upon a svastika to one's own right: Oṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Oṃ, obeisance to Agastya, the son of Avarṇāpāda. Outside of that:
Oṃ lūṃ, homage to Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand.
p.
3) Rūṃ, obeisance to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand.

Oṃ ṭūṃ, homage to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand. Oṃ kṣūṃ, homage to Nairṛti, who holds a sword in his hand. Oṃ vūṃ, homage to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand. Oṃ yūṃ, homage to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand. Oṃ kuṃ, homage to Kubera, who holds a mace in his hand. Oṃ mūṃ, homage to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand. Oṃ āṃ vrāṃ vraṃ, homage to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand. Oṃ hlāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu.
Salutation to the one who holds the moon in his hand.
Having thus worshipped Śambhu, having gone to the ground on one's knees, and having prostrated and made a formal request, one should receive his command.
O Śambhu, since I was previously appointed by you to the Śiva-sacrifice, remain as the Guru of both the higher and lower realms and act for the benefit of the worlds.
O Blessed One, my heart has been scented by your power; therefore, this man was seen by me for the sake of bestowing grace upon his service, and not out of greed.
And in this matter, O Blessed One, you alone are the authority for all actions; you are the witness, the self-acting agent, the supreme Śaṅkara, the Auspicious One.
Therefore, by presiding over me alone with your special presence, grant that I may attain equality of action with those feet of yours.
Keeping your command in my heart, I perform all rites. For who, O Lord, would be able to act otherwise, even the Lords of Knowledge themselves?
I shall experience the fruit of whatever action I perform.
Having thus received the command of Śambhu.
Oṃ ṭhū&? Homage to Bhairava, the King of Vidyās.

Thus, having recited the *Vidyārāja-saptajapta-uṣṇīṣa* seven times and being embraced by the realization of "I am Śiva," one who desires to reach the supreme further shore should go forth with a joyful mind.
First, outside the flask, there is the worship of the circle of light.
Therein is the meditation on the bull.
White, three-eyed, a bull, radiant, and likewise bearing a trident; he should be meditated upon as the destroyer of sins, with hands shining with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Oṃ, homage to the Bull.
One should meditate upon him as having one face and four arms, the destroyer of all obstacles, radiant with a circle of light, and brilliantly effulgent.
Oṃ, homage to Prabhāmaṇḍala.

Salutation to Vṛṣabha. Salutation to Bhṛṅgīśa. Salutation to Kumāra. Salutation to Ambikā. Oṃ, salutation to Dvāraśrī. Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī. Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. Salutation to Viśvakarman. Salutation to the Trident.
Then, outside the jar-sacrifice (kalaśayāga), one should worship the ten Mothers of the Directions in the sequence starting from the east.
The Svadhākalaśas, holding beautiful flower garlands in their hands and being most resplendent, are the Ākāśamātṛs, single-faced, positioned facing the deity.

Oṃ, obeisance to Umā. Oṃ, obeisance to Durgā. Oṃ, obeisance to Bhadrakālī. Oṃ, obeisance to Svastī. Oṃ, obeisance to Svāhā. Oṃ, obeisance to Śubhaṅkarī. Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī. Oṃ, obeisance to Gaurī. Oṃ, obeisance to Lokadhātrī. Oṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Oṃ, obeisance to the Mothers of the Quarters (Diṅmātṛs).
Then follows the worship of the doors.

On the right branch to one's left: *Oṃ nandine namaḥ* | *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ* | *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ daṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch to one's right: *Oṃ mahākālāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ yamunāyai namaḥ* | *Oṃ chāgalāsyāya namaḥ*.
Salutation to Mahodara.
Above the door.
Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa. [This is for] below the door.
Salutation to the threshold. Salutation to Vāstupuruṣa. Salutation to Brahmā. Salutation to all beings.
Then, in the placement within one's own group, [it is performed] in the middle of the door.
By means of the application of the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, together with the nārāca mudrā.
He states that meditation:
One should meditate upon that [deity] who wields the Nārāca weapon, resembling the sun, fierce, blazing with three eyes, holding a trident and a noose, and the remover of obstacles.
Thus, having cast the flower into the center of the sacrificial ground.

Having warded off the obstacles on the ground with three slaps of the heel, those in the intermediate space with three claps of the palms, those in the celestial realm by looking with divine vision, and those situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions with snaps of the fingers, employing the *huṃ* and *phaṭ* syllables;
There, having offered the bali for the spirits (bhūtabali) as will be described;
Whatever beings dwell upon the earth, having received the oblation offered according to the prescribed rite;
May they arrange their residence elsewhere and forgive me; let there be homage to them.
Having recited this, one should perform the ritual for the departure of the elemental spirits.
In the northern direction, having meditated upon Śalabharudra together with his Śakti, one should worship him with his mantra.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the locust-like Śālva, the king of birds; destroy my enemies, destroy them! Hauṃ gha gha huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
I worship the sandals of Śalabharudraśrī; obeisance!
To her left.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Śalabhīśvālī! Destroy my enemies, destroy them! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
O Śalabhā Devī, I worship the venerable sandals; obeisance!
Oṃ sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the glorious Sudarśana weapon. Thus, in the eastern direction.
Oṃ hrīṃ 2 prasphura 2 sphura 2 ghoraghoratara-tanurūpa naṭa 2 pracaṭa 2 karṣa 2 ghātaya 2 huṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ aghorāstrāya namaḥ.
Thus for the right [hand].
Arise, O woman! Why do you sleep? Fear has come upon me; whether it is possible or impossible, O Blessed One, pacify it for me, svāhā!
Salutation to Vanadurgā; thus [one worships] in the west.
[He should place] the Pāśupata weapon in the intermediate directions with: *ŚLĪM PAŚU HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ*. Having remembered Gaṇapati in the center, he should worship him.

Immediately thereafter, having entered [the pavilion], he should contemplate there the arrangement of the weapons of the world-protectors, such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and others, for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.

Standing in the south, facing north, and sitting with his face toward the Aghora-mukha [of the Śiva-linga] due to the power of burning away sins, he should worship Vāstupuruṣa in front of the pitcher-altar.
He speaks of meditative concentration (dhyāna).
One should meditate upon Vāstupuruṣa as white, three-eyed, with a gentle face, two-armed, holding a rosary and a trident, and the destroyer of obstacles.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāstupuruṣa.

Then, the worship of the elements (bhūtapūjā) is performed in order upon the pitcher and the sacrificial altar, starting from the east: Oṃ lāṃ to Kṣiti (Earth), obeisance! Oṃ rauṃ to Agni (Fire), obeisance! Oṃ sauṃ to Yajamāna (the Sacrificer), obeisance! Oṃ sauṃ to Sūrya (the Sun), obeisance! Oṃ vauṃ to Jala (Water), obeisance! Oṃ yauṃ to Vāyu (Wind), obeisance! Oṃ sauṃ to Soma (the Moon), obeisance! Oṃ hauṃ to Ākāśa (Space), obeisance! Then, one should begin the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
Having smeared the two hands with fragrance, sprinkled them with the Astra-mantra, and enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra, one should drench them with Amṛta.
For example:

Having meditated on the *śakti* that has arisen from the *kanda*-place, one should contemplate it as having reached the *dvādaśānta*; then, having meditated on the *śakti* that has arisen from that place, one should contemplate it as having reached the *bindu*-place; then, having taken the nectar (*amṛta*) from that place and visualized it exiting through the nostrils via the *dvādaśānta*, one should contemplate the two hands being bathed. And one should meditate thus.

Immediately thereafter, having formed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*), one should visualize the Support Power (*ādhāraśakti*) at the base of the thumbs, the lotus at its tip, and the Form (*mūrti*) above that. Therein is the venerable Lord Netrabhaṭṭāraka; the five limbs (*aṅga*) from the thumb to the little finger [are assigned], and the Weapon (*astra*) is on the nails.

Starting from the right index finger and ending with the left index finger is the eightfold Bhairava; starting from the left index finger and ending with the right index finger is the eightfold Bhairava.
Then, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the partless [deity] along with its limbs and the Goddess upon the two thumbs. Thus ends the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
Now, the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).
"Oṃ laṃ, I perform exhalation; homage. Thus, one should expel the impure vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) through the right nostril for a duration equal to the time taken to utter twelve *praṇavas*.
Oṃ vaṃ, I perform the filling; homage! One should cause the pure, white *prāṇa*-wind to enter through the left nostril for as long as it takes to recite twenty-four *praṇavas*.
Oṃ raṃ, I perform *kumbhaka*; salutation.

One should restrain that very vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) within by means of a motionless state like a water-filled jar for as long as it takes to recite thirty-six *praṇavas*. Yaṃ, I perform *ūrdhvarecaka*; salutation. One should lead that very restrained air upward through the piercing sequence of the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the *brahmarandhra*. Or...
One should slowly expel the breath through the left nostril as far as possible; this is the withdrawal (*upakarṣa*).
Oṃ haṃ, I establish the self whose nature is space; homage!

Having dissolved the mind, ego, and intellect into the Supreme Reality by means of the upward breath (*ūrdhvarecaka*), one should join the self—residing in the heart-lotus, subtle like a firefly, and appearing like a shimmering star—to the End of the Twelve (*dvādaśānta*) through the process of piercing the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmāraṇdhra*).
Having meditated upon the body as empty, one should rest. Thus ends the purification of the subtle body. Thus ends the process of extraction.
"Oṃ kṣyūṃ, I wither this body; obeisance. Thus, one should contemplate the Praṇava in the form of the Sun as pervading the entire body.
Thus ends the earth-element concentration (pārthivī-dhāraṇā).

"Rakṣaraya-ūṃ, I burn the body; obeisance. Having thus meditated upon the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) at the big toe of the right foot, one should contemplate the body, both internally and externally, as having been reduced to ashes by its flames.
Thus ends the Āgneyī-dhāraṇā.
"Yūṃ, I perform the leaping upward; homage!"—thus one should contemplate the physical body as being dispersed toward the ten directions by the wind. [This is the] Vāyavī [mantra].
"Oṃ vaṃ, I bathe the body; homage. Thus, one should contemplate that place as being washed by the water of the Śākta nectar falling from the *dvādaśānta*.
Thus ends the section on Vāruṇī.
Oṃ haṃ saṃ! I am composed of consciousness; in this there is no other, and here no object of meditation exists.
"The mind, merged in the state of bliss, has attained a state of equal flavor. Thus [ends] the section on Space.

In this way, the fivefold retention (*dhāraṇāpañcaka*)—the five elements beginning with earth and ending with space; the fivefold city as the five subtle atoms (*māṇu*); the fivefold causal deities from Brahmā up to Sadāśiva; the fivefold organs of action such as the ear; the fivefold faces beginning with Sadyojāta; and the fivefold states beginning with waking—all such manifold expansion (*prapañca*) resides within the Supreme Śiva, who is the void beyond the void, whose nature is supreme illumination, who is free from the web of conceptual construction, who transcends all qualities (*guṇātīta*), and who is the sixth.
One should contemplate [the self] as dissolved in the venerable Niṣkala-bhaṭṭāraka, who rests in the supreme ether and abides at the limit of the twelve.

Just as the lethal nature of poison itself is warded off by the power of a mantra, but not its essential nature, so too there is the dissolution of the identification with the body, but not the destruction of its essential nature; this is the intended meaning.
Thus, when the body composed of the six sheaths has been dissolved, one should meditate upon the Self as consisting of supreme bliss.
The sense is: "I myself am Śiva."
Oṃ hāṃ, I enliven the divine body; homage! Having meditated upon the seat-side [of the deity] starting from the ritual action (karma).
Salutation to Ādhāraśakti at the *kanda*. Salutation to Dhātrī up to the navel. Salutation to Payorṇava at the navel. Salutation to Mūla and salutation to Kanda; salutation to Nāla up to the heart.

Having visualized the Yoga-pīṭha seat together with the feet [of the deities] such as Dharma and the rest within the heart, one should meditate upon an eight-petaled white lotus seat with a pericarp in its center.
Salutation to the petals. Salutation to the solar disc. One should meditate upon the white petals. Salutation to Brahmā, the presiding lord thereof.

One should meditate upon Brahmā, who has four faces and four arms. [Recite: "Obeisance to the filaments. "Obeisance to the lunar disc. One should meditate upon the filaments as yellow and white; to their presiding deity, Viṣṇu, obeisance. One should meditate upon Viṣṇu as being black in color. [Recite: "Obeisance to the pericarp."

*Namaḥ* to the fire-maṇḍala. One should meditate upon the pericarp as having the color of its own [corresponding] syllable. *Namaḥ* to Rudra, the lord thereof. One should meditate upon Rudra as white. Then, *namaḥ* to Īśvara. One should meditate upon Īśvara as white. Thereafter, one should place the great preta known as Sadāśiva, who has a corpse for a seat, laughing and conscious. He is red in color, radiant with his own splendor, and adorned with three eyes.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Sadāśiva, who is seated upon a great corpse.

Oṃ, obeisance to the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) on the petals; obeisance to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) on the filaments; Oṃ, obeisance to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) in the pericarp.
Having worshipped the four Vedas upon the honored seat, one should then, from the twelve-finger space of experience (*bhogadvādaśānta*), [visualize] the Blessed One in the form of a shimmering star.

By means of the upward breath-retention (*ūrdhvarecaka*), following the sequence through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the center of the brows, and the palate, one should unite [the deity] with the form of the Blessed One situated in the heart-lotus; then, following the sequence from that twelve-finger space, one should join [Him] within His heart.
The meaning is that one should make oneself Śiva.
"Amṛtīkaromi namaḥ. With these words, I drench my body, both externally and internally, with the nectar-water of Śakti falling from the *dvādaśānta*, saying "namaḥ."

Homage to the lower covering; homage to the upper covering; homage to the middle covering. Oṃ, homage to *sattva*; homage to *rajas*; homage to *tamas*. There, having meditated upon the Supreme Lord with the visualization "the deity is one's own self" (*svadhā*) within the pericarp, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Oṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva at the aperture of the crown; salutation to the Sadāśiva-tattva on the forehead.
Salutation to the principle of Īśvara in the middle of the eyebrows. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Vidyā in the palate.
Salutation to the principle of Māyā at the throat.
Salutation to Kālatattva in the heart.
Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Niyati at the navel.
Homage to the principle of the Puruṣa, on the penis.
Salutation to the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva) at the feet.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the three principles (tritatva).
He offers salutation to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) at the aperture of the skull.
Now, *namaḥ* to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) at the center of the eyebrows.
Oṃ, homage to the reality of the self; [place this] at the heart.
Salutation to the embodiment of nectar throughout the entire body.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) and the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) by means of the six limbs.
Furthermore, one should place the root-mantra upon the entire body: *oṃ mūrtyai namaḥ*, *śuddhadehāya namaḥ*. One should worship the deity with the five mental offerings (*mānasa-pañcopacāra*).

And the fire-oblation (*homa*). Then one should perform the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*). On the sacrificial ground, having worshipped the weapon (*astra*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) to its right of oneself, [one should proceed].

One should meditate upon the Weapon [mantra] of the God, which has three eyes and two arms, facing [the practitioner], blazing as it devours the flood of obstacles and bringing about the destruction of great sins.

Then, with a seat made of two blades of *darbha* grass, the purification of the ritual substances (*dravya-saṃskāra*) is performed. Then, having sprinkled the three vessels with the *astra-mantra*, encircled them with the *varma-mantra*, veiled them with the *kavaca-mantra*, and worshipped them with the *praṇava*, one veils the three vessels with the mantra: "Haṃ, I veil the three vessels; Huṃ, obeisance. Thus one veils them.

Having worshipped with the mantra "Obeisance to the vessels for the rite of animal sacrifice and cessation," and having worshipped with the eight-limbed *arghya* accompanied by a pair of *darbha* blades as a seat;
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, clarified butter, curd, rice, barley, and white mustard seeds— this is proclaimed as the eightfold arghya offering.
Lāṃ, salutation to Pṛthivī, the mother of the world.
Thus for the rice grains.
And for Trijaṭa: "Obeisance to Piṅgala Rudra."
Mustard seeds.
Oṃ, homage to Brahmā, the beloved one in the forest of sound; [offer] barley grains.
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods; salutation to the one of great strength. [Offer] flowers.
Oṃ jrīṃ, O Sāvitrī, consumer of sins; obeisance to Sāvitrī! Hūṃ phaṭ! [To the] darbha grass.
Oṃ svāṃ svāṃ svāṃ, salutation to Soma; [offer] water. Oṃ tatsat, salutation to the ancestors; [offer] sesame seeds.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Sarasvatī, the Mistress of Speech, the bestower of eloquence; [offering] milk.
Oṃ phaṭ, to the weapon, phaṭ; [this is] the clarified butter.
Oṃ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ, homage to all substances, to all materials, which are the most excellent of all things.
One should place these in the vessels; thus, the eightfold nature of the *arghya* arises through the intention of offering.
In that regard, one should first prepare the price for the mantra (vidyārgha) and the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, as seen by others, for the purpose of worshipping the Lord.
The knowledge of the Self is Śiva-prakṛti [and] Puruṣa, by means of the five principles (tattva).
By means of the digits (kalā) of the Sun, Moon, and Fire. Among these, first are the solar digits (sūryakalā).
Oṃ to Mārīcī, Jvālinī, Dhūmrā, Tapantī, Tāpinī, Pācinī, Havirvāhā, Tejovatī, Śatadhāmā, Sudhāmā, Padmagarbhā, and Tamopahāriṇī— these are the twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun.
Now, the portions of Soma.
Oṃ, to Pūṣā; to Yamā; to Sumanasī; to Prīti; to Prītikārī; to Vṛtti; to Vṛtikārī; to Saumyā; to Marīci; to Aṃśumālinī; to Śaśinī; to Hṛdgatā; to Lakṣmī; to Chāyā; to Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalā. Homage to Amṛtā!
Thus end the digits of the Moon. || 16 ||
Now, the fire-arts (āvahnikakalās).
Oṃ to Dhūmrā; to Nīlaraktā; to Kapilā; to Visphuliṅginī; to Jvālā; to Tejovatī; to Havirvāhinī.
To Kavivāhinī, to Raudrī, to Saṃhārakāriṇī. Thus [end] the fire-elements (vahnikalā). 10.

With the root mantra together with the five limbs, accompanied by the five principles of Self, Knowledge, Śiva, and Nature, one should worship the offering of knowledge (*vidyārgha*) in one's own breath. Therein, the observation of the instruments is performed through the vision of another.
O Goddess, that which is unobstructed, perfectly real, eternal, and free from conceptual construction—that is said to be the supreme state, the ultimate goal beyond the eightfold path.
Thus is the sprinkling of all substances from the *vidyā-argha* vessel. Then, in the center, one should worship the *nirodhārgha* with the root mantra alone.
There, one should display the Niṣṭhura-mudrā. Nearby: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Thus is the ritual of the Śiva-water.
Near that, on his own right side, he should worship the Pāśupata weapon with the root mantra together with its ancillaries and the Devīka-mantra, using the Pāśupata-weapon mantra.
Oṃ ślīṃ paśu hūṃ phaṭ, [homage] to the Pāśupata weapon, phaṭ!
Oṃ, phaṭ to the heart; homage!
ŚLĪṂ, PHAṬ SVĀHĀ to the head; VAUṢAṬ to the crest-lock; PHAṬ HŪṂ to the parrot-like armor; HŪṂ VAṢAṬ to the eyes; PHAṬ PHAṬ PHAṬ to the weapon.
Thus concludes the worship of the three vessels for the animal sacrifice (paśvargha) according to the rite of cessation.
In these, one performs the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) with the Amṛta-mudrā.
One sprinkles oneself from the mantra-offering vessel (arghapātra) with the mantra: "I bow to the white one... (naumi śvetmaiti).
Having performed self-worship with the root mantra seven times, one should perform the worship of the Guru starting from the northeast and ending in the southeast.
Having sprinkled the palms of the hands with the water of Śiva, the water of the weapon, and the water of knowledge, and having performed the veiling gesture (avaguṇṭhana).
Having washed one's hand with scented water using another hand, one should worship the deity along with his retinue, omitting the seat, while anointed with fragrance.
And so it is said:
Endowed with the five faces and presided over by Śiva, he is Śiva himself.
The one who severs the noose is proclaimed as Kṣemī Śivahasta.
It is as follows:
With saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, tagara, and priyaṅgu, they prescribed this procedure for the scented water according to the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śaṅkara.
Having thus prepared the scented water and having washed both hands with it.

Oṃ, homage to the moon-maṇḍala; [place this] on the left hand. Oṃ, homage to the sun-maṇḍala; [place this] on the right. Thus, having worshipped the maṇḍala with perfumes using the middle and thumb fingers of those two hands, and having offered flowers placed by the other hand, one should worship the root mantra together with its limbs, faces, and seat.

One should perform the conjunction of mantras, the conjunction of the channels, and the act of supreme transformation for the All-pervading Lord who resides in the hand in another manner. It is as follows:
Uttering the mantra from the heart through the central abode via the *suṣumnā* path, having pierced the *bindu* situated between the eyebrows and previously torn asunder all knots,
one enters the supreme abode at the *dvādaśānta*. Then, descending again from the *dvādaśānta* to the space between the eyebrows,
one gradually takes hold of the collection of mantras resting in the hand— appearing in a blazing, radiant form— through the path of the left nostril by means of that same [left] nostril path.
Having brought it to the midpoint between the eyebrows, one should pierce the cranial aperture from that midpoint with something as fine as the point of a needle and lead it to the dvādaśānta.
Thus ends the conjunction of mantras.

Again, having brought [the breath] from the *dvādaśānta* to the center of the eyebrows, and having performed exhalation (*recaka*) through the path of the right nostril from the center of the eyebrows,

one enters the heart of the All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*) who exists in the form of the mantra held in the hand; then, reaching the *dvādaśānta* via the heart-path of that All-pervading Lord held in the hand,
and having performed inhalation (*pūraka*), one should enter one’s own heart through the right nostril— this is the "joining of the channels" (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).

Then, from one's own heart to the *dvādaśānta*, and from that *dvādaśānta* back to the heart, and everywhere like a bow-shaped wheel, one should contemplate the radiant, partless (*niṣkala*) Lord extending from the heart to the hands.
Thus is the process of supreme transformation.
Thus, having visualized the hand as being completely filled with a mass of blazing mantras, one should recite the root mantra and place the right hand upon the heart.
Having placed a flower from the left hand into the right hand, one should place that right hand upon one's own head.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Hand of Śiva.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having divided the area into nine compartments using a powder of *vāśā* and *lipta*, one should bring nine vessels, ranging from those made of gold down to those made of clay.

"Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I purify the vessels, haḥ phaṭ! Having thus consecrated [the water] seven times, one should sprinkle the vessels with the Sword of Knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) fashioned from thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass. Then, one should sprinkle that [Sword of Knowledge] with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*).
Oṃ haiṃ, I envelop the vessels; hūṃ.

Thus, it is veiled by the *kavaca* (armor-mantra). Beginning from the central square and proceeding in order from the east onwards, the nine principles (*tattvas*)—Śiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyā, Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Puruṣa, and Prakṛti—are deposited. [These are placed] in the center, the east, south, west, and north as Supratiṣṭhā and Suśāntā.
One should worship the fire called Amṛta and the rising of Śukra; then, with the Heart mantra, one should worship the cow dung in the east, and with the Head mantra, the cow urine in the north.

One should place curd in the east with the *śikhā* mantra, milk in the center with the *varman* mantra, ghee in the south with the *astra* mantra, and water infused with *kuśa* grass at the northeast for the eyes.
This is precisely it: one should apply cow dung with the heart-mantra over water. Having recited once, "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart," [one says] "Laṃ, obeisance to the Sadyojāta form."

Thus, [one should offer] cow dung at the head with the thumb; cow urine at the north with the head [mantra]. Reciting "Hīṃ Sirase Svāhā" twice over [the substances], one should recite "Oṃ Vaṃ Vāmadevāya Namaḥ" and pour one *pala* of cow urine into the northern [direction].
Having consecrated the curd in the eastern direction and at the crest-lock [of the deity] three times with "HŪṂ ŚIKHĀYAI VAUṢAṬ," [one should offer it].
Oṃ, homage to the heart of Aghora. In the east, [place] a *pala* of curd; in the center, milk with the *varman* mantra: *Hraiṃ Kavacāya Hūṃ*.
Having consecrated it four times with the mantra: "Yaṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa," place one *pala* of milk in the center.
On the right, [place] ghee with the weapon-mantra: *Oṃ haḥ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*. Having consecrated it five times.
Oṃ kṣaṃ, homage to Īśāna, the head.
One should pour ghee, measuring half the size of a thumb, into the right [hand].
One should offer water with kusha grass to Ishana with the [Netra] mantra.
Oṃ hauṃ, vaṣaṭ to the eyes! Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva!
Let us know that Great Lord; let us meditate upon Him who is pierced by speech; may that Śiva inspire us. || 3 ||
Thus, one should pour a *pala* measure of water with *kuśa* grass into the northeast.
Or alternatively:

Or else, having placed one *palam* of cow-dung and clarified butter measured at half a thumb-breadth, or two, three, four, or five [thumb-breadths], and another *palam* of *iṣadīśī* [medicinal plant], along with *kuśa* water measuring one *palam*.
Or alternatively:
Cow dung, cow urine, clarified butter, curd, and milk as the fifth—[these are purified] by means of the Sadyojāta, Vāma, Rūpin, and Puruṣa [mantras].

One should consecrate the cow-dung and other materials in their respective order with the Īśāna mantra; however, the kuśa-water should be consecrated with the Gāyatrī, the Dhāman, or the Saṃhitā mantra.
Having consecrated the water with kusa grass using the complete mantra-formula: *oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ kuśodakāya namaḥ*.
Then, placing each preceding one in front, he should join them together.
One should place cow dung in cow urine; cow urine in curd; curd in milk; milk in ghee; and ghee in water infused with *kuśa* grass.
The Īśvara-tattva is situated in the southeast; the Māyā-tattva is situated in the southwest; the Māyā-tattva situated in the southwest [extends] to the Niyati-tattva situated in the northwest.
One should join the principle of *niyati* residing in *vāyu* with the principle of *prakṛti* residing in *īśāna* within the water mixed with *kuśa* grass.
All of that should also be placed individually in a vessel upon the lotus previously drawn in the southeast corner, atop the jar-maṇḍala.

Furthermore, having stirred the six limbs within the ocean of nectar and having rendered them immortal, one should worship Ananta with "Oṃ Anantāya Namaḥ" beneath the vessel; and on the left above the vessel, [worship] Aghora and Aghorīśvarī with "Oṃ Kheṭaka. One should worship [the deity] in its partless (niṣkala) form, along with its limbs (aṅga), faces (vaktra), and enclosures (āvaraṇa).
Having enveloped [everything] with the Kavaca mantra,
one should sprinkle oneself and the sacrificial ground with that [water].
Thus concludes the procedure for the five products of the cow.
Then, standing in the southern direction and facing north on the sacrificial ground, he should worship the sword of knowledge made of thirty-six darbha grasses.
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! Homage to the sword of wisdom, which consists of the thirty-six principles.

Then, with that five-product mixture (*pañcagavya*) over which the weapon-mantra has been recited seven times, or with a seat made of seven blades of *darbha* grass, or with the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), one performs the sprinkling of the ground.
Thus, having purified the arrow-head, one should meditate upon the earth as being completely filled.
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I perform the act of scraping; phaṭ!
In this way, there is the removal of loose soil and the extraction of the splinter.

The processes of making [the ground] adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*), filling with pearls (*mauktikāpūraṇa*), pounding (*ākoṭana*), sprinkling (*secana*), leveling (*samīkaraṇa*), and sweeping (*mārjana*)—these purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are performed mentally. Thus is the purification of the ground (*bhūmiśuddhi*).
Then follows the smearing with the five products of the cow and scented water.
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the anointing, haḥ phaṭ. Then follows the casting of the rays.
Sesame seeds, parched grain, dūrvā grass, auspicious white mustard seeds, white flowers, and abundant fragrant incense.
This auspicious powder is mixed with sandalwood paste.
The discharge of the *vikara* weapon by means of the *astra*.
One should meditate upon the transformations in the form of the world-protectors' weapons.
And with a fine powder or a bundle of kuśa grass, one should sprinkle [the area] starting from the southwest (Nairṛta) and ending in the northeast (Īśāna).
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the sprinkling, phaṭ!
Having sprinkled the sacrificial ground with fragrant water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),...
The worship of Śrī in the western direction in the center of the altar.
Having invoked Śrī with the *dhruva* mantra—she who holds a lotus in her hand, possesses beautiful eyes, sheds white flowers, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, gazing upon the sacrificial hall, seated in the Brahma-position, and auspiciously facing the door.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Śrī.
Then, one performs the worship of Gaṇapati to one's left.

"Holding [the spear] in his right hand... With the root mantra and its limbs, perform the worship. To one's own right, perform the worship of Kumāra. [Worship] the bell fashioned of gold with the root mantra and its limbs. Then, in ascending order, perform the worship of the planets. Their petition [is as follows]:
May all the blessed planets, and whatever others are considered secondary planets, all of them grant their presence for the pacification of obstacles.
To the left of oneself, ending with Īśāna, is the worship of the Guru.
O Mother Gaṇanāthāmbikā, O sandals of my Lord, grant me permission as I worship the Teacher of the World, so that I may become a successful performer of the rite.
Then, having worshipped the sacrificial altar with the root mantra and its ancillaries.
Then, having drawn a svastika in the northeast, one should draw a lotus near it.

Then, having brought the *śivakalaśa*, having sprinkled it with the water of Śiva using the *astra-mantra*, having wiped it with a white cloth, having marked it with scented water, and having worshipped it with water filtered through a cloth,
[one should offer oblations] with mango leaves, *aśvattha* leaves, mustard seeds, *dūrvā* grass, gems, medicinal herbs, *sahadevī*, *bilva* fruit, and *jātī* fruit.
Having filled it with betel nuts and other such items.
Having perfumed it with fragrant substances, one should place the Śiva-kalaśa, in the form of Amṛteśvara, upon a worshiped seat on a svastika in the northeast.
One should worship [the deity] along with the limbs using the root mantra and the fivefold [mantra].
In this very manner, having worshipped the water-pot—which is the embodiment of the glory of nectar—with the mantra, one should place it upon a lotus.
Then, one should place upon them the sword of knowledge, fashioned from thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass with the tips pointing northward.
Then follows the ritual of the union of the bhaga and the liṅga.
The heart of Bhaga is the Liṅga; the heart of the Liṅga is Bhaga. Salutation indeed to you, that Bhagaliṅga, Umā-Rudra.
One should touch [it] with this mantra.
One should perform the rites of invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (sannidhāpana), firm fixation (sannirodhana), and the transformation into nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa).
In this manner, one should display the mudrās.
The recitation of the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Regarding enjoyment, it is said: "In secret"; regarding liberation: "Whatever action we perform, whether good or evil."
O Śaṅkara, for me who stands upon the auspicious state, destroy [all obstacles] with "hūṃ haḥ."
Thus, according to the ritual procedure, one should cast a flower into the vase.

Then, the Guru, having taken the mantra-vase and having placed the weapon-vase (astra-kalaśa) into the hand of the disciple, should cause a stream [of water] to fall in the directions starting from the east.
O Indra, come hither! Stay! Be present! Be near! Be restrained! O Blessed One, salutations to you!
Reciting thus: "O Agni, O Yama, O Nairṛta, O Varuṇa, O Vāyu, O Kubera, O Īśāna, O Brahmā, O Viṣṇu," one should cause the stream to fall.
Then the Guru, reciting the Bhairava mantra, should place the Śiva-pitcher upon a lotus; while reciting the Astra-mantra, he should place the water-vessel (vārdhānī) upon a svastika in the northeast.
There, in the northeast, having worshipped the weapon-vessel (astra-kalaśa) with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should perform the special worship upon the Śiva-vessel (śivakumbha).

Aghora with his limbs and faces; Aghorīśvarī with her limbs; Niṣkala with his limbs; Mṛtyuñjaya with his consort and limbs; the Bhairava-enclosure; the seven enclosures beginning with Vidyā; the eight Mothers beginning with Brahmyā; the eight forms beginning with Kṣiti; the eight names beginning with Bhava; Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Kumāra, Viṣṇu, Durgā, Kulavāgīśvarī, Mahātripurasundarī, Kubjikā, and Śārikā.

One should worship the mantras of Śāradā, the illustrious Mahārājñī, Jvālāmukhī, Siddhalakṣmī, and others, along with their limbs and six ancillaries, at the appropriate times according to one's capacity.
With the visualization "in the left [hand] a shield," one should meditate upon the deity residing in the flask, together with his limbs and retinue.
Oṃ, homage to the path of mantra. Homage to the path of word. Homage to the path of phoneme. Homage to the path of world. Homage to the path of principle.
Salutation to the path of Kalā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kalā of Nivṛtti.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of the kalā of cessation (nivṛtti).

Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the power of establishment (pratiṣṭhā-kalā). Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the power of establishment. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the power of knowledge (vidyā-kalā). Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the power of knowledge. Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the power of peace (śāntā-kalā). Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of the power of peace. Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to that which transcends peace (śāntyatītā). Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the lord of the power that transcends peace.
Salutation to Sadāśiva.
Having thus fully worshipped the Śiva-vessel, one should also worship the weapon-vessel (astravārdhānī).
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! To the weapon of infinite power, phaṭ! Oṃ! Salutations to you who possess the forms of Rudra; to the Pāśupata weapon, which is impenetrable, phaṭ!
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, for the weapon, phaṭ! Oṃ phaṭ, for the weapon, phaṭ!
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, to the weapon of wisdom, haḥ phaṭ. Thus.
To the Brahmāstra; to the Brahmaśirastra; to the Agnyāstra; to the Lokapālāstra; to the Pāśupatāstra; to the Aghorāstra.
To the divine weapon.
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, for all weapons, haḥ phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to the sword; to the shield; to the noose; to the goad; to the arrow.
To the Pināka-bearer; to the Excellent One; to the Fearless One; to the Shaven-headed One; to the Khaṭvāṅga-holder; to the Lute-player; to the Hand-drum-player; to the Bell-bearer.
To the trident; to the vajra; to the staff; to the battle-axe; to the mallet.
And one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors, such as the vajra and others.

Then follows the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). Having meditated upon the Power (*śakti*) arising from the center of one’s own *kanda* and reaching as far as the *dvādaśānta* in the form of a flame, it exits through the right nostril and enters the left nostril of the deity. Having reached the heart, it proceeds from the heart through the throat, the palate, and the space between the eyebrows in sequence to the *dvādaśānta*, where it takes up the nectar (*amṛta*). Then, exiting through the right [nostril] of the deity—
In this very manner, O Goddess, having entered and emerged from the guardians of the world who are Bhairavas, she should enter the heart by way of the left.
Thus ends the junction of the channels.
Furthermore, the reconnection of the mantras.

One should contemplate oneself as merged into Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu into Brahmā; Brahmā into Īśāna; him into Kubera; him into Vāyu; him into Varuṇa; him into Nairṛta; him into Yama; him into Indra; him into the host of Vidyās; him into Somarāja; him into Meghanāda; him into Manmatha; him into Vikarāla; him into Krodharāja; him into Śikhivāhana; him into Kapāleśa; him into Astra; and him into Netra.
One should contemplate that [syllable] in the armor, that in the crest-lock, that on the head, that in the heart, that in the Goddess, and that dissolved in the Supreme Lord;
this is the "unification of the mantras" (mantra-sandhāna).
Now follows the process of supreme perfection.

Having uttered the root mantra from one's own heart, one should place [the phonemes] in sequence at the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā— namely, the letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, the *bindu*, the half-moon, the *nirodhinī*, the *nāda*, the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*), *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, *samanā*, and ending with *unmanā*. Having experienced rest at the "end of twelve" (*dvādaśānta*),
one should again enter one's own heart by the order of descent and contemplate the Lord together with his retinue and his Goddess.
Thus is the process of supreme transformation.

Then, having performed the special worship (viśeṣapūjā) at the mantra-vase, and having performed the worship of the weapon-vase with the weapon-mantras, one should recite the root-mantra one hundred and eight times: "Come, be present; protect the sacrifice; fulfill all deficiencies. O Supreme Lord, you are the soul of the universe and the power of the universe; remove all evil."
Having thus received the command, one should perform the worship in the jar-maṇḍala.
The worship of Gaṇeśa on one's left.
Worship of Sūrya in the southeast; worship of Kumāra in the center.
And one should worship Śrī, Sarasvatī, and Viśvakarman.
Oṃ lūṃ, homage to Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand. Rūṃ, homage to Agni, who holds a śakti in his hand. Ṭūṃ, homage to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand.

KṢŪṂ, salutation to Nairṛta, who holds a sword in his hand. VŪṂ, salutation to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand. YŪṂ, salutation to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand. KUṂ, salutation to Kubera, who holds a mace in his hand. SŪṂ, salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand. ĀṂ VRĀṂ BRAṂ, salutation to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand. HLĀṂ, salutation to Ananta, who holds a discus in his hand. OṂ RŪṂ, salutation to Agni. OṂ HRĀṂ HRĪṂ SAḤ.
Salutation to Sūrya. In the center.
Oṃ vūṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ srūṃ, homage to Candra. In the east.

p. 13) Oṃ *kuṃ* to Kuṃkumāra, obeisance! Oṃ *rhūṃ* to Aṅgāraka, obeisance! In the southeast (*āgneya*). Oṃ *hlāṃ* to Viṣṇu, obeisance! Oṃ *shrūṃ* to Budha, obeisance! In the south (*dakṣiṇa*). Oṃ *lūṃ* to Indra, obeisance! Oṃ *rsrūṃ* to Jīva, obeisance! In the west (*paścima*). Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ.

To Vāgvādinī Sarasvatī, salutation! Oṃ Hrīṃ, to Bhārgava, salutation! In the north: Oṃ Āṃ Brāṃ Braṃ, to Brahmā, salutation! Oṃ Kṣmryūṃ, to Śanaiścara, salutation! In the southwest (nairṛta): Oṃ Gūṃ Gāṃ, to Gaṇapati, salutation! Oṃ Yūṃ, to Rāhu, salutation! In the northwest (vāyu): Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lord Rudra! Oṃ Hrīṃ, to Ketu, salutation! In the northeast (īśāna): Oṃ Hlāṃ, to Brahmā, salutation! Oṃ Hrīṃ...

Salutation to Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda. Outside the sacrificial ground, to the north: *Oṃ hlāṃ, salutation to Ananta*; *Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Agastya*. To the south. Then, in the center, is the enclosure of Bhairava (*bhairavāvaraṇa*). First, having worshipped Amṛteśvara, Amṛtalakṣmī, and the Niṣkala [form] in the upper pitcher, and having worshipped Bhairava together with his Goddess in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one worships the enclosure of Bhairava in order starting from the east.
Oṃ kṣamaraya-ūṃ, obeisance to Kapāleśa Bhairava in the east. Oṃ hara-ūṃ, obeisance to Śikhivāhana Bhairava in the southeast.

Oṃ kṣūṃ, obeisance to Krodharāja Bhairava—[in the] south. Oṃ jhrūṃ, obeisance to Vikarāla Bhairava—[in the] southwest. Oṃ hvūṃ, obeisance to Manmatha Bhairava—[in the] west. Oṃ haraya-ūṃ, obeisance to Meghanāda Bhairava—[in the] northwest. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Somarāja Bhairava—[in the] north. Oṃ hrkṣmlvyūṃ, obeisance to Vidyārāja Bhairava—[in the] northeast.
Now, the worship of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the goddess’s son Vaṭukanātha. [In the] south.

To Vaṭuka-Bali in the north; to the Yoginīs in the west; to the Guardian of the Site (Sthānakṣetrapāla) in the east; to the Bali for the Bhūtas in the center; to Rājarājeśvara in the northeast; to Viṣvaksena in the southeast; to Vetāla-Bhairava in the southwest; to Bahukhātaka in the northwest; and to Maṅgalarājānaka in the [northwest].
To Ānanda Rājānaka, to Saṅkhābhidhatta Taruṣka Rājānaka, to Pañcāla Rājānaka, and to Rudragaṇeśvara.
Now, [the section on] Heruka and the others.
Hrāṃ kṣaṃ kṣūṃ, homage to Heruka! [In] the east.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ lāṃ kṣeṃ, salutations to Tripurāntaka; in the southeast (āgneya). Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ kṣīṃ, salutations to Agnivetāla; in the south (dakṣiṇa). Hūṃ, salutations to Agnijihva; in the southwest (nairṛta). Oṃ hrīṃ kṣūṃ hūṃ, salutations to Kurpara; in the west (paścima). [Salutations] to Kāra; in the northwest (vāyu). Oṃ kṣāṃ yūṃ kṣīṃ, salutations to Vikarāla; in the north (uttara).
Āṃ yūṃ kṣmīṃ, obeisance to Ekapāda in the northeast; kṣrūṃ yūṃ kṣāṃ, obeisance to Bhīmarūpa in the center; obeisance to Ḍāmara above; obeisance to Hāṭakeśvara below.
Then, having offered the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the food offering (naivedya).
Oṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ, O you who have the form of substance, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! Thus.
Having offered clarified butter, milk, sugar-cane juice, honey, and likewise grapes— as the *pañcamṛta* food offering—
one should address the Lord.
Then, having performed a salutation and honored the disciple, one should have him sit on one's own right side. One should cause him to perform worship as follows:
"Oṃ, salutations to the light of one's own self. "We bow to the Lord of the universe, the Great Consciousness. Thus is the face-bath.
p.
14) Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, I offer this sacred thread; obeisance. Thus is the mantra for the sacred thread. With benedictions, the tilaka and flower should be given.
I bind this bracelet upon you—you whose mind is fixed on the worship of Bhava—so that you may attain the unshakable, eternal state that is free from worldly existence.
May Lord Śiva protect the inhaled and exhaled breaths, the eyes, ears, nose, mind, head, and hands—though these are natural—to you who drink [the nectar].
May the Blessed One, the remover of evil, take away your misfortune.

May all the hosts of spirits be for peace; may Nārāyaṇa protect my heart with effort. To my own self, whose nature is Śiva, [I offer] water for sipping, perfume—obeisance! Water for the guest-offering—obeisance! Flowers—obeisance!
For the sake of turning back from the great delusion of the desert wilderness of saṃsāra, let this nectar-like eye, this lamp of Śiva, be accepted.
O Śiva, may this incense, which has the form of Kālāgnirudra, which destroys all sins, and which generates all prosperity, be accepted.
He has two arms and one face, is serene, and holds a lotus in his hand.

One should meditate upon the solar disc situated in the center of the fiery orb, circular and clothed in red garments, resembling the sun itself, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
For the purpose of pleasing one's own chosen deity, through this formal dedication (*saṅkalpa*) of incense and lamp, may there be success: *dhūpo namaḥ*, *dīpaṃ namaḥ*.
Salutation to Gāyatrī.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. (Recite three times.)
We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon the one with the elephant’s trunk; may that Dantī inspire us. 3. We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon the knowledge of the Sun;
may that Sūrya inspire us. 3. We know Kārttikeya, the six-faced one; may that Kumāra inspire us. 3.
To that Great Lord, whose speech is purified, [I offer] obeisance; may Śiva grant us [his grace]. (3) To Amṛteśa, whose body is the void, [I offer] obeisance; may Netra grant us [his grace]. (3)
We know the one of many forms; may that terrible one [grant] us [peace]. 3. We know the one of many forms; may Aghoreśvarī [grant] us Rudra [peace]. 3.
To the Supreme Swan, to the Great Swan—may that Swan protect us; three times. We know that Puruṣa, the Great God—may that Rudra protect us; three times.
All this is of the nature of Śiva, proceeding from Śiva alone; may Śiva, who contains Śiva within himself, impel everything toward Śiva. 3.
To Vāsudeva, whose crest is the *lakṣa*, may Viṣṇu grant that to us—3 times. To Subhagā, who wears a garland of desire, may Durgā grant that to us—3 times.
Aiṃ, to the Goddess Tripurā; Klīṃ, to Kāmeśvarī; may that Klīnnā inspire us. (3) To Tatpuruṣa, the Great God; may Nandin inspire us.
(3) To Mahāsena, whose face is fire; may Skanda inspire us. (3) To the one with sharp horns, whose feet are the Vedas; may the Bull inspire us. (3)

To Nārāyaṇa, to Vāsudeva; may Viṣṇu protect us—3. To Mahāmbikā, to the perfection of action; may Lakṣmī protect us—3. To her born from the lotus, to the consort of Viṣṇu; may Dhara protect us—3. To her born from the lotus, to the one whose mouth is the Vedas; may the Creator protect us—3. To Vainateya, to the one with golden wings; may Garuḍa protect us—3. To the one born from the weapon of Śiva, to the one born from the mouth of Śiva; may Speech protect us—3.

Today, on this [specified] lunar day, [I perform the worship] of Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Viśvakarman, the deities of the doorways, Prajāpati Brahmā, and the deities of the water-pots (kalaśa)— Brahmā, Viṣṇu... [page 15]

To the deities of Maheśvara; to Cāturvedeśvara with his attendants; to Ṛtupati; to Nārāyaṇa; to Durgā; to Tryambaka; to Varuṇa; to Yajñapuruṣa; to the deities of the host of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa) beginning with Agniṣvātta; to Svacchandabhairava with his retinue; to the god Bhava; to the god Śarva; to the god Paśupati; to the god Ugra; to the god Bhīma; to Mahādeva accompanied by his Gaṇas; and to Īśvara and Pārvatī.
[Salutations] to Hara accompanied by his consort, to Nandin and Mahākāla together with their retinues, to Gaṅgā and Yamunā, to Meṣāsyā and Chāgalāsyā,

to Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, to the treasure of the conch (Śaṅkhanidhi), to the treasure of the lotus (Padmanidhi), to the great treasure (Mahāpadmanidhi), to the cause of all causes, to the deities of the ritual offerings for the creation, destruction, and animal-sacrifice, to the water of Śiva, and to the Gurus on the left— namely the Guru, the Paramaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru.

[Salutations] to the supreme preceptors and gurus, to one's own gurus, to the eleven planets beginning with Āditya, to Brahmā with his retinue, to Viṣṇu with his retinue, to the deities of the mantra-pitcher, to the deities of the weapon-pitcher, and to Vāsudeva. || 8 || Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ, [salutation] to Sūrya. || 6 || To Vināyaka. || 13 || To Amā (the New Moon), and so forth. To Indra, the lord of the gods, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand; to Agni, the lord of splendor, who holds a spear in his hand.
To Yama, lord of the *pretas*, who holds a staff in his hand; to Nairṛti, lord of the *rākṣasas*, who holds a sword in his hand; to Varuṇa, lord of the waters, who holds a noose in his hand;

to Dhvaja, lord of living beings, who holds a banner in his hand; to Kubera, lord of the *yakṣas*, who holds a mace in his hand; to Īśāna, lord of all, who holds a trident in his hand; and to Brahmā, lord of the Vedas, who holds a lotus in his hand.
Of Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the three worlds who holds the discus in his hand; of Agni and Āditya; of Varuṇa and Candramas; of Kumāra and Bhauma; of Viṣṇu and Budha;
of Indra and Bṛhaspati; of Sarasvatī and Śukra; of Prajāpati and Śanaiścara; and of Gaṇapati and Rāhu.

[The mantras] of Rudraketu, of Brahmadhruva, of Ananta and Agastya; of Kapāleśabhairava, of Śikhivāhanabhairava, of Krodharājabhairava, of Vikarālabhairava, of Manmathabhairava, of Meghanādabhairava, of Somarājabhairava, and of Vidyārājabhairava; [the mantra] of the illustrious Svacchandabhairava situated in the center of these; and of the deities of the seven enclosures (saptāvaraṇa), of the all-encompassing Lord (sakalabhaṭṭāraka), of Aghora, and of Aghoreśvarī.

Of Niṣkalabhairava; of Amṛteśvara, whose aim is nectar; of Ānandabhairava together with his Goddess; *KṢAṂ* for the face of Īśāna; *YAṂ* for the face of Tatpuruṣa; *RAṂ* for the face of Aghora; *VAṂ* for the face of Vāmadeva; *LAṂ* for the face of Sadyojāta; [the seed-syllables] of the six limbs;
[the mantras] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; and of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalavikaraṇī.
To Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī; to Brahmā, the lord of the Nivṛtti-kalā;
and to Viṣṇu, the lord of the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā.

To Rudra, the lord of the *vidyā* and *kalā* levels; to Īśvara, the lord of the *śāntā* level; to Sadāśiva, the lord of the *sāntyatītā* level; to Mahātripurasundarī and the other deities of the *praty-aṅgirā* class, including Siddhalakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, and the goddess Kubjikā; and to the paths of mantra, word, phoneme, world, principle (*tattva*), and energy (*kalā*).
[The mantras] of Mālinī Durgā with six arms, of Durgā with eight arms, of Durgā with eighteen arms,
of the Blessed Goddess Śārikā, and of the Blessed Goddess Śāradā.

To the illustrious Queen Śrījvālā Bhagavatī; to the illustrious Vīḍā Bhagavatī; to the illustrious Śivā Bhagavatī; to Vajreśvarī; to Kāmeśvarī; to Bhagamālinī; to Bhuvanamālinī; to Dīkṣādevī; to Pāpāntakāriṇī; to Mantramātṛkā; to Mantraḍāmarikā; to Bhadrakālī; to Tārā; to Pustakavāgīśvarī; and to Gaṅgā.

To the Blessed Lady; to the Blessed Lady Vitastā; to Agni together with his retinue; to Vaṭukanātha, the son of the Śrīdevī; to the Yoginīs who move through their stations; to Viśvaksena, the Lord of the Kings of Spirits (Bhūtarāja-rājeśvara); to the King of Vetālas; to Maṅgalyarājānaka of Bahukhātaka; to Rudrarājānaka; to Saṅkhābhidhattattaruṣkarājānaka; to Pañcālarājānaka; and to Heruka.
Of Tripurāntaka; of Agnivetāla; of Agnijihva; of the one named Kalā; of Kapālin; of Ekapāda; of Bhīmarūpin;

of the one named Tāraka; of Hāṭakeśvara; of Rājarājeśvara; of the field-protectors beginning with Aja, and of all the deities who are field-protectors; of Kūrma; of Dhruva; of Ananta; of Hari; and of the deities presiding over the dwelling-place (Vāstoṣpati).

For the sake of warding off the sins accumulated by myself through speech, mind, and body, and for the sake of pleasing my chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), I shall perform the worship of the vase (*kalaśapūjana*), the worship of the sacrifice (*yāgapūjana*), and the worship of the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapālapūjana*).
Oṃ, do so! Having scattered sesame, mustard seeds, and barley:
In the same way, so too is the posture.

"To Mahāgaṇapati, to Kumāra," and so forth—"I worship you all; Oṃ, worship! "Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra," and so forth—"I shall invoke you; Oṃ, invoke! "I invoke the Lord of the Gaṇas; may he, peaceful, come with his two arms holding a rosary and a ring."
The lion-throne is resplendent with an axe and a vessel; his pair of left hands is for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke the god Kṣetrapāla, the great lord.
He dwells within all embodied beings, from worms and insects to moths; he is the house, the field, the forest, the grove, the yakṣa, the bhūta, and the piśāca.
One should worship the Gaṇas, Gandharvas, Devas, and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). "May this offering, flowers, sacrificial porridge (caru), and incense be accepted."

I invoke the Lord who shines with serpents, whose garments are the quarters of space, who has three eyes and holds a trident in his hand; he of dark countenance, the remover of sins and suffering, the divine lord of the field, most wondrous, for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke the Lord, the Master, the husband of Pārvatī, who is mounted upon his bull-throne and adorned with serpent ornaments.
White in color, of great splendor, adorned with white garlands and radiant light—please accept this offering, these flowers, this sacrificial oblation, and this incense.
I invoke the god Viṣṇu, who possesses a universal form, who resembles the flax flower, who is clad in yellow garments, and who is the infallible Acyuta.
For those by whom Govinda is honored, no fear exists. [Bali]
I invoke the king of the gods, seated upon his elephant, holding the sharp thunderbolt, honored and as radiant as the moon.
And [he sees] the Destroyer, holding a trident together with his power (śakti), three-eyed and stainless in his left hand for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke Agni, who holds the Veda-mudrā and a rosary in his own right hand, and possesses the finest parrot.
Likewise, for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice, there is a fire together with its sacrificial pit, as well as a staff, the tri-kṣa, and the supreme three-eyed one.
I invoke Yama, who is supreme to the Lord, marked with a trident and vajra, seated upon the back of a buffalo, and possessing three eyes.
And holding a lute together with its neck, he has four arms on the left side for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke Nivṛtti, who is intent on the worship of the moon-crested Lord [Śiva], and who holds a goad and a sword in her right hands.
In his left [hand], he holds a shield together with a noose; he is seated upon a bull for the purpose of protecting me from the ass.
I invoke Varuṇa, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, who is intent on worship, and who holds a noose and a sword in his right hand.
On the left [is] him, equipped with a shield and a noose, seated upon a crocodile, for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke Vāyu, who holds a vessel of air, initiated by his own pair of hands, and devoted to the Supreme Lord.
In his left hand, he holds a water-pot together with a rosary, seated upon a trembling deer for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.

I invoke Dhanada, seated upon his human vehicle, holding in his own hand the Cintāmaṇi jewel as well as a rosary; accompanied by the lion-bannered [Kubera], bearing the moon and a book, O Lord, for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke the Lord who wears a crown of moon-crests, the Imperishable One, who carries a trident in his right hand.
Or likewise, he holds a mirror and a linga in his hands, and similarly on the left, a bull-vehicle, being three-eyed for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke him who is seated upon the lotus throne, bearing the gesture of the Vedas and the rosary of beads.
Carrying a staff and a water-pot, he was constantly bearing Brahmā, who is devoted to the Supreme Lord, for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I constantly invoke Viṣṇu, who holds a rosary and a fruit, situated on my own right side.

Or else, he should hold a trident joined with a skull in his right hand and a mallet in his left, seated upon the tortoise posture (kurmāsana) as another form of Śiva for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
Then one should perform the invocation of the planets in their proper sequence; indeed, all the planets, beginning with Āditya, are invoked by means of the hundred [verses].
I invoke the Lord of Day, who bears the sacred thread upon his right eye, as well as the smoke-colored foot and the banner.
With his two hands he holds the seven-horsed chariot and a mass of rays; he has three eyes and is the refuge for those with three eyes, for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke Śaśin, who holds a rosary in his right hand and bears a banner with a smoke-colored emblem.
With his pair of hands fixed upon a deer, he is a mass of rays with three eyes, the refuge of the Three-eyed Lord for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke the son of the Earth, who bears the sacred thread and bracelets made of lotus stalks, and who is seated upon his peacock vehicle.
Holding a discus in his left hand, possessing a red complexion, three-eyed, and the refuge for those with three eyes, he exists for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke the white-complexioned Mother, adorned with a crown and necklaces, holding a rosary and bracelets in her right hands, and seated upon Garuḍa.
Holding a water-pot in his left hand, white in color and beautiful, with three eyes, he is the refuge for those with three eyes and exists for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke the preceptor of the gods himself, who holds the thread and ring of the sacrificial cord, and who is seated upon the elephant-vehicle.
Holding a discus in his left hand, possessing a yellow complexion, three-eyed, and the refuge for those with three eyes, he exists for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke the fierce Lord Kavi, who possesses the form of Īśvara, who holds a thread and a rosary in his hands, and who is seated upon the monkey-vehicle.
Holding a water-pot in his left hand, white in color, possessing three eyes, he is the refuge for those with three eyes, for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke Śani, who has the fierce form of Antaka, who holds a rosary and a bracelet in his right hand, and who is seated upon a human vehicle.
Likewise, he holds a water-pot in his left hand; he is the three-eyed refuge for those with three eyes, for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke Rāhu, who wears earrings and a garland, whose head alone remains, and who has taken away his own sacrificial portion (svadhā).
Seated upon his lion-throne, with a most formidable face, three-eyed and the refuge for those with three eyes, he exists for the sake of protecting the sacrifice.
I invoke him who is accompanied by ten serpents, with Dakṣa and Ikṣa joined to him, and with a water-pot in his left hand.
To him whose banner has a very long body black with a mass of darkness, who is three-eyed, the refuge of the three-eyed one, and distressed by the protection of the sacrifice;
I invoke the Lord who is of the nature of Brahman, whose feet are ever uplifted, who is eternal, whose body is the wings [of the bird-form], whose limbs are red, and who is immovable.
I invoke the god Agastya, who is served by the gods, the Lord who eternally assumes the form of Viṣṇu and bears a formidable form.
I invoke the Lord who wears a crescent moon as his crest-jewel; may he, the glorious bearer of the skull, accept this garland of skulls.
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice, [I take refuge] in the five-faced, three-eyed, and beautiful ten-armed one, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
I invoke that Bhairava whose vehicle is the peacock, who possesses a crimson radiance and wears a garland of charming young skulls; he who has five faces and three eyes.
I invoke that stainless King of Wrath, who resembles a fresh cloud and is adorned with a garland of skulls, together with his radiant splendors.
The five-faced one.
I invoke the formidable form of the Lord, radiant as fire, adorned with a garland of lovely severed heads, possessing five faces.
I invoke the Blessed One, the form of the Lord, that Manmatha who wears a garland of charming young skulls, the five-faced one.
I invoke that stainless Meghanāda, who possesses the luster of a smoke-colored body, who wears a garland of skulls, and who has five faces.
I invoke him who resembles the moon held in the hand, the stainless King Soma, adorned with a garland of skulls, and possessing five faces.
I invoke the King of Vidyās, who resembles a white jewel, whose head is adorned with a garland of skulls, and who has five faces.
I invoke Maheśa, whose arms are as bright as Vasu and the moon, who is independent and whose supreme self-form is as pure as a flawless gem.
Rudrāsana, three-eyed, with a mass of matted hair adorned by the crescent moon, five-faced, the supreme cause, and immeasurable.
While Bhairavī remained in wonder for a moment at the thought that the god had three and five eyes.
We praise Svacchandabhairava, whose singular form is the universe, whose self is the universe, who is the cause of the creation and other processes of the universe, and whose body is supreme light.
Transcending the universe yet consisting of the universe, joined with the eight Bhairavas, it is self-peaceful, partless, pure, all-pervasive, and stainless.
I worship that splendor which is consciousness, the knower, and a dense abyss of bliss, the refuge of all; salutations indeed to that Aghora, whose nature is more terrible than the most terrible.
O Goddess Durgā, worshipped by the Asuras, I invoke you for the sake of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, dissolution, and grace.
Grant me an excellent woman for the accomplishment of dharma, kama, and artha; [grant me] the conch, discus, mace, sword, noose, goad, bow, and arrows.

[One should worship] in sequence the eight-armed Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune: "May this water for honor (arghya), this water for the feet (pādya), and this incense (dhūpa) be accepted."
I invoke Durgā, who holds the trident, the discus, the sword, and the arrows.
Bearing a bow, a conch, a shield, and the threatening gesture in her hands during the sacrifice, I invoke the goddess Pārvatī, the boon-granting Umā.
"Come, O Goddess, beloved wife of Hara, you of beautiful limbs, who increase prosperity; O Jagannāthā, O Mīnā, O delighter of the heart!"
O Pārvatī, granter of boons, gentle one, who are eternally dear to your devotees!
May this water for honor and this water for the feet, as well as this incense, be accepted. I invoke the Goddess Śārikā, the Supreme Sovereign.
In this enchanting sacrifice, I invoke the goddess Śāradā, the bestower of boons, who is the source of all accomplishments.
I invoke the goddess Rājñī, the bestower of sovereignty, who is worshipped eternally by Śāṇḍilī and resides on Śrīśaila, possessing six arms.
I invoke the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī, who dwells within the half-body of Bhūteśvara and is seated upon a lion-throne.
In this very great sacrifice, I invoke the Goddess Bhagavatī, who is accompanied by Kāmeśvara, though she is fearful within the ritual.
I invoke the Goddess Lakṣmī, the bestower of all prosperity, who holds a vessel of spirituous liquor in her hand, is adorned with necklaces and ornaments, and takes the form of a swan.
Seated upon a lotus, resting her chest against the lotus-navelled one, I invoke the goddess Bhadrakālī, the Great Sovereign.
I invoke the goddess Bhadraṅkarī, who possesses a splendor like a cloud during the sacrifice of mantras, the supreme Dakṣiṇā Kālikā.
She possesses the brilliance of a great cloud, is formidable, and is accompanied by Mahākāla.
The Lord has fifteen eyes, five faces, and a form that bears the half-moon as complete as the full moon.

Wearing the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, he holds in his left hands a fine bell, the gesture of protection, and a mallet; likewise, a noose, an arrow, a great staff, a khaṭvāṅga, a lute, and a ḍamaru drum.
He holds a sword, a supreme goad, a vajra-weapon, a severed head, and likewise a shield in his left hands; and with his right hands,
he holds an axe, a bow, and a trident, possessing a radiance that surpasses ten million suns.

Thus, I meditate upon the God of gods, seated upon the Rudra-throne in the center of a lotus, joined by the goddess Vāmā and Gayā, adorned with a necklace of great scorpions, and bestowing fearlessness.
I shall invoke these deities; Oṃ, invoke!
"May those beings depart," and so forth. *Oṃ* 12—exhalation (*recaka*); *Oṃ* 24—inhalation (*pūraka*); *Oṃ* 36—retention (*kumbhaka*). One should perform the upward exhalation very slowly.
Then, with the Astra mantra, [one should purify] the vessel for the water for the feet (pādya).

Having thus prepared the fragrant water according to the ritual with saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, tagara, and priyaṅgu, one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) in due order during the performance of the collective worship (*saṅkarārcana*) to Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and the others, saying: "Obeisance! (*namaḥ*).

One should discard the remainder of the water for the feet (*pādya*). Again: *phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*. Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, curd, rice grains, barley, and white mustard seeds—this is proclaimed as the eightfold *argha* offering.
"Obeisance to Soma"—with these words, [one offers] water from each respective vessel.

Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī, the Mistress of Speech, the Bestower of Speech; [offer] milk. Oṃ jrīṃ, obeisance to Sāvitrī, the Consumer of Sin; [offer] *darbha* grass. Aiṃ, obeisance to Rudra, who has three matted locks and a yellowish-brown upper garment; [offer] mustard seeds.
Oṃ tat sat, obeisance to the ancestors; [I offer] sesame seeds.

Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods; salutation to the one of great power—this is the flower offering. Yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ, salutation to all the most excellent essences; salutation to all substances.
O Blessed Ones, [accept] the water for honor (arghya) twice. [Salutations to] Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and the others.
This is the offering of water for washing the feet; homage!

To Mahāgaṇapati and Kumāra, and so forth; O Āditya, accept this anointing; fragrance, obeisance! To Mahāgaṇapati and Kumāra, and so forth; O Āditya, obeisance to the water-offering (argha); obeisance to the flower!
To these deities, salutation with incense; salutation with light.
Salutation to the garments of these deities.
May the entire ritual procedure for the worship of these deities, beginning with the offering of the *arghya*, be completely fulfilled.
Phaṭ! To the weapon, phaṭ!
To these deities, [I offer] the *apośāna*; obeisance! To the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), obeisance!
Now, let these deities be gratified by this sacrificial fee consisting of sesame, gold, silver, and a gold coin;
let them be pleased.
With water and sesame seeds poured over the left shoulder, O one of the Śiva lineage, may Śiva be pleased for the sake of the ancestors' attainment of the state of Śiva.
Having given canopies, bells, banners, parasols, chowries, mirrors, dance, song, and so forth, as well as jewel-lamps and the like.
Having placed a full vessel containing salt pills and other such items, one should make a formal petition.
As follows:
O you, O lords of the Gaṇas, now make this place free from obstacles!
I shall perform the worship of Hara for the sake of protection in this world and the next.
May all the Blessed Planets, and whatever others are considered secondary planets (upagrahas), all of them remain present for me to pacify obstacles.
O Indra, O you who possess the splendor of Indra! For the sake of pacifying obstacles in this direction, you must remain vigilant until the completion of the rite, by the command of Śiva.

"O Agni! O Yama! O Nairṛta! O Varuṇa! O Vāyu! O Kuvīra! O Īśāna! O Brahmā! O Ananta! Having thus proclaimed the command of Śiva to the world-protectors (lokapālas) and having offered the *nirodhārgha* water, he should proceed to the vicinity of the fire.
Homage be to all yogins, and salutations again and again to the perfected ones (siddhas). O Lord of the formed and the formless, O Grasper, homage to you who possess a multitude of powers.
Having performed half a circumambulation and having offered the *nirodhārghya* with the words "sannidadhvam," he should go near the fire.
Oṃ, homage to Svacchandabhairava!

Oṃ. Having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the purification of the seat. For this venerable mantra for purifying the seat (*āsana-śodhana-mantra*), Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chanda*), Kūrma is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the purification of the seat. Prīṃ! O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are held up by Viṣṇu.
And you, O Goddess, uphold me; make the seat pure.

Salutation to the Seat. Salutation to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti). Salutation to Kūrma. Salutation to Ananta. Having sat upon the seat, one performs the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra.
Salutation to the Sword of Knowledge, whose nature consists of the thirty-six principles.
Having thus performed the *upayāma* rite and worshipped the *astra-kalaśa* on one’s own right side,

and having performed the procedures of drying (*śoṣaṇa*), burning (*dahana*), and so forth through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the worship of the three vessels for the *argha* of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) according to the prescribed rule. With the mantra "I sprinkle with that, phaṭ," one should gaze upon the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) while reciting the root mantra (*mūla*).
