One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit with "Astrāya Phaṭ. One should strike the sacrificial pit with "Astrāya Phaṭ. One should sprinkle water upon the sacrificial pit with "Huṃ."
Thus ends the fourfold set of formative predispositions.
I perform digging, sweeping, removing the soft earth, pounding, purifying, and sprinkling—phaṭ!
"Thus, salutation to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), whose nature is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). This is the worship.
The vajrification by means of the mantra: *phaṭ*, I perform the vajrification, *phaṭ*.
For example:
(21) The lines are made adamantine with the weapon-mantra; there are three lines facing east and one facing south and north. This is proclaimed as the "thunderbolt" (vajra).
The covering of the pit is performed with *darbha* grass blades pointing eastward, accompanied by the recitation of the Astra-mantra.
Having drawn a circle, then a triangle above it, then a hexagon above that, and then a circle above that, whereon a seat is placed.
Salutation to Mukunda. Salutation to Īśāna. Salutation to Purandara. Salutation to Brahmā. Salutation to Svadhāsāgara.
Homage to Ratnadvīpa. Homage to Kalpavṛkṣa. Homage to Indu. Having thus worshipped and sprinkled [the image] with arghya water.
Upon that, one should worship the seats (pīṭhas).
Salutation to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti). Salutation to Kūrma. Salutation to Ananta. Salutation to the Earth. Salutation to the Ocean of Nectar (Sudhāsāgara).
Homage to Ratnadvīpa. Homage to the Kalpavṛkṣa. Homage to the Ratnavedikā. Homage to the Cintāmaṇigṛharāja.
Salutation to the Jewel Lion Throne. Salutation to the Root of Bliss. Salutation to the Stem of Consciousness. Salutation to the Lotus consisting of the Principles (tattva).

Salutation to the petals consisting of *prakṛti*. Salutation to the filaments consisting of *vikāra*. Salutation to the pericarp beginning with the fifty seed-syllables. [Salutation] to Dharma (four times). [Salutation] to Adharma (four times). Salutation to [Name] Devatā. Having thus worshipped:
Having prepared a seat of fifty-four *darbha* grass blades on the right side of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and having placed it in the center of a ball of cow dung, one should worship it.
Salutation to the seat of Brahmā. Having invoked him with "O Brahmā, come hither," [one says]: "Be present! Be present! O Lord, remain near! I veil you; salutation!"
Āṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of all worlds. One should worship him with water for the feet and other offerings.
Thereafter, having placed a single darbha grass blade facing east in the center of the pit with the Astra-mantra, one should fashion a crossroads.

With the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should contemplate the sacrificial pit as being made of vajra. This is the vajrīkaraṇa (the rite of making it adamantine). With the mantra "Namaḥ," one should draw a square within the pit using kuśa grass.
In the middle is the Āvamadhyabhāga fire; on the west is the Āhavanīyabhāga fire; on the north is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; and on the south is the Gārhaspatya fire.
Thus ends the making of the path fit for travel.
Behind that is the seat; there, one should visualize Vāgīśvarī.
One should worship Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and resembles the color of indigo mixed with the juice of a deity, joined in union with Vāgīśvara, by means of ritual offerings.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with beautiful eyes and a most excellent complexion, she was endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.

Having meditated upon the Goddess in this manner, one should install her in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa)— seated in the Brahma-position, auspiciously facing the entrance— while recollecting the visualization of the Goddess along with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Upon the seat.
Oṃ, homage to the seat of Vāgīśī. Having thus performed the worship of the seat.

Hāṃ, O Vāgīśvarī, come, come! [Perform] the invocation and other rites as previously described. "Oṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Having thus worshipped her with water for the feet and other offerings:
Having visualized the goddess as lying supine upon the head of Īśa and in her fertile season, one should display the *yoni-mudrā* for the sake of her presence.
One should seek to obtain fire by means of a vessel covered over another vessel, using either a sun-crystal or from the hearth of a Vedic scholar.
Having brought the blazing fire situated within the vessel.
Oṃ phaṭ! I perform the sprinkling of fire, phaṭ. Likewise: the gazing; the veiling.

Oṃ hūṃ, I veil the fire with hūṃ. The veiling is performed with the armor-mantra (kavaca). Oṃ raṃ, homage to Agni. Oṃ, homage to Agni, whose essence is the power of gnosis (jñānaśakti). Thus is the worship.
Oṃ phaṭ! I expel the flesh-eater, phaṭ!
Having thus ignited a blade of darbha grass, one should cast it toward the southwest.
May there be purification for Agni Kravyāda; Svāhā! Water with sesame seeds.

Then, having uttered the root mantra, take the fire-vessel with both hands, smell it at the tip of the nose, and by means of the root mantra, grasp the crest of the flame as the consciousness of the fire.
Having caused the fire to enter the heart through the left nostril by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), unify it with one's own conscious fire.
Then, exhaling through the right nostril while uttering the root mantra, cast the fire into the vessel.

Oṃ Raṃ, obeisance to Agni. Worship with the six limbs. Perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) with the root mantra. Firmly grasping the divine identity of Śiva, thinking "I am indeed Śiva," and meditating on the fire as being of the nature of semen (*śukra*), one should conceive of Māyā as Vāgīśvarī and say: "Obeisance, I cause the fire to revolve within the womb."
Having thus rotated three times, [one should say]: "Into that womb, Oṃ Hūṃ, I join; Namaḥ. One should cast it in the direction of Nairṛti.

Then, having gazed at the fire with the *mūla-mantra* and having sprinkled the fire with *arghya* water while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ," he should strike it with *darbha* grass while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ. Having sprinkled the fire with *arghya* water while reciting "Huṃ," he should worship within that fire as follows:
"Rāṃ, obeisance to Jaṭharāgni; Rīṃ, obeisance to Vaindhavāgni; Rūṃ, obeisance to Bhaumāgni. Thus, having performed the worship.

Having meditated upon the unity of the stomach-fire, the fire of the *bindu*, and the terrestrial fire, one should unite the consciousness of the purifier (fire) with the syllable *raṃ* within it; then, having consecrated the fire with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), made it nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā* with the syllable *vaṃ*, and sprinkled the fire with the weapon-mantra *astrāya phaṭ*.
Having veiled the fire with the syllable *Hūṃ* and worshipped it with the root mantra, one should take up the fire with both hands, lift it, and while touching the ground with the knees,

whirl it three times over the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Reciting the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*), one should cast the fire toward oneself into the womb of Vāgīśvarī with the thought "I am He" (*asmi aham*)— perceiving the fire as the life-force (*jīva*) of Paramaśiva.

Then, having worshipped with "Salutation to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara," one should contemplate the union of Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara, and join that consciousness into the embryonic channel (garbhanāḍī) of Kāmeśvarī.
Thus, having covered the womb with *kuśa* grass for the protection of the fetus: "I cover the womb of Vāgīśī; obeisance!"

Thus is the covering of the womb with *darbha* grass. "Oṃ Phaṭ! I fashion the enclosure (*akṣavāṭa*); obeisance!"—with these words, using eight *darbha* blades with their tips intact and pointing upwards, one forms the enclosure in the ten directions within the center of the *darbha*.

Then, having prepared a seat of *darbha* grass and having meditated with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) recited seven times upon the form of the bracelet residing in the right hand of Vāgīśī, one should offer it with: "Oṃ phaṭ!
I bind the bracelet of Vāgīśī; obeisance! One should then give [the mantra].
One should meditate on it in the form of a bracelet situated upon the right hand.
Oṃ rāṃ, salutation to Agnigarbhā. Thus is the worship.
Then, one should display the Jvālinī mudrā.
Having made the two wrists level, with the fingers of both hands pressed together.
Having joined the two middle fingers, one should insert the thumbs into their center.
Thereafter, one should kindle the fire with this Jvālinī mudrā.
Then, one should kindle the fire with the fire-mantra.
"Cit-piṅgala, slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! O Omniscient One, grant knowledge! Svāhā! Having thus kindled the fire, he should join his palms in reverence.
I bow to Agni, the kindled fire, the consumer of oblations, who is like pure gold, stainless, radiant, and whose faces are turned in every direction.
p.
23) One should establish [the fire]. Then, with sesame seeds: *oṃ juṃ agner garbhādhānaṃ karomi svāhā*. *Ā* three times.

Thus: *Oṃ juṃ, may the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) of Agni be accomplished, svāhā! Ā 3! Vyoṃ, O Agni, become a male, namaḥ!* With these words, one should sprinkle water with the tip of a *darbha* blade from the *vidhi-arghya*.

*Oṃ vyom agnaye puṃse namaḥ*—thus is the worship. *Oṃ vyom agneḥ puṃsavanaṃ saṃpadyatāṃ svāhā*. *Ā 3*. *Oṃ īm agne vibhaktāvayavo bhava namaḥ*. Having thus drawn the entire body of Agni with the tips of *darbha* grass.
Oṃ īṃ, homage to the one in the form of fire. Thus is the worship.
Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the visualization of the face of Agni; svāhā! Ā 3! May it be accomplished! 3!
Oṃ, Agni, I perform the visualization of the three eyes; svāhā. Ā 3. Saṃ 3.

Oṃ hūṃ saḥ īṃ! I make the face of Agni the Śivatattva; svāhā! Ā 3! Saṃ 3! Oṃ juṃ īṃ! I make the heart of Agni the Vidyātattva; svāhā! Ā 3! Saṃ 3! Oṃ oṃ īṃ! I fashion the feet of Agni as the Ātmatattva; svāhā! 3! Saṃ 3! Oṃ īṃ! I enliven the head, the chandases, the waist, the feet, and all the limbs of Agni; svāhā! 3! Saṃ 3! Oṃ īṃ! I perform the demarcation of the boundaries of Agni.
Svāhā 3 Saṃ 3. Oṃ Īṃ, I perform the parting of the hair and the opening of the eyes for Agni; Svāhā 3 Saṃ 3. Oṃ Phaṭ, I awaken the seed-syllable of Agni;
Svāhā 3. Oṃ Phaṭ, obeisance to Agni.
Thus is the worship.
"Oṃ phaṭ! Be facing toward the impulse of Agni; homage! Having thus made this request and formed the añjali gesture, one should contemplate that Agni has been generated from Vāgīśī.
Oṃ phaṭ, salutation to Agni, whose nature is the power of gnosis (jñānaśakti). Thus is the worship.
Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the birth-rite for Agni, svāhā. (3 times) Saṃ (3 times).
Oṃ phaṭ! To the weapon, phaṭ! May there be purification from the birth-impurity of the fire, svāhā! (Recite three times; perform the *saṃ* gesture three times.)
The purification of birth-impurity from the sacrificial pit is accomplished by means of a mantra.

Oṃ phaṭ! I perform the opening of the mouth of Agni, svāhā. (3 times) Saṃ. (3 times). Oṃ phaṭ! I perform the sprinkling over the mouth of Agni, svāhā. (3 times) Saṃ. (3 times). Oṃ phaṭ! To the weapon, phaṭ! I sweep around the fire. Thus I sprinkle around it; I sprinkle water all around. Then follows the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*): Phaṭ! I spread the fire, phaṭ! Three stalks of *darbha* grass in the east; five in the south; five in the north; three in the west.
Then, sacrificial fuel sticks one span long, accompanied by two blades of darbha grass and pointing northward, are placed in the east.

With tips pointing eastward on the south; with tips pointing eastward on the north; with tips pointing northward on the west—thus is the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Then, one should place four bundles of grass (*viṣṭara*) in the cardinal directions: "Salutation to Brahmā in the east," "Salutation to Rudra in the south," "Salutation to Viṣṇu in the west."
In the north, "Salutation to Sadāśiva. Then, upon the Jvālāliṅga, one should worship the Śāntikalaśa with the root mantra together with its ancillaries (sāṅga), as follows:

Therein, first, one should worship the All-pervading Lord (Vibhu) together with a seat made of seven darbha grasses, which is yellowish-brown, placed upon a water-pitcher adorned with garlands of flames and liṅgas.
He states his meditation as follows:
One should meditate upon the four-armed Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, who has a blue throat, possesses four faces, holds a trident in his hand, and has a rosary of beads placed in his other hand.
Mounted upon a bull, exceedingly fierce, and endowed with individual powers.
Upon his lap, one should meditate upon the Goddess, radiant as gold, holding a rosary and a water-pot, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and having the form of light.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Bhairava, who has the form of a flame and resides within the flaming liṅga. Thus is the worship of the peace-vase (śāntikalaśa).
p.

24) One should worship the peace-vase (śāntikalaśa) with the root mantra together with its ancillaries. Then, one should worship the ten world-protectors (lokapāla) in the ten directions. It is as follows:
The thousand-eyed Hari mounted upon Airāvata.
At the time of the fire offering (homa), one should visualize Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand and is joined by Śacī. Oṃ lūṃ, homage to Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand. [Direction: East.
One should contemplate him as having five faces and large eyes, always accompanied by Svāhā, mounted upon a parrot, holding a spear in his hand, and possessing nine tongues.
Oṃ rūṃ, homage to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand.
One should always meditate upon Yama, who is mounted upon a corpse, holds a staff in his hand, resembles a dark-blue cloud, possesses large teeth, and has a buffalo for his seat.
Oṃ ṭūṃ, homage to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand.
At the time of the fire-oblation (homa), one should meditate upon the goddess, the mighty-armed three-eyed lord of the world, Nirṛti, who is equipped with a sword in his hand.
Oṃ kṣūṃ, obeisance to the one in the southwest, who holds a sword in his hand. That pure seat of the sea-monster (makara), together with its goddess, is situated in the west.
One should always meditate on him with a noose in hand during the fire offering for the pacification of the multitude of obstacles: *Oṃ vūṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand.*

At the time of the fire oblation (homa), one should visualize the Wind-god as mounted upon a deer, endowed with speed, holding a banner in his hand, joined with a spear, and possessing the brilliance of fire.
Oṃ yūṃ, homage to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand.

For the pacification of obstacles, one should meditate upon Kubera—the three-eyed lord of sacrifices, master of treasures, bestower of all accomplishments, king of the Yakṣas, and wielder of the mace.
Oṃ kuṃ, homage to Kubera, who holds a mace in his hand.
Maheśāna, mounted upon his bull, as pure as clear crystal.
One should always meditate upon the three-eyed Lord, holding a trident in his hand, together with the Goddess.
Oṃ mūṃ, homage to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand.
Brahmā, mounted upon a lotus, four-faced, with a lotus in his hand.
Accompanied by the Gāyatrī, one should meditate upon the supreme treasure-house of the Vedas during the fire-oblation (homa).
Oṃ āṃ vrāṃ vraṃ, homage to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand and is adorned with four arms bearing a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
The wise one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, endowed with splendor and clad in yellow garments.
Oṃ hlāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, who holds a discus in his hand. Oṃ jyaṃ, I perform the emergence of Agni; svāhā! May it be accomplished! (Three times) Three times.
Oṃ jyauṃ, I perform the visualization of Agni as the Sun; svāhā, thrice. May it be accomplished, thrice.
O Agni, be an auspicious fire; salutation! Salutation to the auspicious fire! Thus is the worship.
I perform the naming ceremony for Agni as "Śivāgni," svāhā 3. Saṃ 3. I perform the loosening of the bracelet for Vāgīśī, svāhā ā 3.
Year 3.
Having removed the bracelet that bears the form of Vāgīśī, [one should say]: "Obeisance to Brahmā. [This is] the worship.
To Brahman, Svāhā! (Recite three times). O Brahman, may you forgive me. He should release the previous seat.
Oṃ, thus obeisance to Rudra. To Rudra, svāhā! (three times). May Rudra forgive [me]. One should release the southern seat-grass (viṣṭara).

Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. Oṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu, three times. May Viṣṇu forgive me. One should release the western seat. Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva. Oṃ, svāhā to Sadāśiva, three times. May Sadāśiva forgive me. One should release the northern seat.
Oṃ juṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. [Pūjā: Juṃ, svāhā to Vāgīśvarī, ten times. O Vāgīśvarī, may you be forgiven.
O Śivā, who are skillful in creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and who bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; O Vāgīśvarī, salutations to you! Go now, O Goddess, to the highest realm.
p.
25) Then follows the oblation of fuel-sticks (*idhma*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*) [in length], performed with the root mantra: "I satiate the Śiva-fire, svāhā! (24).
Oṃ. Now follows the consecration of the sacrificial ladle (sruc) and the dipping-spoon (sruva).

Oṃ phaṭ, I perform the sprinkling, phaṭ. [Perform] the veiling (avaguṇṭhana). Sprinkling with auspicious water (śivāmbhas). Likewise: heating (tāpana), whirling (bhrāmaṇa), and again sprinkling. Touching its tip with the tip [of the vessel]. Again, sprinkling, whirling, and heating. Touching its middle with the middle [of the vessel]. Again: "I heat thee, obeisance," "I whirl thee," "I sprinkle thee. Touching its base with the root-mantra (mūla). Then...

Placing the two hands face down with the palms touching at the navel: "To Śiva and Śakti, salutation for the anointing; salutation for the fragrant water (gandha); salutation for the offering (argha); salutation for the flower (puṣpa). Then, turning the hands upward: "Salutation to Śiva; salutation to Śakti."
Then follows the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya).

Having brought the vessel for the clarified butter (ājya), wash it with "Astrāya Phaṭ. Inspect the clarified butter with the root mantra (mūla). Sprinkle it with water while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ. Strike the ghee with kuśa grass blades while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ. Sprinkle it with the arghya water while reciting "Huṃ. Having performed these four purificatory rites (saṃskāra), place the vessel of clarified butter in the northwest corner (vāyu-koṇa). One should then place the vessel for the clarified butter with the mantra "Namaḥ."
This is the heating [hell].
Then, having ignited a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter, one should throw the burnt residue into the fire with the mantra "Namaḥ."
This is the rite of purification.
Then, while reciting the mantra "hum," one should wave the pair of ignited *darbha* blades over the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and cast it into the fire.
Thus is the illumination.
Then, taking a handful of ignited kuśa grass while reciting the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," [he should perform the rite].
Having displayed blades of darbha grass ignited in ghee, one should cast them into the fire.
Thus is the illumination.

Then, having grasped the *pavitra* separately with the thumbs and little fingers of both hands held palm-upward while reciting the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should perform the upward splashing (*utplavana*) of the clarified butter facing east and the downward splashing (*saṃplavana*) toward oneself; then, one should worship the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra together with its limbs (*sāṅga*). By that very act, the consecration as nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is performed; one should worship the clarified butter with the root mantra.
Thus ends the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya).
Laṃ, with the face of Sadyojāta, I unite with Raṃ, the face of Aghora; svāhā! || 3 ||
*Raṃ*, with the Aghora face, I unite with *yaṃ*, the Tatpuruṣa face; *svāhā*. || 3 || *Yaṃ*, with the Tatpuruṣa face, I unite with *kṣaṃ*, the Īśāna face;

*svāhā*. || 3 || *Oṃ hūṃ*, I perform the visualization of the three channels; *namaḥ*. With this, one should place two blades of *darbha* grass, pointing eastward, upon the sacrificial vessel (*ājipātra*). Therein, in the center—
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the power of will (icchā-śakti). Oṃ, obeisance to Suṣumṇā, whose abode is fire. [This is] on one's own left.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti. Oṃ saḥ, obeisance to Iḍā, the abode of Soma; [place this] on one's own right side.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Jñānaśakti. Oṃ juṃ, homage to Piṅgala, the abode of the sun. Now, for Agni:
Oṃ, I perform the conceptual division of the Śiva-fire into three parts; obeisance!
Thus, one should offer two fuel sticks, each a span in length, with their tips pointing upwards.
Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Sun, the refuge of Piṅgalā. Thus is the worship performed on one's own left [side] and the right side of the fire.

Oṃ juṃ, obeisance to Agni, who has his abode in Suṣumṇā; thus [offer] in the center. Oṃ saḥ, obeisance to Soma, who has his abode in Iḍā; thus [offer] on one's own right, to the left of Vahni. Oṃ juṃ saḥ, svāhā to Agni; thus [offer] from the right side of the clarified butter (ājya) into the right side of Vahni. With the root mantra, [offer] svāhā to Soma.
Thus, from the left side of the clarified butter, [it is offered] into the left side of the fire.
From the left side, [it is] on the left side of the fire.
Oṃ juṃ saḥ, svāhā to Agnīṣoma; [thus] from the middle portion of the clarified butter, [he offers] into the middle portion of the fire.
Thus [it is] in the bright fortnight.

*Oṃ juṃ saḥ agnaye svāhā.* Thus, from the right portion of the clarified butter (*ājya*), [he offers] into the right portion of the fire. *Oṃ juṃ saḥ sūryāya svāhā.* Thus, from the left portion of the clarified butter, [he offers] into the left portion of the fire. *Oṃ juṃ saḥ agni-sūryābhyāṃ svāhā.* Thus, from the middle portion of the clarified butter, [he offers] into the middle portion of the fire; this is for the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

Oṃ juṃ saḥ, I perform the consumption of the Śiva-fire; svāhā! || 3 || May it be accomplished! || 3 || Then, having bestowed the *tilaka*, flowers, and blessings upon the patron (*yajamāna*) together with his retinue, [the officiant says]: "I bind this bracelet for you, so that your mind may be fixed on the destruction of the fear of worldly existence."

Worship that which is skillful, stainless, and eternal for the sake of fearlessness. May Lord Śiva protect those breaths—prāṇa and apāna, sight, hearing, smell, mind, head, and hands—even though they are material—which you seek to swallow.
Oṃ! May the Blessed Śiva, the remover of sin, take away your inauspiciousness; may the hosts of all beings be for your peace through effort; may Nārāyaṇa protect your heart.
Thus ends the Kaṅkaṇa-mantra. Now follows the inspection of the clarified butter (ājya).

Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme remover of sin. Clarified butter is the nourishment of the celestial realms; in clarified butter all the worlds are established.
Whatever sin has come upon you from divine, atmospheric, terrestrial, and other sources—may all that go to destruction through contact with this clarified butter.

For the purpose of warding off the sins accumulated by my own speech, mind, and body, for the purpose of destroying all sins without exception, and for the purpose of pleasing my chosen deity, I offer this clarified butter (ājya) to the fire of Śiva; obeisance. Thus ends the visualization of the clarified butter.
He beheld the god Agni, consisting of flames and adorned in many ways, who made the sky itself appear as if adorned with fire, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
The god Hutāśana is white in color, with four arms, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, seated upon a parrot, and bearing a spear in his hand.
Clad in a deer-skin, he was the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer.
At the time of the fire sacrifice (homa), one should meditate upon [the deity] who has three eyes and five faces; having thus meditated upon the Blessed One, the bestower of all accomplishments.

One should meditate upon the Fire-god, fashioned in the form of a horse, possessing the luster of a mass of vermilion, his body-hair filled with flames, enchanting the world by his splendor, his neck adorned with ornaments shining with priceless jewels in the shape of horses, and covering the earth with gems emerging from his senses.

She holds the Śakti, the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles with her right hands, and the *tomara* and *tālavṛtta* fan with her left hands; she eternally bears the seven-tongued sacrificial fire, which is filled with clarified butter and possesses the color of molten gold.

Oṃ juṃ saḥ! May all the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) beginning with the initiation into Śiva-fire and extending from childhood onwards, including those ending with the vow of the student (brahmacarya), be fully accomplished—vauṣaṭ. Thus is the full oblation (pūrṇā).
Then, in his own right month, he should worship Viṣṇu; there, he should prepare a sacred thread (pavitra) provided with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds.
Accompanied by his own name and ending with "namas" through recitation, he is four-armed and adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.

I meditate upon the Lord Viṣṇu, the imperishable, who possesses the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, who is adorned with a forest garland, and who is both the manifest and the unmanifest deity.
We know the seat of Viṣṇu; we meditate upon the meditation on Viṣṇu; may that Viṣṇu inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ, I invoke Bhūḥ-puruṣa; obeisance! Oṃ Hūṃ, I invoke Bhuvaḥ-puruṣa; obeisance!
Oṃ hrīṃ svaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; obeisance! Oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; obeisance!
O Lord Viṣṇu, come, come! O Lord Viṣṇu, welcome! Be present, be present! Manifest your presence, manifest your presence! Haṃ haṃ haṃ! O Lord, accept this water for the feet; salutations!
Oṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ Viṣṇo, accept this water for sipping; svadhā! Oṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ Viṣṇo, accept this arghya offering; svadhā!
Thus, while anointing, say: "Accept [this]. Thus, for the unbroken grains and flowers: "Vauṣaṭ! Thus, for the five-fold worship: "Accept, accept! Vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu."
Thus concludes the worship of the cup-vessel.
Therefore, one should cause them to receive the command.
Whether the sacrifice has been commenced for the sake of the victim or for one's own sake by the practitioners, O Blessed One, may there be no flaw in our sacrifice through Your grace.
Now follows the consecration of the charu.
For the purpose of preparing the *caru* oblation, one should bring fire to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and perform the preparation of the *caru*.

Alternatively, if this [initiate] is intent upon initiation, this is the distinction: having prepared the fire for the purpose of the sacrificial pap (caru), he should place it there well-protected and veiled with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
If the sacrificial pap (caru) has been prepared using fire that is already established as worldly, then this is a purificatory rite (saṃskāra).

Then, having drawn a maṇḍala according to the prescribed rule on the ground to the left of oneself with cow-dung, and having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, [one should offer salutation] there: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti."
Having thus worshipped the seat (āsana-pakṣa), and having placed the sacrificial porridge (caru) upon it, one should worship the caru there with the root mantra together with its limbs (sāṅga).
Having rendered it nectar-like (amṛtīkṛtya) by means of the Amṛteśa-mudrā, and having kindled a blade of darbha grass, [one recites]: "Phaṭ! I perform the lustration (nīrājana); phaṭ!"

Having thus rotated [the vessel] three times over the *caru*, he should cast it into the fire. Having sprinkled it with the water of Śiva (*śivāmbhas*), he should ignite it in the center of the *darbha* grass mat with the *astra-mantra*.
Having placed it for a moment before him together with the mat, and having kindled it and adorned it with the water from the *argha* vessel, he should perform the [six] limbs (*aṅga*) three times.

Oṃ juṃ saḥ, "be heated by yourself," [recited] over the fire; "hā," [recited] over the sacrificial porridge (caru). Oṃ juṃ, "be satisfied," svā [hā], [recited] over the fire; "hā," [recited] over the sacrificial porridge.

Thus: *vyoṃ īṃ hūṃ juṃ phaṭ*. Having placed it over the fire, then, having spread darbha grass on the ground to the right of oneself with the mantra "To the seat, *namaḥ*," one should take down the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

The cooling sprinkling [is performed] through the pervasion of Soma; for the pacification of the *doṣas*, [it is done] with the root mantra together with the six limbs and the *jāti* ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
"Be cool for yourself, vauṣaṭ svāhā"—this [is used] for the sacrificial porridge; "hā"—this [is used] for the fire.
Thus, for the sacrificial porridge (caru): "juṃ, be well-cooled, vauṣaṭ svā. For the fire: "hā," three times.
Thus: Vyoṃ īṃ huṃ juṃ phaṭ. Again, worship with "Salutation to Somavatī."
"Oṃ syūṃ, obeisance to Soma, the maker of nourishment for the world. Then follows the *saṃpāta-homa*. Then, that *caru* [oblation] with the *astra-mantra*.
Oṃ phaṭ! I cover the sacrificial pap (caru); homage! Having thus covered it with *darbha* grass, [one recites]: Oṃ hūṃ! I protect the sacrificial pap; homage!
Thus one should offer the upper flower.
Then, one should visualize a nine-tongued flame above the fire-liṅga and worship it. As follows:
Oṃ, salutation to Prabhā. Oṃ, salutation to Dīpti. Oṃ, salutation to Prakāśa. Thus is the worship. [Salutations] to Marīci, Sthāpinī, Ruci, Karālī, and Līlihā.
Thus, one should contemplate and worship [the tongues] in the form of flames upon the Jvālāliṅga. Now, the worship of the nine tongues within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is as follows:
Salutation to Rājyārthadāyī in the east; salutation to Dāhajananyā in the southeast; Oṃ, salutation to Mṛtyudāyī in the south; Oṃ, salutation to Śatruhāriṇī in the southwest.

Oṃ, obeisance to Vaśīkartrī in the west; Oṃ, obeisance to Uccāṭinī in the northwest; obeisance to Arthadā in the north; Oṃ, obeisance to Muktidā in the northeast; Oṃ, obeisance to Sarvasiddhipradā in the center.
Having thus performed the worship, the fire-oblation (*homa*) concludes with *svāhā*. Then follows the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). [The mantra begins with] "O Lord of the Gate" (*dvāreśa*).
Oṃ juṃ saḥ, I fashion the tongues of the fire of Śiva; svāhā vauṣaṭ!
Now follows the second [verse]. || 3 ||
"May there be the presence of the tongues of Śiva’s fire; Svāhā! Vauṣaṭ! Then, one should contemplate the fire as having been rendered conscious, visualizing the tip of its flame.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god as red in color, wearing matted locks and clad in red garments.
I am seated upon the left lap; the god has two arms and three eyes, sits upon a parrot’s back, and is adorned with a flaming beard.

One should contemplate the god Agni in this manner during the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya): "Obeisance to Agni, who is mounted upon the syllable Śuk, accompanied by Svāhā, and holding a spear in his hand."
Thus ends the worship.
Then, having grasped the tip of the flame of the fire with the syllable *jum* and having meditated upon the consciousness of the fire;

"Oṃ juṃ, I grasp [the essence] at the tip of the flame of the Śiva-fire; salutation! Having thus grasped it with the curved index finger, having taken it in through the right nostril, and having united it with the consciousness residing in the heart by means of the internal fire (analena).
One should proceed in sequence from the heart, throat, palate, and the space between the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

Then, having milked the wish-fulfilling cow of the bodiless god (Anaṅga-dhenū) who has two udders, and having churned her milk, one should perceive that the sacrificial oblation (havis)—clarified butter (ghṛta)—has emerged.

Taking that clarified butter, one should again descend into the heart by the same sequence, perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to one's ability with the root mantra and its ancillaries (sāṅga), and offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). It is as follows: *Oṃ, with the mind as the ladle, [I offer] into the fire of my own self, which is kindled by the oblation of dharma and adharma.*
By way of the *suṣumṇā* path, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses; *svāhā*.
Thus, having united the fire of consciousness with the external fire, one should remember the form of Amṛteśvara within the tongue of that fire through the state of Śiva-nature;

and one should meditate upon that Lord of Gods within oneself, possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons, resembling a jasmine flower, the moon, cow’s milk, and the snowy mountain, the all-pervading Lord.
Resplendent with the luster of a white elephant and the moon, adorned with white ornaments, his limbs smeared with white sandalwood paste and greyed by camphor powder.
It is overflowing with the vast and thick waves of the nectar of the throbbing moon; it has one face and three eyes, and resides in the center of the lunar disc.
Seated upon a white lotus and established in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana).
One should meditate on [the deity] with four arms and wide eyes, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; likewise, one should contemplate a full moon in the left hand.
One should recollect him as being worshipped with entirely white offerings.
Thus, through this meditation, one should worship the God together with his consort and his retinue by means of the five mental offerings. It is as follows:

Having visualized the bulb (kanda) at the navel with its stalk reaching to the heart, and within the heart a white eight-petaled lotus whose petals are Dharma and the other [Bodhisattvas], and upon that a lion-throne and an Ananta-throne, one should worship the Blessed One situated above it.

Thus, having brought about the unification of the external fire, the fire of consciousness, and Śiva, and having also brought about their unification with one's own form, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) in the aperture of the head."
Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Sadāśiva on the forehead; salutation to the principle of Īśvara between the eyebrows; salutation to the principle of Vidyā on the palate.

Salutation to the principle of Māyā at the throat; salutation to the principle of Kāla at the heart; salutation to the principle of Niyati at the navel; salutation to the principle of Puruṣa at the genitals; salutation to the principle of Prakṛti at the feet.
(p. 29) Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the three principles (tritatva).

Oṃ saḥ, obeisance to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva); at the aperture of the crown. Oṃ juṃ, obeisance to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva); between the eyebrows. Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the principle of the self (ātmattattva); in the heart. Oṃ juṃ saḥ, obeisance to the form of Amṛteśvara; throughout the entire body.

Then one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). From the thumb to the little finger, one places the five limbs beginning with the heart; the weapon (*astra*) is placed on the fingernails. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands.

Oṃ juṃ, *namaḥ* to the heart, on the two thumbs; vyoṃ, *svāhā* to the head, on the two index fingers; īṃ, *vauṣaṭ* to the crest-lock, on the two middle fingers; huṃ, *huṃ* to the armor, on the two ring fingers; juṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to the eyes, on the two little fingers; phaṭ, *phaṭ* to the weapon, on the nails.
Having thus performed the *karanyāsa*, one should perform the *dehanyāsa*: "Thus the heart [mantra] in the heart," and so forth; the *astra* [mantra] on all the limbs.
Having thus performed the placement upon the body, one should again place the root mantra upon the entire body.
Oṃ, homage to the one of pure body; Oṃ, homage to the embodiment.
Having thus performed the placement of all the limbs upon the body, one should then form the lotus mudrā and perform the meditation as described.
"O God, [worship] the *svadhā*-vessel," he says.

Having meditated upon his own form as being of the nature of Śiva through the aforementioned meditation, he should then perform the worship of the *argha* vessel with the root mantra and its limbs to the left of himself for the sake of the external sacrifice; he should fashion it as having eight parts, five parts, or three parts, conceived as being situated upon the Ocean of Milk.

Having bound the Amṛtamudrā and sprinkled all the ritual offerings as well as oneself with those drops of water, one should perform a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with seven applications of the root mantra upon an upward line on the forehead, [visualizing] oneself as the very nature of Śiva. One should then perform self-worship (*ātmapūjā*) with the root mantra and its limbs.

Then, outside [the maṇḍala], in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), following the middle tongue of the Śiva-fire, one should visualize the bulb (*kanda*) at the navel, the stalk (*nāla*) extending to the heart, and at the heart, a white eight-petalled lotus; [one should then visualize] the qualities such as Dharma as the feet, the lion-throne and the seat of Ananta, and the form of the Fire-god (*agnimūrti*).
"Oṃ juṃ, I invoke Agni, whose nature is Śiva; obeisance.

Having thus drawn forth the flame previously established [within] from the heart by means of exhalation through the right nostril, one should cast it onto the seat visualized within the external fire.
In this very way, there is a state of unification between the fire of Śiva, the fire of consciousness, and the supreme Lord’s own forms.
Then, having recollected the form of Amṛteśvara through the state of Śiva-nature within the central tongue of the fire situated in the external *kuṇḍa*, and [having recollected] him as well—
One should meditate upon the Lord of Gods within oneself, possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons; having thus recalled the meditation.
Taking a flower in his joined palms (añjali), he should perform the invocation of the deity.
Oṃ, O Blessed One, come, come! Namaḥ—thus is the invocation. O Blessed One, stay, stay! Svāhā—thus is the installation. O Blessed One, be present, be present!
O Blessed One, be firmly established! Huṃ Phaṭ! O Blessed One, be present! O Blessed One, be seated here! Oṃ Hūṃ, O Blessed One, I perform the veiling; Namaḥ!
Thus, having veiled [it]; "O Blessed One, I make [this] nectar; salutation! Thus, having made [it] nectar.
Then: "O Blessed One, accept the water for the feet from this vessel of mantra-offering; homage! O Blessed One, accept the water for rinsing the mouth; homage!"

Thus, "Accept the five-fold service offering, accept, vauṣaṭ! Then one should worship with the root mantra together with its limbs and the goddesses. [The sequence is: the worship of the door; the worship of the Guru; the seat consisting of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and so forth; Aghora with his faces and limbs; Aghorīśvarī with her faces and limbs; the partless (niṣkala) form with its limbs; the Bhairava enclosure; the weapon (astra) enclosure; the seven enclosures beginning with the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa); and the eight Mothers beginning with Brahmyā.
The eight [names] beginning with Bhava.

Having worshipped Heruka and the others, Vaṭuka and the others, the Lords of the Field (kṣetrapālas), and the sixfold path beginning with Mantra, one then performs the worship of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) previously placed there with:
"Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the vessel that cooks the six flavors. Then: "Oṃ svyūṃ saḥ saḥ."

Vauṣaṭ! To the one whose abode is the moon of the state of ten million moons, whose splendor is the splendor of the moon, and who is the source of the flow of the nectar of immortality. Worship with the root mantra together with its ancillaries (sāṅga).

Oṃ juṃ saḥ, I transform the sacrificial porridge (caru) into nectar; *namaḥ*. Thus is the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the nectar-mudrā (*amṛtamudrā*). Then follows the oblation of the remainder (*saṃpāta-homa*): Oṃ, I perform the *saṃpāta*;
*śvā* into the fire, *hā* into the porridge. (31)

In this manner, one should perform the *sampāta* (pouring together) of all substances used for the oblation, such as fuel sticks (*samidh*), parched grain (*yava*), sesame seeds (*tila*), and so forth, by means of three oblations (*āhuti*).

Then, having taken a small portion of the sacrificial food (*caru*)— consisting of fish, meat, cakes, and so forth— from the jars in the sacrificial mandala, or from the *kṣetrapālas*, or from the fire, or from near the fire for the *lokapālas*, one should present it as an offering (*naivedya*) preceded by the ringing of a bell.

Oṃ, I unite the face of Bhairava with the faces of the fires of Śiva; svāhā! With clarified butter (ājya); ā 3. Oṃ, I unite the tongue of the face of Bhairava with the tongues of the faces of the fires of Śiva; svāhā! 3.
Then, having recited the root mantra, [the deity] emerges from the heart through the left nostril by means of the visualization of fire, enters the right side of the Lord of the Altar (sthaṇḍileśa),
and likewise performs the entry and exit for the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas).
"Enter by the right [channel] of the fire"—this is the conjunction of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). Thus ends the means for accomplishing the fire (*agni-sādhana*).
Then, for the purpose of turning [the deity] toward bestowing grace, there is the oblation of fuel-sticks.
Oṃ, I satisfy Amṛteśvara Bhairava, svāhā. [Recite] 108 times; or 54 times; or 27 times; or 14 times.
The tenth part of the [principal] limbs belongs to the goddess. Half of that which belongs to Bhairava belongs to Vāgaṇīśa and all the others; for each of them, it is one [unit].

Now, if the sacrificer is afflicted by disease or other ailments, then, with *akṣīrāku* fuel-sticks, or with white flowers— or in their absence, with white rice— and with powdered sandalwood, one should worship Amṛteśvara for the pacification of disease according to this procedure using the protection mantra (*ārakṣāmantra*).

OṂ JUṂ SAḤ AMṚTEŚVARA BHAIRAVA, protect [Name] from all diseases! SAḤ JUṂ OṂ NAMAS SVĀHĀ. Recite 108, 54, 27, 14, or 7 times. This is one-tenth of the recitation for the limbs (*aṅga*). OṂ JUṂ SAḤ AMṚTA LAKṢYA [Name], protect [Name] from mental anguish, physical illness, and fear! SAḤ JUṂ OṂ NAMAS SVĀHĀ. Recite 54, 27, 14, or 7 times.
Oṃ juṃ, protect the heart of [Name], protect it twice; homage to the heart, svāhā! Vyoṃ, protect the head of [Name], protect it twice; svāhā to the head, svāhā!

Īṃ! Protect the crest-lock of [Name]! To the crest-lock, Vauṣaṭ Svāhā! Hūṃ! Protect the armor of [Name]! To the armor, Hūṃ Svāhā! Jyauṃ! Protect the eyes of [Name]! To the eyes, Vaṣaṭ Svāhā! Phaṭ! Protect all the limbs of [Name]! To the weapon, Phaṭ Svāhā! As it is stated in the *Amṛteśavidhāna*:

With a concentrated mind, one should perform a fire sacrifice using fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa) smeared with milk; for whomever one performs it by name, for that person there will certainly be peace. Thus ends the pacification of poison (juraśānti). Then, with clarified butter (ājya):
*Oṃ juṃ saḥ, I satiate Amṛteśvara Bhairava, svāhā*. [Recite] 24, 27, 14, or 7 times. The representative formula for the limbs (aṅga) is *ā* once. Then...
The Full Oblation: Oṃ juṃ saḥ! May there be the fulfillment (or accomplishment) of the satisfaction of all the wheels of mantras; svāhā vauṣaṭ!
Now follows the second [section].
Oṃ juṃ saḥ, may there be nourishment for Bhairava; svāhā vauṣaṭ. Now, another [mantra]:
Now follows the oblation for the seven coverings.

Therein, first are the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras): Oṃ hrīṃ anantāya svāhā | Oṃ jhrūṃ sūkṣmāya svāhā | Oṃ sūṃ śivottamāya svāhā | Oṃ kṣūṃ ekanetrāya svāhā | Kṣyāṃ ekarudrāya svāhā | Ylūṃ trimūrtaye svāhā | Hjūṃ śrīkaṇṭhāya svāhā | Śrīṃ śikhaṇḍine svāhā | Thus.
Thus [end] the Vidyeśvaras.

[I worship Him] who carries in His various hands a *bījāpūra*, a mace, a bow, three tridents, a conch, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, His own tusk, and a jewel-pitcher.
Flower in the fire: of this Śrī Gaṇapati mantra.

The seer (ṛṣi) is Gaṇaka; the metre (chandas) is Nivṛttigāyatrī; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Mahāgaṇapati; the seed-syllable (bīja) is *gaṃ*; the power (śakti) is *hrīṃ*; the pin (kīlaka) is *kuru 2*; the application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). The ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with *gāṃ* and so forth. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glāṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvaṃ janaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā* (108 times). Then follows the full oblation (*pūrṇā*).
Red-bodied, with red pigment, holding an axe, a rosary, his own teeth, and a vessel of white sandalwood paste in his hands.
I bow to Gaṇeśvara, the elephant-faced remover of obstacles, who is mounted upon a lion-chariot; I bow to the inconceivable one with the face of an elephant and sharp tusks.
"O best of gods, [the one] with the color of lac and vermilion, saluted by the gods. "With vermilion and saffron... [This is] the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra.
Then the libation: "By this mantra-homa, may the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati, together with his limbs and his retinue, be pleased; may he be pleased."
Now follows the *vallabhā* [meter].

I worship the beloved of Gaṇanātha, who has two arms, whose lotus-face is smiling, who wears deep red garments, who is auspicious, and who holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting in her heart. (Offer a flower into the fire.)

Of this mantra of Śrī Gaṇapativallabhā: the seer (ṛṣi) is Gaṇaka; the meter (chandaḥ) is Nivṛttigāyatrī; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Gaṇapativallabhā; the seed-syllable (bīja) is *gaṃ*; the power (śakti) is *hrīṃ*; the pin (kīlaka) is *kuru 2*; the application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*). The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *gāṃ* and so forth.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glāṃ gaṃ, O beloved of Gaṇapati, bestower of boons, bring the hearts of all people under my control; svāhā. (Recite 108 times.)
Then follows the full oblation (*pūrṇā*): with the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full oblation. Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
By this mantra-homa, may the illustrious Gaṇapati-vallabhā, together with her weapons, her vehicle, her retinue, and her attendants, be pleased; may they be gratified.
Then [the oblation] for Sūrya.

I worship Him whose face shines like ten million suns at the end of an aeon, who is the color of a Sindūra-red flower or a Japā blossom, who wears a jeweled crown, has two eyes, and sits upon a white lotus; adorned with various ornaments, with a smiling face, clad in red garments, consisting of pure consciousness, and holding a golden lotus and a jewel-pitcher in His two arms.
Seated upon a white lotus, possessing the luster of a pomegranate flower, with shimmering, radiant, and great splendor, adorned by a circular halo.

One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having one face and two arms, wearing red garments, with white lotuses and stalks held in his two hands resting upon his shoulders and quivering; [one should offer] a flower into the fire.
The rites beginning with the invocation, as well as the water for washing the feet and so forth, [are taken] from the vessel of honorific water (arghapātra).
We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon the knowledge of Sūrya; may that Sūrya inspire us.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Sūrya, svāhā! Ā (ten times). Aṃ, obeisance to the heart, svāhā! Arka, svāhā to the head!
Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, vaṣaṭ to the flaming crest-lock; huṃ to the armor, hūṃ; bhāṃ to the eyes, vaṣaṭ; raḥ to the weapon, phaṭ svāhā. Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā).

May the Sun-god, who is seated in the lotus posture, who is affectionate toward those who have sought refuge, who possesses seven horses and seven reins, and who has two arms, protect us. [The offering] is completed with the root mantra; the libation for the rite of confinement is: "Be present here. Then, [one visualizes] the goddess Visphurā, who has three eyes and two arms, her hands shining as she grants boons and fearlessness.
I meditate upon her seated in the lotus posture, with a smiling face, radiant upon the lap of the Sun; [I offer] a flower into the fire.

Of this Śrīvisphurā mantra: Haṃsa is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (cchanda); Śrīvisphurā is the deity (devatā); Rāṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Oṃ is the power (śakti); Namaḥ is the pin (kīlaka) for the fire-oblation (homa).
The application (*viniyoga*) is as follows: *rāṃ*, and so forth. *Oṃ rāṃ visphurāyai namaḥ svāhā*, [recited] 108 times. The final offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) is performed with the root mantra.
Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa).
Then, [the ritual] for the prince.
[He saw] Kārttikeya, the best of gods, who has six faces and is marked by a cock; he holds a bell and a spear, is radiant, and likewise holds a rosary;
he has two eyes, is mounted upon a Cātaka bird, possesses the form of a child, and has the luster of the moon.
I remember in my heart Kumāra, the primordial bestower of desired boons, who is like the snowy Himālaya mountain, two-armed, encircled by serpents, seated upon the back of a peacock,
and the beloved son of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
The flower for the fire; the invocation and so forth; the water for the feet and so forth.
We know Kārttikeya; we meditate upon the Lord of Śini; may Kumāra inspire us. || 3 ||

Oṃ klūṃ kāṃ, salutations to Kumāra. || 108 || The ritual placement (nyāsa) begins with "kāṃ" and so forth. Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā): [He is] the beautiful king of peacocks, bearing a bell fashioned in his own color, a radiant banner, and a spear.

May the Youthful Kumāra, whose face is like his own teeth and who remains fixed in the age of childhood, grant you prosperity. [The vessel] is filled with the root mantra. This is the libation and the offering for the restraint.
Then [the mantra] of Mṛtyuñjaya.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Gods within oneself, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons, resembling pure pearl-jewels, and having a luster like a mountain of crystal.
The all-pervading Lord, resembling a jasmine flower, a conch shell, cow’s milk, and the snowy mountain, is adorned with white ornaments as beautiful as bright pearls and the moon.
His limbs were smeared with white sandalwood paste and greyed by the powder of camphor; he was bathed in the vast, surging waves of the nectar of the shimmering moon.
He has a single face with three eyes situated in the center of a moon-maṇḍala; he is seated upon a white lotus and stands in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana).
One should contemplate him as four-armed and large-eyed, with hands in the gestures of discourse (*vāda*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), and likewise, one should visualize a full moon in his left hand.
One should meditate upon Him, worshipped with entirely white offerings, having eyes like the moon, the sun, and fire, a smiling face, seated within two lotuses, His excellent hands holding the mudrā,
the noose, the svadhā gesture, the rosary, and the boon-granting pose, and possessing the luster of the moon.

One should meditate upon Paśupati, the conqueror of death, whose body is bathed by the nectar dripping from ten million moons, resplendent with ornaments such as necklaces, and who deludes the entire universe with his beauty.
The Lord of the Gods, whose hair is illuminated by the moon, holds a vessel of nectar in his lotus-hand, as well as a smile that is as stainless as ten million moons and a lotus.

I meditate upon that Śiva, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya), who has the sun, fire, and moon as his eyes, who holds in his ten hands the noose, rosary, and goad, and who is ever auspicious. [Offer] a flower into the fire.

Of this Śrī Mṛtyuñjaya mantra: Mahācamasakaloha is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas); Mṛtyuñjaya is the deity (devatā); *juṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *saḥ* is the power (śakti); *oṃ* is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
The rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth.
Oṃ, may we know the Lord of Nectar; may we meditate upon Him whose body is the void; may that Netra inspire us. || 3 || Oṃ juṃ saḥ haṃsaḥ, protect me, protect me!

So'haṃ saḥ juṃ oṃ. || 108 || Oṃ juṃ, salutation to the heart, svāhā! Oṃ vyoṃ, svāhā to the head! Oṃ īṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock! Oṃ huṃ, huṃ to the armor! Oṃ jyoṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two eyes! Oṃ phaṭ, phaṭ svāhā to the weapon! [The Full Oblation.]
The full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is offered with the root mantra, saying "Svadha to the God. This is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the water of cessation (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, Guhyakālī.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with beautiful locks of hair adorned by a digit of the moon, decorated with various ornaments, three-eyed,
and graced by a white lotus garland.
I meditate upon the Blessed Lady Uttarakālikā, who holds a spear and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who sits upon a corpse-seat, and who is adorned by Mṛtyuñjaya.
Regarding this mantra of Śrī Guhyakālī, the invocation and other rites are performed as in the case of Mṛtyuñjaya. Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ oṃ juṃ saḥ aiṃ klīṃ Guhyakālike hrīṃ svāhā. (108)
The full oblation with the root mantra. Now, for Amṛteśvara.
The primordial God, most beautiful, with the crescent moon upon his crest, possessing faces like the full moon, seated upon a lotus throne.
I take refuge in the three-eyed Lord Amṛteśvara, who is enriched by a vessel of nectar, a water-pot, a lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Of this mantra of Śrī Amṛteśvarabhairava: Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), Amṛteśvara is the deity (devatā), *juṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *saḥ* is the power (śakti), *oṃ* is the peg (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa). [The rites of] invocation and so forth [are performed].
Oṃ juṃ saḥ, obeisance to Amṛteśvara Bhairava. [I bow to] Amṛteśvarī, whose face is like the full moon and who wears a crown of the moon.
I worship her who has the form of that [Amṛteśvarī], the three-eyed one, seated upon the moon in Amṛta. Oṃ juṃ saḥ, obeisance to Amṛtalakṣmī.
Now, [the ritual] of Aghorabhairava.
"Behold the god with fifteen eyes"—thus, for a moment, there is meditation on Bhairavī; [then] a flower in the fire.
Of this mantra of the venerable Aghora-Bhaṭṭāraka, Kālāgnirudra is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda), the venerable Sakala-Bhaṭṭāraka is the deity (devatā);
*oṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *hūṃ* is the power (śakti), and *kuru 2* is the peg (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

Having performed the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and having offered water for the feet (pādya) and other honors from the argha vessel according to the rules, one should perform the placement of mantras on the faces and limbs (vaktrāṅganyāsa) upon oneself. Then [recite]: "We know the one of many forms;
we meditate upon the one with hollow eyes; may that terrible one inspire us. (3 times).

Then the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with the root mantra: || 108 || *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the weapon, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, *svāhā*. *yaṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *raṃ* to the face of Aghora, *svāhā*. *vaṃ* to the face of Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *laṃ* to the face of Sadyojāta, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *saṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *kṣaṃ* to the tuft of hair, *svāhā*. *haṃ* to the armor, *svāhā*. *kṣa
Svāhā! Laṃ, to the face of Sadyojāta, svāhā! To the Aghoras, the all-pervading self, the heart, obeisance, svāhā! Tha, to the Ghoras, to Brahmā, the head, svāhā!

To those who are most terrible and more terrible than the terrible, to Jvālinī, to Śikhā, Vauṣaṭ! To Sarvataḥ, to all the Sarvas, to Piṅgala, to the Armor (Kavaca), Hūṃ! Juṃ Saḥ! To the one whose form is light, to the three eyes, Vaṣaṭ! Homage to you, O forms of Rudra; to the Pāśupata weapon, which is impenetrable, Phaṭ!
Then, for the full oblation (pūrṇā), at the end of the root mantra "kheṭaka" on the left, [one says] "vauṣaṭ"; this is the full oblation.

Now, regarding Aghoreśvarī: I cannot approach her, the queen of the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, who transcends the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, and who is Śivā, consisting of supreme bliss.

Of this mantra of the venerable Aghoreśvarī: Kālāgnirudra is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); the venerable Aghorīśvarī is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hūṃ is the power (śakti); [Hūṃ] twice is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

The rites beginning with invocation and those beginning with the water for the feet [are performed]. We know the one of many forms; we meditate upon the Sovereign Lady Aghorī; may that Rudra inspire us. || 3 ||

Oṃ hrīṃ aghorīśvaryai hūṃ phaṭ (108 times). The assignment (*nyāsa*) begins with *hāṃ* and so forth. *Kṣaṃ* to the face of Īśāna, svāhā. Likewise, the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is performed with the root mantra.
Then, for the Niṣkala [mantra]: "Madhyaprāṇa" etc. For this Śrī Niṣkala Mantrarāja, Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Triṣṭubh is the meter (chanda);

the deity (devatā) is Paramaśiva, whose essential nature is Śrī Saccidānanda; Hūṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Oṃ is the power (śakti); Namaḥ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
We praise Svacchandabhairava, whose body is supreme light, the single form of the universe, the soul of the universe, and the cause of the creation and other processes of the universe.
We praise Svacchandabhairava, who transcends the universe yet consists of the universe, who is joined with the eight Bhairavas, who is both with parts and without parts, and who is the peaceful one.
A flower in the fire.
The rites beginning with the invocation, as well as the ritual water-vessel, the *argha* offering, and so forth.
Let us know the Supreme Swan; let us meditate upon the Great Swan; may Śiva impel us toward that. || 3 ||
Oṃ hūṃ! Salutation to the partless, pure Bhairava; svāhā! || 108 ||
HĀṂ, obeisance to the heart, svāhā! And so forth. Svāhā to Vāmā and the others; svāhā to Kapāleśa and the others;
svāhā to the weapons, such as the sword and the rest.
Svāhā to the deities of the seven enclosures. Then, the full meditation: at the end of the root mantra, "vāme kheṭaka," perform the full libation.

May the Lord Svacchanda, together with his limbs [retinue], that Goddess, and his entire entourage, be pleased; may he be pleased. "Be present"—this is the *nirodhārghya* (the water of obstruction). Then, for Lakṣmī and Vāsudeva:
He is white in complexion and is always marked by right arms holding a conch, mace, lotus, and discus, while his left arms are joined with a book, a mirror, a foremost lotus, and a water-pot.

I bow to the all-pervading Lord Śrī Vāsudeva, the bestower of boons, who shines resplendently mounted upon Garuḍa, who is the object of compassion for his devotees, and whose body is marked by Lakṣmī as his left half.

Of this mantra of Śrī Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva: Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda), Śrī Viṣṇu is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hau is the power (śakti), Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering of] flowers is in the fire.
(40) The invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
Let us know Vāsudeva; let us meditate upon the Half-Lakṣmī; may that Viṣṇu inspire us. || 3 ||

Oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī Vāsudeva; svāhā. (108 times) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī; svāhā. (108 times) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart of the True Being of Pure Knowledge; svāhā. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the Head, the embodiment of all sovereign powers and qualities; svāhā. Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Crest-lock, the form of all power, Jvālinī; vauṣaṭ. Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the Armor, the embodiment of incomparable strength; huṃ. Oṃ hāṃ, [obeisance to] the Immeasurable...
Vaṣaṭ to the two eyes for splendor! Oṃ Hraḥ, Phaṭ Svāhā to the weapon (astra) whose form is irresistible valor! Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā).

O Lord whose hands are beautiful with the lotus of knowledge, the sprout of nectar, the full jar, and the sweetmeat—be gracious! O you who possess the intoxicating luster of lightning, you are the splendor Lakṣmī herself, the unbroken embodiment of the Self, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa.
I worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, whose face is like the full moon, who wears yellow garments, who is seated upon a lotus, who is attended by Lakṣmī, and who possesses four arms.
At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* is for the full libation (*pūrṇātarpaṇa*). "*Sannidhatsva*" (be present) is for the obstructing water-offering (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, [the offering] for Annapati.
With his very graceful body, he held with his right hand a piece of food, like a fragment of sugar, placed upon a silver vessel.
He who meditates upon Vāmana, holding a jar filled with nectar in his left hand, casts off all suffering.

Of this mantra of the illustrious Dadhivāmana: Indu is the seer (ṛṣi); Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ); the illustrious Dadhivāmana is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering is] a flower in the fire.
The invocation, the offering of water for the feet, and so forth, as well as the self-deposition (ātmannyāsa).
We know Vasudeva; we meditate upon Narayana; may that Vishnu inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of gods, the one of great strength; give food, svāhā! || 108 ||
Oṃ, salutation to the heart, salutation, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, the head, svāhā! To the Lord of the Gods, the crest-lock, vauṣaṭ! To the Greatly Powerful One, the armor, huṃ svāhā!
Give food, give food, to the eyes, vaṣaṭ svāhā! To the weapon, phaṭ svāhā! Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā).
Fair as a pearl, adorned with excellent ornaments of fresh jewels, seated upon the moon, his lotus-face beautified by clusters of locks of hair hanging down.

With our two lotus-hands, we worship Him who holds a golden pitcher filled with pure water and curd-rice placed upon a silver vessel, endowed with supreme qualities. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*). This is the offering for the rite of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Then one should offer three full oblations.
From whose opening and closing [of the eyes] this fivefold set of causes— namely earth, water, fire, air, and ether— along with Brahmā and the rest, certainly arises and surely goes to destruction.
I bow to that light called the "Partless" (niṣkala), which is eternally bound by the noose consisting of the five kalās beginning with Māyā, yet remains free from the stain of all kalās.
Oṃ juṃ saḥ! May there be satisfaction for the entire wheel of mantras; svāhā! (1)

The five-faced one, the bestower of boons, whose vehicle is the king of bulls, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, Śaṅkara, the independent one, whose matted locks are adorned with a crescent moon and a garland of human skulls.

We praise you, whose pair of lotus feet are lauded by Brahmā and others, who removes the influence of time, who is partless, who grants the boons desired by the universe, and who utterly destroys the fear of worldly existence.
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the nourishment of Bhairava, svāhā! || 2 ||

Peaceful, seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of the moon, five-faced and three-eyed, he carries in his right hands a trident, a vajra, a *dha* (?), a sword, an axe, and bestows fearlessness.
I bow to Maheśa, who holds a serpent, a noose, a bell, and a hand-drum in his left hands, is adorned with various ornaments, resembles a mass of crystal, and has a smiling face.
I fulfill the ritual procedure for what is deficient or redundant; svāhā! || 3 || Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa).
One should preserve the remaining clarified butter for the purpose of the oblation to the goddesses.
Now follows the oblation of barley and sesame seeds.
Therein, first is the *vyāhṛti* oblation: Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā. Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā. Oṃ svaḥ svāhā. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā.
Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā. Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā. Oṃ svaḥ svāhā. Oṃ mahaḥ svāhā. Oṃ janaḥ svāhā. Oṃ tapaḥ svāhā. Oṃ satyaṃ svāhā.
Now, the meditation on Gāyatrī.
Likewise, in the *Prapañcasāra*:

With faces like the *mandāra* flower, yellow pigment, collyrium, and the *japā* fruit, his body is variegated by twenty-four syllables, while his crown is adorned with a crest-jewel shining like the moon.

Holding a bow, a noose, a goad, a lotus, and the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), she who is called Abjā, Cāri, and Darā, and who possesses the qualities of Guṇa and Kapāla, shall be the deliverer from worldly existence (*bhava*) and the savior (*tāriṇī*) of one’s desired goals.
[Offer] flowers in the southeast (*agni*).

[Perform] the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, as well as the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. Perform the internal placement (*nyāsa*) upon oneself. *Oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt.* (The Gāyatrī Mantra)
Oṃ tat savitur hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā. Oṃ vareṇyaṃ śirase svāhā. Oṃ bhargo devasya śikhāyai vauṣaṭ.

Dhīmahi kavacāya hūṃ; dhiyo yo naḥ netrābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ; pracodayāt astrāya phaṭ svāhā. The tenth part [is offered] with "muktāvidruma"; the *pūrṇā* [offering] is with [the same]; the *tarpaṇa* is with [the same]; and the *nirodhārgha* is with "sannidhatsva."
Now, in another way: first, that of Brahmā.

I worship Śiva— the primordial one, who laughs, whose crown is the crescent moon, who is beautified by ten million moons, who holds a Veda and a rosary in his hands, and who displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he who is seated upon a jeweled throne, possessing four faces or five faces.

Of this Śrī Caturmukha mantra, Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda); Śrī Caturmukha is the deity (devatā); Hrāṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hsauḥ is the power (śakti); Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

*Hrāṃ hsauḥ | Oṃ |* Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). [Offer] a flower into the fire; [perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. *Oṃ hrāṃ hsauḥ, grant, grant the supreme reality-siddhi of the Four-Faced One, svāhā!* (108)
The full oblation and the libation are performed with the root mantra.

I worship Vedeśvarī, who has four arms and the luster of a thousand times ten million suns, who has three eyes and is adorned with necklaces and a crown; she is intensely radiant, possesses five faces, and is embraced by the lap of the Four-faced One.

Of this venerable Gāyatrī mantra: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and the venerable Mother of the Vedas, Gāyatrī, is the deity (devatā). Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Śrīṃ is the power (śakti), and Bhaiṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

Oṃ sauḥ hsauḥ—thus is the ritual placement (nyāsa). [Perform] the invocation, the offering of water for the feet (pādya), and so forth. Oṃ, we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. 3.
oṃ sauḥ hsauḥ sauḥ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ bhaiṃ glauṃ gāyatrī śrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ prīṃ strīṃ svāhā || 108 ||
The full oblation with the root mantra; the libation; the offering of water for averting obstacles.
Then follows the oblation of barley and sesame seeds to Gaṇeśa and the other deities.

One should meditate upon Indra, the king, who wields the thunderbolt and possesses many eyes; who is mounted upon Airāvaṇa, auspicious, and surrounded by beautiful Apsarases. [One should offer] a flower into the fire. (p.

The rites beginning with invocation and ending with the offering of padya (water for the feet) and so forth [are performed]. *Lūṃ*, obeisance to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand. One should meditate upon Agni, seated in the vīrāsana posture, with the *kūrca* grass as his limb, possessing a sacrificial cord and a spear, mounted upon a goat, tawny in color, and with tawny eyes.
Rūṃ, salutation to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand.
One should meditate upon Yama, the Lord of the Departed, who holds a staff and a noose in his hands, seated upon a buffalo, wrathful, and the destroyer of obstacles during the fire sacrifice (homa).
Ṭūṃ, obeisance to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand.
In the same manner, one should meditate upon Nirṛti, who holds a sword in his hand and sits on an excellent seat—the formidable lord of the Rākṣasas—for the pacification of all obstacles.

*Kṣūṃ*, obeisance to Nirṛti, who holds a sword in his hand. One should meditate upon Varuṇa in the west—white in color, holding a noose, seated upon a fish, and bearing a mace—as the supreme protector during the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Vūṃ, salutation to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand.

One should meditate upon Vāyu, who wears yellow garments, holds a smoky-colored banner in his hand, and is mobile; he is seated upon a deer for the sake of protection and is the dispeller of all obstacles.
Yūṃ, obeisance to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand.

One should remember the Lord of Yakṣas with devotion for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha—him who is mounted upon a ram, holds a mace in his hand, is yellow in color, and has a man as his vehicle.
Salutation to her who possesses the speed of a boar and holds a mace in her hand.
Holding a trident in his hand, mounted upon a bull, adorned with a crown of matted hair, white in complexion, joined by Gaurī, three-eyed, and clothed in an elephant hide—he is to be meditated upon.
Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand.
Brahmā is gentle, four-faced, and possesses a large abdominal region; he bears a long beard, a lotus stalk, a water-pot, kusha grass, and a lotus.
The one to be meditated upon is the remover of obstacles, who was created by Śruti and whose seat is the lotus born from water.
Oṃ āṃ brāṃ braṃ, homage to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand.
One should meditate upon Halāyudha, situated in the direction of the netherworld (Pātāla), mounted upon a tortoise.
He beheld the white Lord of Serpents named Ananta, possessing a thousand hoods.
Hlāṃ, homage to Ananta, who holds a plow in his hand.
Thus are the Lords of the World.
Then follows the oblation to the planets. Among those, first is that for the Sun.
Bearing a smoke-bannered staff and a garland in his two hands, along with a mass of rays; the seven-horsed Sun is red, three-eyed, and of the nature of fire.
He beheld the Lord manifest before him, radiant and beautifying the ground with a thousand rays of light.

I worship the primordial god Mihira, who possesses seven horses, holds a noble banner in his hand, and resides upon a lotus. Of this Śrīsūrya mantra, Śatacihna is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrīsavitā is the deity (devatā), Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Śrīṃ is the power (śakti), and Hsauḥ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

[Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the water for the feet (pādya). [Recite: "We know Aditya; we meditate upon Martanda; may that Surya inspire us. (3) Oṃ Raṃ Agnaye Svāhā. Oṃ Hrāṃ Jhrīṃ Saḥ Vīreśvara Bhairavāya Svāhā. (108 times, or 54, or 27, or 14, or 7 times. Oṃ Hrāṃ Jhrīṃ Saḥ Vīralakṣmyai Svāhā. [This is] the offering (arghya) for the Goddess. Oṃ Hsauḥ Śrīṃ Āṃ [to] Grahadhirāja.

To Āditya, svāhā! || 108 || Oṃ, obeisance to Aṃ Āditya, svāhā! Oṃ Aṃ, to the bearer of the conduct of Śiva, svāhā! Oṃ Aṃ, to the one with the color of the pomegranate flower, svāhā! Oṃ Aṃ, to the one born in the region of Kaliṅga, svāhā! Oṃ Aṃ, to Kaśyapa, svāhā! Oṃ Aṃ, to the one of a thousand rays, svāhā! Oṃ Aṃ, to the lord of the planets, svāhā! Oṃ Aṃ, to the kinsman of the lotus, svāhā! To the one who grants boons to the sacrificer, Aṃ!
Svāhā! Full! The offering for cessation.
May the great-rayed one rise, the one who brings fearlessness through his splendor; may the thousand-beamed, radiant Āditya be pleased with me.
"Be present" is the cessation. Now, concerning the moon:
Always bearing a mass of rays, a garland, and a smoky banner, white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, may the three-eyed Lord come for our protection.

One should meditate upon the Moon, the lord of the planets, within the lotus of the heart— resplendent with the luster of a conch, beloved, situated upon the crown of Lord Śiva, possessing a form of pure love, and holding a pair of lotuses in his hands.

Of this venerable Moon-mantra: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the venerable Soma is the deity (devatā). Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Śrīṃ is the power (śakti), Krīṃ is the pin (kīlaka);

its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth. We know the Maker of Night; we meditate upon the One of Cool Rays; may that Soma inspire us.
Oṃ blūṃ, svāhā to King Varuṇa! Oṃ hsrīṃ saḥ, svāhā to the Cool-rayed One (the Moon)! 108 oblations as before.

Oṃ śrīṃ krīṃ caṃ, obeisance to Candra, svāhā. || 108 || Oṃ, obeisance to Kaṃ, to Soma, svāhā. Oṃ kūṃ, to the Lord of the sixteen digits (kalās), svāhā. Kaṃ, to the one born at the place of Yamunā, svāhā. Kaṃ, to the one of the color of a kunda flower, svāhā. Kaṃ, to the son of Atri, svāhā. Kaṃ, to the Lord of the constellations (nakṣatras), svāhā. Oṃ kaṃ, to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer (yajamāna), svāhā.

The *pūrṇā* libation and the *tarpaṇa*. "The king of the twice-born, the greatly meritorious lord of the stars, especially the sovereign of medicinal herbs—may that Soma be pleased with me. "Be present" is the *nirodhārghya*.
Now, concerning Mars.

Adorned with a water-pot and a garland of *akṣa* seeds, having the excellent peacock as his vehicle, red in hue, three-eyed, wearing a garland—the son of the Earth, Mars, may he protect us. I meditate in my heart upon the compassionate Bhauma (Mars), who resembles molten gold, who sits upon a lion-throne, who holds a lotus and a sword in his hands, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by gods and demons, and who is the lord of the planets. Regarding this Śrī-Bhauma mantra: Aṅgāra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), Śrī-Bhauma is the deity (*devatā*), and "Oṃ" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Śrīṃ is the Śakti; Kaṃ is the Kīlaka. The application is in the fire sacrifice (homa). [Offer] a flower to the fire; [perform] the invocation (āvāhana), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the red-limbed Kumāra. Aiṃ hsauḥ śrīṃ drāṃ kaṃ, svāhā to Bhāma, the lord of the planets. [108] Ā, as before.

Oṃ rhrūṃ aṅgārakāya svāhā || 108 || Oṃ śrīṃ saḥ, O Maṅgala, lord of the planets, remove 2 my affliction; bestow 2 prosperity! Oṃ śrīṃ saḥ phaṭ svāhā || 108 || [With clarified butter: Oṃ namaḥ caṃ aṅgārakāya svāhā || Oṃ caṃ to the youth who observes vows, svāhā || Oṃ caṃ to the son of the Earth, svāhā || Oṃ caṃ to him whose birth was in Avantī, svāhā || Oṃ caṃ to Bhāradvāja, svāhā || Oṃ...

Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the one of red color! Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to Bhāradvāja! Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the one of red color! Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the one with eight thousand rays! Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the one of fierce splendor! Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the crusher of enemies! Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer! [The vessel is] full. "Be present"—this is the water of obstruction (*nirodhārgha*). [This is] the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
By him, whose son has won eternal fame throughout the world, and by that noble-souled Bhauma, his enemies have been slain.
