May Bhauma be pleased with you today; may he always be well-disposed toward me. This is the *nirodhārgha* [offering]. Now, for Budha:
Seated upon the Garuḍa-throne, he holds a rosary and a water-pot.

May the three-eyed Budha, richly adorned with a crown and necklaces, protect me. I meditate upon Budha within the lotus of my mind— he who is the son of Soma, seated upon a swan, two-armed, with the form of a conch and the moon, holding a noose in his hand, a treasure-house of compassion, his limbs graced by ornaments.
Of this glorious mantra of Budha, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Bodha is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with *ṭāṃ* and so forth; offering flowers into the fire, the invocation (*āvāhana*), and the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.
Oṃ hūṃ viṣṇave svāhā. Oṃ hrāṃ kroṃ ṭaṃ to Budha, the Lord of Planets, svāhā. (108 times) Oṃ śrūṃ to Budha, obeisance, svāhā. (108 times) Oṃ hrīṃ to Budha, svāhā.
As in the previous case.

Oṃ, homage to the wise one (*budha*), svāhā! Oṃ ṭaṃ, homage to the one who maintains the conduct of Viṣṇu, svāhā! Ṭaṃ, homage to the lord of forms, svāhā! Ṭaṃ, homage to the one born in the land of Magadha, svāhā! Ṭaṃ, homage to the one whose complexion is his own natural color, svāhā! Ṭaṃ, homage to the son of Atri, svāhā! Ṭaṃ, homage to the one with eight rays, svāhā! Ṭaṃ, homage to the one whose body is great intelligence, svāhā! Ṭaṃ, homage to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer, svāhā! Full libation (*tarpaṇa*).
May Budha, the bestower of intelligence, the son of Soma, and possessor of great luster—standing in the chariot of Āditya—be pleased with me.
The price of cessation.
Now, concerning the individual soul (jīva).

May this Jupiter, who has three eyes, carries a water-pot, is mounted upon an elephant, is adorned with a bull, garlands, and perfumes, and is endowed with knowledge, protect us—he who possesses the luster of a white water-lily.

I remember in my heart-lotus the Guru, who is composed of light, who holds a trident and a spear in his hands, whose lotus feet are praised by the eldest of the lords of gods, who is a treasury of wisdom, who appeared as a fish, and who has two arms.
Of this venerable Bṛhaspati mantra, Gṛtsa is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and the venerable Bṛhaspati is the deity (devatā).
The application (*viniyoga*) in the home [is as follows]: flowers in the fire; the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth with lotuses and other [offerings].
Lūṃ indrāya svāhā || Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ vlu-īṃ aiṃ glauṃ to Bṛhaspati, the lord of the planets, vīṃ ṭhaḥ śrīṃ ṭhaḥ aiṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā || 108 ||

*Ṛṣrūṃ*, obeisance to the living soul, *svāhā*. || 108 || *Oṃ hrīṃ*, to the one who is ever-present with enjoyment, *svāhā*. || 108 || With clarified butter: *Oṃ namaḥ*, obeisance to Bṛhaspati, *svāhā*. To him who maintains celibacy, *svāhā*. To him who is the lord of the protectors of progeny, *svāhā*. To him who is born in the Saindhava region, *svāhā*. To him who belongs to the lineage of Aṅgiras, *svāhā*. To him who has the luster of yellow orpiment, *svāhā*. To him...
Svāhā to the one with incomparable rays! Svāhā to that giver of boons to the sacrificer! Full libation for satisfaction!
May my preceptor, the priest of the king of the gods, who has ascended the summit of Mount Meru and is a knower of all scriptures, be pleased with me.
The price for cessation. Now, regarding semen.
May the three-eyed one, yellow-hued and accompanied by Kāvyā, Ukṣā, and Kalaśā, protect you; he is seen in some great scriptures holding a treasure and a book in his hands.
Resembling molten gold, two-armed, compassionate, clad in yellow garments, and holding a pair of lotuses and a trident.
I meditate upon Śukra, who is served by the Asuras, seated in the Krauñca posture, with two eyes, and whose pair of feet rest upon the lotus of my heart. Of this Śrī-Śukra-mantra:

The sage is Krauñcāṅgāra; the metre is Bṛhatī; the deity is Śrī Śukra; the application is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] a flower in the fire. [Perform] the invocation and so forth, the water for the feet and so forth. Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech, obeisance to Sarasvatī, svāhā! || 108 || Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhārgava, svāhā! || 108 ||
Oṃ aiṃ jaṃgīṃ, obeisance to Śukra, the Lord of the House; svāhā! (108)
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the most excellent of the Asuras; [offer] with clarified butter (ājya). Oṃ namaḥ, svāhā to Pañcaśukra. Svāhā to the one who maintains the conduct of the Moon (Inducarya).
Dhaṃ paṃ, svāhā to the Lord of Māyā! Paṃ, svāhā to Bhojakaṭa Janman!

*Paṃ* to the one with seven rays, *svāhā*. *Paṃ* to the lord of the asuras, *svāhā*. *Paṃ* to the one with the color of cow’s milk, *svāhā*. *Paṃ* to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer, *svāhā*. [Full Oblation. [Libation.]
May Śukrācārya, whose radiance is equal to the moon, who is the preceptor of the Asuras, and the conqueror of all enemies, be pleased with me.
The offering for cessation. Now, for Saturn.
The three-eyed one stands upon a corpse, holding a water-pot, a rosary, and garlands; he is dark-complexioned, adorned with a staff, a rosary, and bracelets, and wears a dark garland.

I meditate upon Śani, who has the luster of blue collyrium, the beloved son of Mihira, the lord of planets, holding a noose and a serpent in his hands, the two-armed one who instills fear in gods and demons,
within the lotus of my mind.

Of this auspicious mantra of Śanaiścara: Kutsa is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda); the auspicious Śanaiścara is the deity (devatā). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa), [as well as] for the flower, the invocation, the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
Oṃ prīṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, to the universal sovereign of the planets, Śanaiścara, klīṃ aiṃ saḥ svāhā. || 108 ||
Kṣmryūṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara, svāhā! || 108 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Śanaiścara of black complexion! Smlvyūṃ svlyūṃ jmryūṃ, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā to Śanaiścara, the remover of all diseases! 10.

Oṃ hrīṃ mardinyai svāhā. This is the Śakti. Oṃ namaḥ yaṃ śanaiścarāya svāhā. Yaṃ yamacaryadharāya svāhā. Yaṃ saurāṣṭrajanmane svāhā. Yaṃ kāśapāya svāhā. Yaṃ rājavartavarṇāya svāhā. Yaṃ kṣayaṅkarāya svāhā. Yaṃ mahāmṛtyudhikāriṇe svāhā. Yaṃ chāyāsutāya svāhā. Yaṃ.
Svāhā to the one who grants boons to the sacrificer! Full oblation! Satiating libation!
May Śanaiścara, the son of the Sun, who is black in color, thin-limbed, and resembles a dark cloud— may he, together with Sauri, be pleased with me.
The offering for the cessation [of obstacles]. Now, for Rāhu.
May Rāhu, who has the form of a head, adorned with garlands and earrings, delighting in his lion-throne and fond of seizing the nectar, protect you.

I meditate in my heart upon Rāhu, the lord of planets, who has the form of the moon, Mitra, and Antaka; who is both terrible and resembles lapis lazuli, possesses two arms, and is the supreme protector of the three worlds and the bestower of desired boons.
Of this Śrīrāhu-mantra:

The seer is Gautama; the meter is Gāyatrī; the deity is Śrī-Rāhu; the application is in the fire-oblation (homa); [the offering is] a flower in the fire; [this applies to] the invocation, the padya-offering, and so forth.

Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ, to the Lord of all Obstacles, svāhā! Oṃ krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ ṭaṃ, to the bearer of the mallet, to Rāhu, īṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ bhaiṃ, svāhā! || 108 || Yūṃ, obeisance to Rāhu, svāhā! || 108 || Oṃ hūṃ, to the lover of nectar, svāhā! [Offer] with clarified butter.

Oṃ, obeisance, peace to Rāhu, svāhā! Peace to Gaṇapati, the observer of vows, svāhā! Peace to the Lord of the Gandharvas, svāhā! Peace to the one born from the heat of the sun, svāhā! Peace to him whose lineage is Paiṭhana, svāhā! Peace to him who resembles the *atasī* flower, svāhā! Peace to the one with eighteen thousand rays, svāhā! Peace to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer, svāhā! Full oblation. Libation.
Red-eyed, with a smoky hue, the conqueror of enemies and possessor of great strength; armless, dwelling in the intermediate space together with Rāhu—may he be pleased with me.
The offering for Nirodha is finished. Now, for Ketu.
Restrained by ten serpents, he was equipped with a banner, three eyes, and a massive body; his skin was like the color of the water at the confluence of the Vata and Anna rivers.

I worship in my mental lotus the Ketu, the sole hero who possesses a tail, who strikes fear into people, who resembles a dark rain-cloud, who wears black garments, and who holds a spear and a trident in his hands.

Of this Śrī Ketu mantra: Agni is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda); Ketu is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering of] flowers into the fire, the invocation (āvāhana), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, to Rudra; svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ krūṃ, to the comet of fierce form, aiṃ sauḥ; svāhā! (108 times) Hrīṃ, obeisance to the comet; svāhā! (108 times) Oṃ hrīṃ, to the light-comet; svāhā! [Offer] with clarified butter (ājya).

Oṃ namaḥ kṣaṃ ketave svāhā || Kṣaṃ agnicaryadharāya svāhā || Kṣaṃ dhūmravarṇāya svāhā || Kṣaṃ jaiminīyāya svāhā || Kṣaṃ antarvedī-sambhavāya svāhā || Kṣaṃ mahāmṛtyudhikāriṇe svāhā || Kṣaṃ yajamānavarapradāya svāhā || Pūrṇā || Tarpaṇam ||
May Ketu, the son of Agni, possessed of great splendor and the destroyer of all planets, who agitates all living beings—may he with his banner be pleased with me.
The price for cessation. Now, for the permanent [offering].
The son of Uttānapāda, Dhruva, is the form of Viṣṇu, possessed of great merit; seated above all, he is the four-eyed one, the supreme Śiva, eternally auspicious.

Of this venerable *dhruva-mantra*: Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Jagatī is the meter (*chandas*), Dhruva is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*). [The offering of] flowers into the fire, the invocation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth.

Oṃ hlāṃ, svāhā to Brahmā. Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda. (108) Oṃ tat sat! He who is omnipresent, supreme, even more supreme, and all-pervading—the Great Brahman—abides having pervaded all; he whose form is most beautiful like a conch shell, and who is praised by the lords of sages.

May the Pole Star (Dhruva), who circumambulates the circle of stars, who is honored by the foremost of the Seven Sages, and whose dwelling is established in the direction of the preeminent Kinnaras, grant us prosperity. May he be our upward-facing support.
Oṃ, homage to Dhruva, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the one in the form of a bird, svāhā! Homage to the sovereign of the northern quarter, svāhā! Homage to the most excellent of sages, svāhā!
Svāhā to the one who grants boons to the sacrificer! Full oblation! Libation! The steadfast king, of great merit, is established in the northern direction.
May Sadhrūva, the most excellent among the sages, be pleased with me. This is the offering for cessation (nirodhārgha).
Now follows [the hymn] of Agastya.
White-complexioned, with eyes like the petals of a lotus and a face like the full moon, he holds a pair of lotuses in his hands and is intent upon the lotus posture.
O beautiful one, Agastya, born from a jar, dwells most firmly in the southern direction; he is the drinker of the lord of rivers (the ocean) and is forever the enemy of Vātāpi, the foe of the gods.
For this Śrī Agastya mantra: [offering] to Agni; flower; [and the rites of] invocation, water for the feet, and so forth.
Oṃ, svāhā to Agastya!

Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Agastya, the son of Avarṇapādā. (108) With clarified butter: Oṃ, obeisance to Agastya, svāhā. Oṃ, svāhā to the one born from a jar. (108) Svāhā to the enemy of Vātāpi. Aiṃ, svāhā to the one who drank the ocean. Oṃ, svāhā to the lord of the southern quarter.
Svāhā to the one who assumes the form of Viṣṇu. Oṃ, svāhā to the body of Kṛṣṇa. Oṃ, svāhā to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer. [The full oblation.
The libation.
May Vātāpi, that destroyer of people who was swallowed whole by him, and likewise the ocean, and also the enemy of the Vindhya mountains, be pleased with me.
Agastya, having become a water-jar, remains stationed in the southern direction.
The ocean has been brought to exhaustion; may the enemy of the Vindhya mountain be pleased with me.
The price for cessation.
Whoever performs the fire-oblation according to this rite for the Brahma-maṇḍala attains all desires and enjoys infinite fruit.
Then follows the fire offering for the seven enclosures.
Svāhā to the deities of the seven enclosures. Then, one should offer three full oblations (pūrṇāhutis).

One should meditate upon the God seated on a lotus throne, resembling the Himālaya mountain, with one face and three eyes; in his right hands he holds a full pitcher, the gesture of boon-granting (vara), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), while in his left hand he holds a full moon.

I bow to the Goddess who holds a conch and a lotus in her hands, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who has one face and three eyes, and who bears the crescent moon— the lord of stars— revered by the three worlds.
Oṃ juṃ saḥ! May there be satisfaction for the entire wheel of mantras; svāhā! || 1 ||

I worship the Lord, who is adorned with five faces—white like pearls, yellow like turmeric, white as a pearl, red like a hibiscus flower, and dark blue—and who possesses three eyes on each; who wears a crescent moon upon his brow and shines with the brilliance of ten million full moons;
who holds in his hands the trident, axe, sword, thunderbolt, fire, lordly serpent, bell, goad, noose, and the weapon that destroys fear;
and whose limbs are radiant with immeasurable ornaments.
Oṃ hūṃ! May there be nourishment for Bhairava; svāhā! (2)

Oṃ, I bow to him who has the luster of a bandhūka flower, who possesses three eyes, who bears a crescent moon, whose face is smiling, and who holds in his hands a trident, a skull-cup, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, with a beautiful laugh; whose body is embraced by the hand of his beloved, who rests upon Sumbha’s left thigh, whose lovely jewel-lotus shines in her palm,
and who is adorned with shimmering ornaments made of gems.
Oṃ, I fulfill the ritual procedures that are deficient or excessive; svāhā!

By this offering of sesame seeds, for the purpose of warding off the sins accumulated through speech, mind, and body by myself, and for the purpose of pleasing the goddess [named] so-and-so, may all the deities be satisfied and grant their boons.
Oṃ. Now, the procedure for the clarified butter oblation (ājyahoma) for the goddesses is written.
Therein, first, Durgā.
Resembling the Bandhūka flower and gold, adorned with a beautiful serpent-garland, and holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
With my hands, I take refuge in the three-eyed Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, who holds the moon and the digit as ornaments, and who is supported by Umā.
Of this venerable Nīlakaṇṭha mantra: the seer is Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter is Anuṣṭubh.

The deity is Śrī Durgeśvara Nīlakaṇṭha. *Hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Oṃ* is the power (*śakti*). *Namaḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire sacrifice (*homa*). *Oṃ hsauḥ hrīṃ*—thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). [Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites. *Oṃ hsauḥ hrīṃ nīlakaṇṭhāya namaḥ svāhā*. (Recite 108 times.)
At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" constitutes the full oblation (pūrṇā). This is the libation (tarpaṇa) and the water-offering for obstruction (nirodhārgha).
Now, [the ritual] for Durgā.
Holding in her left hands a trident, a sword, a great spear, discs, a conch, a shield, a bow, and a threatening gesture, she stands upon the back of a great buffalo demon;
may she, who resembles a blade of durva grass, destroy our sins for the attainment of our desires.

I worship Durgā, who resembles the *dūrvā* grass, who has three eyes and a shimmering crown, who holds a conch, a lotus, a sword, an arrow, a shield, a trident, a bow, and the gesture of threat (*santarjanī*), who is seated upon the throne of the buffalo, and who resides on the nine-fold seat of the syllable *Ar*.
Seated upon a lion, crowned with the moon, and resembling emerald, she holds a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows in her four arms; adorned by women with their eyes,
wearing armlets, necklaces, bracelets, jingling girdles, and tinkling anklets, and shining with jeweled earrings— may Durgā, who removes all misfortune, be for your protection.
For this Śrī Durgā mantra, Maheśvara is the seer (ṛṣi).

The meter is *anuṣṭubh*, the deity is the illustrious Goddess Durgā, *duṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *oṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). This is the application in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
An offering of flowers into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
We know her as the Fortunate One; we meditate upon her who wears a garland of desire; may that Durgā inspire us. || 3 ||
If the oblation is for the purpose of protecting the fetus, then there is an oblation of sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
Oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai namaḥ svāhā || 108 || [Recite] 54 times, or 27 times, or 14 times, or 7 times. This is the tenth part (daśāṃśa) for the limbs (aṅga).

Oṃ, homage to the heart, svāhā! Hrīṃ, svāhā to the head! Duṃ, vauṣaṭ svāhā to the crest-lock! Duḥ, hūṃ svāhā to the armor! Gā, vaṣaṭ svāhā to the eyes! Yai, phaṭ svāhā to the weapon! Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā): Holding a discus, conch, sword, shield, arrow, bow, trident, and the threatening gesture, she who stands upon the severed head of Mahiṣa is like none other than the ninefold primordial [Goddess].
May there be prosperity through Durgā. With the root mantra. Now, Vanadurgā.

May that Samādhi—who is both a noble chariot and the form of a supreme charioteer; who, being honored by the virtuous, bestows joy through his generosity even upon those who are deluded by contempt; who grants the attainment of desired goals;
and who possesses the power to prevail—protect you constantly with supreme well-being, O Giridurga!

Of this *Śrī-Vanadurgā-mantra*: Suratha is the seer (*ṛṣi*); *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chanda*); *Śrī-Vanadurgā* is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is according to the purpose in the fire-oblation (*homa*). [The offerings are: flowers in the fire; the invocation (*āvāhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. "Arise, O Puruṣī! Why do you sleep? A great danger has come upon me.
Whether it be possible or impossible, O Blessed One, pacify that for me! Svāhā! (108). As before.
Arise, O woman! Homage to the heart, svāhā!

Why do you sleep? To the head, *svāhā*! Fear has come upon me; to the crest-lock, *vauṣaṭ svāhā*! Whether it be possible or impossible, to the armor, *hūṃ svāhā*! Therefore, O Blessed One, to my eyes, *vaṣaṭ svāhā*! Quench it, *svāhā*! To the weapon, *phaṭ svāhā*! Now, Gaurī:
She whose radiant body resembles molten gold, who bears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, and who holds a conch in her hand amidst the flames.
May that Durgā, seated upon a golden lotus throne, granting the boons of protection and fearlessness with her hands, bestow prosperity upon you today. Regarding this mantra of Śrī Gaurī:
Sumadhyastha is the seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī Gaurī is the deity (devatā), and its application is in the fire sacrifice (homa).
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Durgā, daughter of Gauri and the Mountain; svāhā, svadhā, vauṣaṭ, hrīṃ, kṣvīṃ, phaṭ, svāhā. [The syllables are 28.]
The oblations, according to their full extent.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Durgā, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura; svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the bearer of the red skull-cup; svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Goddess Durgā, the crusher of Duṃdubhi; svāhā! Oṃ, O Siṃhadurgā, O Mistress of the Lion, eighteen-armed one, fierce as Rudra, of terrible form, huṃ phaṭ, obeisance; svāhā! (Thirty syllables.)

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, O Durgā, O Deliverer from Destruction, huṃ blūṃ svāhā. Thus are the mantras for the thirty-six-armed form. Hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ—these are the limbs (aṅgas). Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā).

Drawing her bow back to her ear, she makes the sound of thunder; ringing her own bell, she strikes the Dānava’s hard chest with her trident while holding his throat with her hand. She offers the blood and fat splashing from his body to Cāmuṇḍā.

O Goddess praised by the gods, whose feet are free from the miserable states of existence, whose lower lip is crimson, and who, together with [your consort], protect us from the difficult path of evil rebirths.
Oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai svāhā vauṣaṭ. Thus is the full oblation (pūrṇā). Now follows the libation (tarpaṇa).
Oṃ! Prosperity, humility, beauty, patience, heaven, earth, and fortitude.

She is nourished by modesty, she is the noble one, she is the one who restrains speech, and she is indeed never false; those who know you as Durgā, as Vedagarbhā, and as Ambikā—[to them you grant your grace].
Addressing her as Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, Kṣemī, and Kṣemakarī, they, with bodies bowed in reverence, gratified her both in the morning and in the afternoon.
For by your grace, everything they desire shall come to pass.
By this mantra-homa for the sake of attaining the goal as it truly is, may the many Durgās be pleased; may the many Durgās be gratified. This is the *nirodhārgha*. Now follows the *śārikā*.

I take refuge in the auspicious Vāmadeva, the embodiment of Śiva, who possesses the luster of ten million full moons, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, who holds a skull-bowl, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a mace, and a sword in his hands, and whose body is adorned with ashes and garlands of bones.
Of this mantra of Śrī Vāmadeva: Kālāgnirudrabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Triṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Śrī Śārikeśvara Vāmadeva is the deity (devatā);
Hrāṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Vāṃ is the power (śakti); Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

An offering of flowers into the fire; the invocation and the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings; the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with *vāṃ* and so forth: *oṃ hrāṃ vāṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*. (108)
At the end of the root mantra is the *pūrṇāhuti*. The libation (*tarpaṇa*).

The offering for the cessation (*nirodhārgha*). She who is radiant with the seven seed-syllables, whose form possesses the brilliance of the seven suns, whose pair of lotus feet are bowed to by the Seven Sages, and who removes the suffering of the seven worlds; she who fashioned the cage of the manifested universe as a mere thread and released Pradyumna—may that Blessed Goddess, joined with the seven, protect us.
May the illustrious Śārikā protect us!

I worship in my heart Śārikeśī, who possesses the splendor of the rising sun, who bears the crescent moon upon her crest, whose arms hold the excellent sword, the discus, and the gesture of fearlessness, who is seated upon a lion-throne, and who is merged with the left side of Śiva.

Of this mantra of the illustrious Śārikā: the seer (ṛṣi) is the illustrious Mahādeva; the meter (chandaḥ) is Triṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is the blessed goddess Śārikā; the seed-syllable (bīja) is ŚĀM; the power (śakti) is ĀM; the pin (kīlaka) is HRĀM; its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
A flower in the fire.
The invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth; the self-assignment of mantras (nyāsa) within one's own self.
Oṃ hrīṃ, let us know Śārikā; let us meditate upon the seven-syllabled mantra; may that Śilā inspire us. 3.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ pheṃ āṃ śāṃ śārikāyai namaḥ || 108 || The ritual placement (nyāsa) begins with *śrāṃ* and so forth. Likewise, the deities of the surrounding retinue (*āvaraṇadevatā*) are as follows: Oṃ hrīṃ aṃ amāyai svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ kaṃ kāmāyai svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ caṃ cārvāṅgyai svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ ṭaṃ ṭaṅkādhāriṇyai svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ taṃ tārāyai svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ paṃ pārvatyai svāhā |
Oṃ hrīṃ yaṃ yakṣiṇyai svāhā. Oṃ hrīṃ śāṃ śārikābhavatyai svāhā. Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā).

May that goddess Śārikā—who has arisen from the peak of a mountain split open by the host of gods, who is surrounded on all sides by eight goddesses equal in number to the Vasus, who is the pacifier of sins, who bears the form of a flame, who bestows wealth, and whose body is adorned with a skull red as the blood of a Śārikā bird—be ever with us.
[Recite] the root mantra: *Vauṣaṭ Svāhā*. [This is] the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
I bow to Pāṃśārikā, the Mistress of the Sacred Seat (Pīṭheśvarī), who sits upon the peak of Pradyumna and is adorned by the circle of Mothers, for the sake of the sacred stone.
By this mantra-homa, may the Blessed Śrī Śārikā, together with Vāmadeva, along with her retinue, weapons, and limbs, be pleased; may she be gratified.
"Be present!"—this is the water-offering for cessation (*nirodhārgha*). Now, [the mantra of] Śāradā:

That face which possesses the radiance of a thousand suns, the luster of a mass of camphor, with its slopes of tawny-red matted hair, and is resplendent with the necklace-like ornaments of the hoods of serpents;
I worship Śiva, whose face is smiling, whose body is adorned with the crescent moon, and who constantly holds a sword, a skull, a boon-granting gesture, a trident, and a bow in his arms.

Of this venerable Śiva-mantra: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda); the venerable Lord of Śāradā, Śiva, is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Śrīṃ is the power (śakti); Namaḥ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
A flower in the fire.
The invocation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth; the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with *hrāṃ* and so on; [the Gāyatrī]:
"We know Sadāśiva, we meditate upon Tryambaka; may that Śiva inspire us. (3)
Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Śiva. (108 times) Gūṃ śrīṃ oṃ, obeisance to Śiva. (108 times) Oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Śiva.
(108 times) The full oblation with the root mantra. The libation. The water for the final restraint. Now, the worship of Śāradā.

Seated upon Śrīśaila, Pārvatī has a smiling countenance, holds a trident in her hand, possesses eyes like fire, sun, and moon, is the mother of the three worlds, has six arms, and is the embodiment of all power.

May the Blessed Lady Śāradā, who is accessible through devotion, who was initiated by Śāṇḍilya, who is followed by her attendants, who sits upon a lion-throne, and who indeed bestows desired fruits— may she, who is as radiant as the orb of the rising sun, possessing the splendor of millions of flames of fire, whose eyes are the shining moon and fire,

who is beautiful with a network of tinkling bells made of various jewels, and who holds a trident, a spear, a noose, and a multitude of vessels filled with nectar— may she grant us blessings. I bow to her.

May Śāradā—seated upon a lion-throne, with a smiling countenance, endowed with six arms, holding a mirror, a staff, a jar, nectar, a book, a rosary, and a trident that fulfills the hopes of practitioners; three-eyed and single-faced, adorned with precious ornaments, possessing a yellow luster—protect the three worlds! [I bow to her] who has six arms, three eyes, a smiling face, and whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the sage Śāṇḍilya.
I meditate in my heart upon the blessed Goddess Śāradā, who stands upon a mountain, holding a trident, seated upon a lion-throne,
possessing three eyes, and bearing a bow, arrows, a spear, a bell, a vessel of *svadhā*, and a rutting elephant.
May this autumnal season, radiant with the golden hue of [the goddess] holding her weapons, be for your prosperity and grant you all fruits.

Of this mantra of the Blessed Śrī Śāradā: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), the Blessed Śrī Śāradā is the deity (devatā), *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *namaḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Flowers, the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth, [are offered] into the fire.
We know Śāradā; we meditate upon her who possesses seven syllables; may Sarasvatī inspire us. || 3 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *oṃ hrāṃ klāṃ*, and so forth. *Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to the Blessed Lady Śāradā, hrīṃ svāhā.* (108 times) *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lady Bhairavī, O Sovereign of Speech, O Great Bestower, O Possessor of Great Power, to the Blessed Lady Śāradā, hrīṃ svāhā.* (108 times)

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, obeisance to the heart, svāhā! O Vāgīśvarī, svāhā to the head! O Mahāpradā, vauṣaṭ svāhā to the crest-lock! O Mahāprabhāve, hūṃ svāhā to the armor! Omiti Bhagavatī Śāradā, vaṣaṭ to the eyes! Hrīṃ svāhā, phaṭ svāhā to the weapon!
Now, the divisions.
Oṃ śmrīṃ, svāhā to Śāradā. || 108 ||
The placement [of mantras] beginning with *śmām*, etc.; or alternatively:
Hrīṃ hya jhreṃ for the head; jhūṃ for the crest-lock; hūṃ for the armor; hūṃ for the eyes; oṃ phaṭ for the weapon; and the full oblation with the root mantra.
Seated upon a three-eyed tiger, clad in red garments, autumnal in splendor, holding the sun and moon, a bow and arrow, a spear, a sword,
and the gesture of fearlessness; that Goddess, always bearing a sharp dagger, with a face as lovely as the full moon, adorned with garlands and earrings— may she protect us supremely.
Always [worship] Śāradā; [fill the vessel] with the root mantra; then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
I bow to Śāradā, the mistress of the sacred seat (pīṭheśvarī), who bestows eloquence in Kāśmīra, who is united with Vijayeśvara, and who increases the intellect.
Salutations to that Bhavānī, who is skilled in destroying the afflictions of existence, who is Śāradā, and whose white lion-throne resembles an autumnal cloud.
By this mantra-homa, may the Blessed Lady Śāradā, together with her weapons, her limbs, her retinue, and her attendants, be pleased; may she be gratified.
The offering for cessation. Now, the queen.

I meditate in my heart upon the Lord of Beings, who shines like jasmine and the moon, who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, who holds a skull, a noose, a goad, and a trident in his hands, who possesses three eyes, who is white with sacred ash, and who smiles.
Of this mantra of the illustrious Bhūteśvara: Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda); the illustrious Rājñīśvara Bhūteśvara is the deity (devatā);
HŪṂ is the seed-syllable (bīja); HRĪṂ is the power (śakti); OṂ is the pin (kīlaka).
The application for the domestic rite: flowers in the fire;
the invocation, water for the feet, and so forth. *Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ*, salutation to Bhūteśvara. (108 times).
The full oblation with the root mantra; the libation.

I bow to that Queen of the Ultimate Reality, whose form possesses the twelve suns as its circumference, who sits alone upon the lion-throne, encircled by serpents, who has attained the sovereignty of the Goddess whose movement transcends the senses, and who embodies the splendor of Bharga.
Her eyes are like the cool-rayed moon, the rising sun, and fire; she has four arms and is seated upon a lotus throne.

I worship the Great Queen, the Sovereign who dwells on Mount Himavat, bearing a conch, a lotus, a trident, and a sword. Of this mantra of the illustrious Mahārājñī: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda).

The deity is Śrī Mahārājñī; *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *sauḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *klīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire sacrifice (*homa*). [Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth.
We know the one whose ears are like the sun; we meditate upon the jewel of light; may that Queen inspire us. || 3 ||

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ klīṃ sauḥ, to the Blessed Lady Rājñī, hrīṃ svāhā. || 108 || Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lady Rājñī, svāhā. || 108 || Oṃ lhrūṃ, to the Great Queen, the Pervader of the Universe, svāhā. || 108 ||

Then, [the priest] offers the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra and *vauṣaṭ*: "I worship the Queen, who possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns, who has three eyes, who is seated upon a lion-throne, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread, whose hands hold a sword, a lotus, an excellent water-pot, and a vessel of nectar, and whose lotus-face is in full bloom. Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*). By this mantra-oblation, may the Blessed Queen Śrī Rājñī, together with Bhūteśvara, along with her weapons, her vehicle, her retinue, and her attendants, be pleased.
May they be pleased.
Now, the flame.

I bow to Mahādeva, the Lord of Consciousness, who has three eyes, whose crown is adorned with the moon, who is red-hued, who possesses the fierce laughter and the splendor of the sun at the end of an aeon, who is seated upon a bull, and who holds a trident and a skull-cup in his hands.
Of this mantra of the glorious Mahādeva: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); the glorious Jvālāmukhīśvara Mahādeva is the deity (devatā);
*hrāṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *hauṃ* is the power (śakti); *oṃ* is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
Flowers in the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
Oṃ hrāṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Mahādeva. || 108 ||
The full oblation is performed with the root mantra. Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa).

(52) She is situated upon a mountain of flames, three-eyed, presiding over the three seats, adorned with a profusion of fire, and possessed of a beautiful face that is never seen by ordinary mortals. Abiding in the center of the lotuses of the six wheels, she holds a choice mace, a lotus, and displays the gestures of fearlessness; she is the embodiment of consciousness, the fulfiller of all aims.
I bow to Jvālāmukhī, the illuminator.

Of this mantra of Śrī Jvālāmukhī: Vaiśvānara is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); the venerable goddess Śrī Jvālā is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Śrīṃ is the power (śakti), and Huṃ is the bolt (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
[Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
We know Jvālāmukhī; we meditate upon her who devours the world; may that Jvālā inspire us. || 3 ||

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ jvālāmukhi, devour all my enemies, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (108) Oṃ hrīṃ [to] the heart, śrīṃ [to] the head, jvālāmukhi [to] the crest-lock; devour all my enemies, kava [to] the armor, huṃ phaṭ [to] the eyes, svāhā [to] the weapon. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kṭnrlhūṃ? [to] the sandals of Mother Jvālāmukhī, obeisance. (108) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ phuṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lady Jvālā.

Then, in my true heart, I remember Jvālāmukhī, whose hair is encircled by full flames, who holds a lotus, a conch, a sword, and a mace, who is seated upon a lion throne, and whose pair of feet are yellow.
O Jvālāmukhī, O Great Flame, you whose eyes are tawny with flames!
"O Jvālā, O Tejas, O Mahātejas, O Jvālāmukhī, salutations to you! With the root mantra followed by "vauṣaṭ," one performs the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and thereafter the libation (tarpaṇa).
By this mantra-homa, may the Blessed Lady Śrījvālā, together with Mahādeva, along with her weapons, her vehicle, her retinue, and her attendants, be pleased;
may they be gratified.
Now follows the goddess Dīkṣā.
Likewise, in the right [hands], there are a trident, a sword, a goad, a severed head, a flaying knife, and a skull-cup filled with blood.
I bow with devotion to the Great Mistress of the gods, who is seated upon the throne of Rudra and possesses eight faces.
In the fire, [one performs] the invocation of the flower, the water for the feet, and so forth; with the hand, one performs the oblation of sesame seeds and clarified butter.
Oṃ hūṃ bhuvanamālini hrīṃ. (108) The full oblation and libation are performed with the root mantra.
The eight-syllable mantra known as Vidyābhuvanamālinī destroys sins such as the uprooting of tawny-colored creatures through mere remembrance.
O Maheśvarī, you burn away the heap of sins of Mudgala; O Goddess, O best of women, when you have been worshipped, you have entered the path of his ears.
Or she is the meditator, the one whose form is the universe, the giver of liberation, and the destroyer of bondage.
By this mantra-homa, the Great Goddess is consecrated along with her weapons. This is the offering for the rite of restraint (nirodhārgha).

Now, I bow to the Mother, Pāpāntakarī, whose hands are marked with the noose, the goad, the rosary, and the lotus; who has a lotus-like form, a gentle countenance, and three eyes; who rests upon a beautiful lotus; who is red in hue; who bestows abundant happiness upon her devoted worshippers; and who is intent on bringing an end to all evil.
An offering of flowers into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, homage to the Blessed One, O Gaurī, pure in speech! Purify! Awaken! Sāṃ sāṃ klīṃ svāhā! [The syllables are 26.]
The full oblation with the root mantra; the libation.
Even after destroying the entire universe filled with Brahmins, he is not tainted by those sins, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
By this mantra-homa, she brings an end to evil.
Now, Kulavāgīśvarī.

I perpetually bow to the Goddess Vāgīśvarī, the Guru of the Kula, who dwells in a grove of Kadamba trees, who resides within the white and black pericarp of a red triangle, and whose lotus-hands are endowed with a sacred book and a rosary of beads.
Of this mantra of Śrī Kulavāgīśvarī: the seer (ṛṣi) is Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter (chandas) is Paṅkti; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Kulavāgīśvarī;
*aiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *sauḥ* is the power (*śakti*); *klīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*); its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
The flower offering into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
We know the Lord of Speech; we meditate upon the Lord of Desire; may that Śakti inspire us. || 3 ||
Aiṃ Hrīṃ, may we know Vāgīśa; Klīṃ, may we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; Sauḥ, may that Śakti inspire us. || 3 ||

Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, obeisance to the sandals of Mahātripurabhairavī Kulavāgīśvarī Ambā. || 108 || Oṃ Klīṃ Hrauṃ Śrīṃ Hūṃ Jhaṃ, O Kulavāgīśvarī who holds a crocodile in her hand! Aiṃ Ṭhaḥ Jhaṃ Ṭhaḥ Dhrīṃ Ṭhaḥ Svāhā. || 108 ||

Aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ; klīṃ śirase svāhā; auḥ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; Tripurabhairavī kavacāya huṃ; Kulavāgīśvarī netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ; Ambāpādukābhyo namaḥ svāhā astrāya phaṭ. Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā).
I worship Kulavāgīśvarī, who holds a trident and a sword in her two arms, who is beautiful and radiant like fire, who has three eyes, and who is seated upon a lion throne.
At the end of the root mantra, [say] *vauṣaṭ*. Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
I bow to that Mother of the Gods, upon whom this triple world—from the cosmic egg to the outer shell—is strung like beads upon the great thread of the Imperishable.
By this mantra-homa, may Kulavāgīśvarī, together with her retinue and attendants, be pleased; may they be gratified.
Now follows Kāmeśvara.
Bhairava is mounted upon the pericarp, resembling the rising sun; he is endowed with great energy, possesses three faces, and is imperishable.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, having an elephant hide as his upper garment, holding a trident and a sword in his hands, he resounds with the ringing of a bell and a hand-drum.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, he has oxen for his nose-ropes and terrible scorpions.
Resembling a twilight cloud and endowed with smiles and graceful dances, [he beheld] the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī seated upon his lap.
The Goddess, who resembles a heap of vermilion, possesses a luster equal to rubies; she shines like the rising sun and is augmented by divine splendor.
Illuminating the ten directions with rays of light arising from herself, she had four arms and one face, and was adorned with a bow and arrows.
She is adorned with a book composed of all-encompassing wisdom, and graced by a crystal rosary held in her hand.
Clad in red garments and adorned with red flowers, she was bound with a girdle and anklets, and embellished with necklaces and armlets.
She has the appearance of a sixteen-year-old maiden, adorned with jar-like breasts, and she shines with the knitting of her eyebrows, which are split like the bow of the God of Love.
One should meditate upon her who has three eyes and a beautiful face, who is immersed in a flood of nectar, who faces the God of gods, and who is smiling.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess, who assumes such a form, who removes the suffering of those who bow before her, and who is endowed with the four seats (catuṣpīṭha).
An offering of flowers into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth; then the Gāyatrī.
Oṃ, may we know Vāgīśa; may we meditate upon Kāmeśa; may Śiva impel us toward that. || 3 ||
With the hand, one should perform the oblation of parched grain mixed with curd, honey, and milk.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ, obeisance to the sandals of Kāmeśvara Bhairavanātha, svāhā! (108 times) Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to the sandals of Ambā Tripurabhairavī, svāhā! (108 times)
The factors do not exist. As it has been said:
Thus has been declared this goddess, the Vidyā Tripurabhairavī, who is endowed with the names and the feet [of the mantra], yet is devoid of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Then follows the full [offering].

I perpetually bow to Kāmeśvarī, the Guru of the Kula, whose full body is completely filled with vermilion, who is endowed with two hands holding a bow and arrows, and whose lotus-hands are joined with a fine book and a rosary.
At the end of the root [mantra], the full oblation (pūrṇā). The libation (tarpaṇa). By this mantra-homa, the respectful offering for cessation (nirodhārgha).
Now follows Vajreśvarī.

I bow to the auspicious Vajreśvarī, whose luster is like the red of the Atasī flower in the fire at the end of an eon; her body is adorned with fine garments, necklaces, gems, and earrings; she possesses three eyes, and her hands are joined with the goad, the noose, the arrow, the bow, and other weapons.
An offering of flowers into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
Oṃ, let us know the one of great fortune; let us meditate upon her who is eternally moist; may that Śakti inspire us. || 3 ||
Hrīṃ klīnne aiṃ kroṃ nityamadadrave hrīṃ. || 108 ||

Aiṃ hya hrīṃ hrīṃ klīnne, for the head (śiras). Klīnne hrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ kroṃ, for the crest-lock (śikhā). Kroṃ aiṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ nitye, for the armor (kavaca). Nitya hrīṃ hrīṃ madanetrebhyaḥ, for the eyes (netra). Mada hrīṃ hrīṃ drave astrāyāstrāya phaṭ svāhā, for the weapon (astra).
The oblation (homa) consists of camphor, saffron, musk, and clarified butter. [This is] the full oblation (pūrṇā).
May this Earth, whose six hands shine with a bow, a noose, a goad, a cloud, and two citron fruits— she who is the source of the Vedas,
the three-eyed one, and the supreme Goddess Kamalā— always abide with you, O Unborn One, as your beloved.
The libation; the offering for cessation.
Now, the divisions of Mahātripurasundarī; therein, first, those of Kāmeśvara.

I worship Kāmeśvara, who possesses the luster of ten million moons, who bears the moon upon his crest, who has three eyes, and whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as the trident and the sword.

Of this mantra of Śrī Kāmeśvara: the seer (ṛṣi) is Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter (chandas) is Paṅkti; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Kāmeśvara; the seed-syllable (bīja) is Śrīṃ; the power (śakti) is Hrīṃ; the pin (kīlaka) is Klīṃ.
The application for the domestic rite: flowers in the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.

Then, the fire sacrifice (*homa*) is performed with the root mantra. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* is uttered for the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*). By means of this mantra-homage, the respectful offering of restraint (*nirodhārgha*) is made. Now, Bālā.

May the young maiden, who colors the quarters of space with networks of rosy rays, who holds a rosary, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, and who is enriched by other excellent hands resting upon a full-blown white lotus— may she, whose form is eternal bliss, dwell forever within my heart.
She possesses the splendor of a thousand suns risen all at once, and her hands bear the marks of the knowledge-gesture, the rosary, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.

I worship you, Tripurā, whose lotus-face is adorned with three blue-lotus eyes and who is radiant with a necklace of pearls. I meditate upon the youthful goddess (Bālā) seated upon a reddish lotus, clad in red garments, adorned with the crescent moon, resembling the rising sun, and possessing three eyes; her hands bestowing knowledge, a rosary, and the gesture of granting fearlessness. Holding a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary in her hands, she is worshipped by all the gods and possesses a red rosary.
This Bālā Tripurā, who rests upon the moon-crested Lord, should be meditated upon by all as the object of meditation.
Of this mantra of the illustrious Bālātripurasundarī: the seer is the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is Paṅkti, and the deity is the illustrious Bālātripurasundarī.

Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), sauḥ is the power (śakti), and klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). This is the application (viniyoga) in the fire sacrifice (homa). [The offering of] flowers in the fire, the invocation (āvāhana), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
Aiṃ! We know the Goddess Tripurā; we meditate upon Vāgīśvarī; may She, Liberation, inspire us. (3)
p.
55) The root [mantra] is 108 [times]. Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇā).

I meditate upon you in my heart, adorned with a moon-crest and a digit of the autumnal moon, white as the autumnal moon, consisting of fifty syllables, three-eyed, and holding in your lotus-hands a book,
a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and the gesture of exposition.
With the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is offered. Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
"By means of this mantra-homa [one should worship] the gross [form], seated upon a red lotus, with the luster of a pomegranate flower."
With four hands joined by a noose, a goad, a bow, and an arrow; three-eyed and single-faced; most beautiful, adorned with various ornaments.
One should contemplate the form of the Goddess, endowed with every kind of auspicious beauty.

Of this mantra of the venerable Tripurabhairavī: Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandaḥ), the venerable Fifteen-Syllabled Tripurabhairavī is the deity (devatā), Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Sauḥ is the power (śakti), Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

The ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*. [Offer] a flower into the fire; perform the invocation, the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth. *Aiṃ tripurādevyai vidmahe klīṃ kāmeśvaryai dhīmahi sauḥ tannaḥ śaktiḥ pracodayāt* || 3 ||
The root. || 108 ||

She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, wears saffron-colored silk, a garland upon her head, and has breasts smeared with red pigment; she holds a rosary, the Vidyā, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā.
I bow to the Goddess who stands upon a lotus, her lotus-like face graced by three eyes, holding a firm lotus in her hands, and adorned with a crown of jewels and the cool-rayed moon.
At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" is used for the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa) with this mantra-homa.
Then [there is] Mahātripurasundarī.
Then [he beheld] the goddess, who resembles a lotus, reddened by the rays of the rising sun, like a hibiscus flower, and comparable to the pomegranate blossom.
Resembling a ruby and appearing like saffron-water, she was adorned with a shimmering crown, rubies, and a network of tiny bells.
Her lotus-like face is like a swarm of black bees; on her forehead is a soft fillet, slightly curved like a half-moon.
She whose eyebrows are shaped like the Pināka bow, the supreme sovereign of fair-browed women, her eyes rolling with the playful movement of waves of bliss and joy.
She wore golden earrings spread with a mass of shimmering rays, and the full expanse of her beautiful cheeks surpassed the orb of the moon, the nectar-essence of the world.
Her nose was perfectly defined by the lines of creation fashioned by Viśvakarman and others; her lips, resembling the bimba fruit of copper and coral, were like nectar.
She surpassed the ocean of the essence of sweetness with the charm of her smile; endowed with incomparable qualities, she was graced by the region of her chin.
The great goddess Kambugrīvā, with arms as graceful as lotus stalks, her delicate lotus-hands having the appearance of red lotuses.
The surface of the sky was overspread by the radiance of the nails of her lotus-like hands, and her uplifted breasts were adorned with strings of pearls.
Her waist was beautifully adorned with the three folds of skin, and she was graced by a navel that resembled an eddy in the river of loveliness.
Her hips were adorned with a girdle fashioned from priceless jewels; the line of hair upon her rounded buttocks was like a choice goad for the elephant of her pelvic orb.
The sovereign lady, whose thighs were as delicate as the graceful trunk of a plantain tree, was adorned with a pair of shanks resembling the stems of a plantain tree in their beauty.
To her whose lotus feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels of those who bow before her;

She possesses a luster that dispels the heat of suffering, resembling the brilliance of a hundred moons; her feet possess the hue of the *aḍima* flower, surpassing the redness of vermilion and the Sindhu river.
Clad in red garments and adorned with red ornaments, she has four arms and three eyes, and she holds five arrows and a bow.
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with camphor and whole nutmegs; her body was crimsoned with the intense saffron and musk of the great deer.
Abounding in all the splendor of amorous attire, adorned with every ornament, she is the one who generates delight for the world and brings joy to the universe.
The Goddess who attracts the world, whose form is the cause of the universe, who consists of all mantras, and who is beautiful with every auspicious fortune.
Having meditated upon the Mahātripuramudrā—which consists of all prosperity, is eternal, and resembles supreme bliss—one should [perform the invocation] with the Āvāhanamudrā.
By means of the previously mentioned external *subhagā* mantra, joined with the *namaskāra*, the supreme practitioner [worships] Mahātripurasundarī.

I worship in my heart Kāmeśvarī, who embodies the form of Śiva and Śakti, who holds a crescent moon, whose beauty is like molten gold, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire, and who bears with her lovely arms the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a sacred book, and a rosary of teeth.

One should meditate upon the Sovereign of sovereigns, seated upon a lotus, robed in crimson, possessing a reddish glow, with three eyes, and adorned with a jeweled crown and beautiful gem-studded earrings. She is radiant, flashing with hands that hold a noose, a goad, the bow of Love, and an arrow. Her body is illuminated by a shimmering pearl necklace rolling upon the slopes of her full and lofty breasts. She possesses a luster equal to ten million suns, has four arms, and three eyes.
I worship Śivā, who tears asunder the noose, goad, bow, and arrows; I worship Lalitā, who is crimson in hue and holds in her hands the bow, arrow, noose, and goad.
O Smara, meditate upon her who rests smilingly on the lap of Kāmarāja, held firmly in his embrace.
Of this King of Mantras of the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī.
The seer is Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

Śrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). The application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering of] flowers in the fire; the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth.
Aiṃ, we know the Goddess Tripurā; Klīṃ, may we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; Sauḥ, may that Śakti impel us toward union with Klīnna. || 3 ||
The fire-oblation is performed with the root mantra. || 108 ||

Śrāṃ Aiṃ Ṭhoṃ! Salutation to the Heart, whose essence is the power of omniscience; Svāhā! Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ! Salutation to the Head, whose essence is the power of eternal contentment; Svāhā! Śrūṃ Sauḥ Aiṃ! Vauṣaṭ Svāhā to the Tuft (Śikhā), whose essence is the power of absolute independence!
Śreṃ eṃ 1? To the armor (kavaca) whose essence is the power of absolute freedom, hūṃ svāhā! Śrauṃ klīṃ 2 To the eyes whose essence is the eternally undecaying power, vaṣaṭ svāhā!
ŚRAḤ SAUḤ SAKALA HRĪṂ ANANTĀSTRATAḤ ŚAKTYĀTMANE ASTRĀYA PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. This is the root-homa according to another method.
To the three peaks within the Great Wheel whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, in the Bindu, to the sandals of Ambā Mahātripurasundarī, obeisance, svāhā!
Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ. To the heart 3, to the head 3, to the crest 3, to the armor 3, to the eyes 3, to the weapon.
The fire-oblation (homa) is performed as previously described for the three cities (tripurī). Now, the meditation for the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti):

One should meditate upon the face of Śrī, which is like the full moon with a tilaka of musk on her slightly reddened limbs; she is encircled by garlands of caṇpaka, mālatī, and jasmine, and her crescent-moon crown is adorned with them.
I bow to the pair of lotus feet of Sundarī, whose lofty breasts are adorned with pearl necklaces, who is decorated with red garments, and who resounds with the tinkling of her anklets.

Her form is established in three syllables and three groups of three syllables, and she is resplendent with the three supreme mudrās; with her four arms, she holds a goad, a noose, a multitude of arrows, and a bow.

May the Mother of the World be victorious with the three goddesses, as well as with the eight goddesses renowned as the guardians of the directions, and with the eight [goddesses] numbering eight Vasus;
at the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" constitutes the full oblation (pūrṇā). Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa).

Having thus performed the recitation according to his capacity at the outset, the best of practitioners—the Brāhmaṇa—should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with ten parts of the total, using fuel-sticks made from the Brahma-tree.
Or likewise, with Svayambhū flowers smeared with the three sweets according to the prescribed rite, this Vidyā then becomes effective for the pacification of the flood of great obstacles.
O Goddess, you are the bestower of all desires, and the giver of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In a vulva-shaped pit, one shaped like the female organ, circular, or half-moon-shaped; or in a nine-triangle wheel, a square, or an eight-petaled lotus.

In a vulva-shaped pit (yoni-kuṇḍa), one becomes eloquent, and there is the supreme attraction of the female organ (bhaga); in a circular pit, there is prosperity (lakṣmī), and in a half-moon shape, all three [qualities] arise.
In a triangular or nine-cornered *kuṇḍa*, the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) arises; in a quadrangular one, there shall be peace, prosperity, nourishment, and freedom from disease.
O King, when there is a lotus-mark, all prosperity arises before long; O fortunate one, by means of the eight-spoked wheel, one shall obtain the desired fruit.
O Supreme Goddess, by offering oblations of Mallikā, Mālatī, and Jātī flowers soaked in clarified butter and honey, even a mute person becomes a lord of speech.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, by offering parched grain mixed with curd, honey, and milk, one is liberated from diseases and the fears of karma, death, and the like.
By this mantra-homa, may the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī— along with her Lord, her retinue, her limbs, her command, her weapons, and her attendants—
the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, being worshipped with supreme service, be satisfied.
Now follows the pure sesame oblation (śuddha-tilahoma) for the Sarasvatī mantras.
Her face, arms, feet, belly, and chest are adorned with the fifty distinct letters; she possesses radiant matted hair, wears a digit of the moon, and is as white as the moon or a jasmine flower.

I bow to that Bhāratī, who holds a rosary, a water-pot, and a book in her excellent hands, who has three eyes, who sits upon a lotus, whose appearance is pure, and who bears the weight of full breasts and hips.
She is endowed with four arms; in one hand she holds a rosary made of crystal beads, while another holds a white lotus, and yet another a cup and a book.
May that Goddess of Speech, whose radiance shines on all sides like jasmine, the moon, a conch, and crystal, dwell forever, ever-gracious, within our mouths.
Of this mantra of the venerable Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī.

Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi). Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ). Śrīmātṛkāsarasvatī is the deity (devatā). Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja). Hrīṃ is the power (śakti). Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka). The application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
An offering of flowers into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) begins with *hrāṃ* and so forth. "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. (3)
Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī, svāhā. || 108 ||

The *pūrṇāhuti* at the end of the root mantra is *vauṣaṭ*. Alternatively: Of this venerable *Mātṛkā-sarasvatī* mantra, Brahmā is the *ṛṣi*; *gāyatrī* is the meter; the venerable *Mātṛkā-sarasvatī* is the deity; the consonants are the seeds (*bījas*); the vowels are the powers (*śaktis*); and the seed of Brahmā is the pin (*kīlaka*).
The application at home.

With the hand, perform the *śuddhatilahoma* (oblation of pure sesame seeds). [Perform] the invocation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ tatsavitur vareṇyam bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt* || 3 || *hsauḥ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ*
Haṃ Kṣaṃ Hsauḥ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Svāhā! || 108 ||
Aṃ kaṃ 5 āṃ to the heart; iṃ caṃ 5 īṃ to the head; uṃ ṭaṃ 5 ūṃ to the crest-lock; eṃ taṃ 5 aiṃ to the armor; oṃ paṃ 5 auṃ to the eyes;
aṃ yaṃ thuṃ aḥ phaṭ to the weapon.
Now follows the second [verse].
Hsvūṃ, obeisance to Vidyāvidyeśvarī, svāhā. (108) Oṃ rkṣjhrūṃ, obeisance to Vāgbhaveśvarī, svāhā. (108) Oṃ hrīṃ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech, svāhā. (108)
Now, Vaikharī: Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, obeisance and svāhā to Vaikharī, the Mistress of Speech, the bestower of speech. || 108 ||
For all [these], there is an oblation of pure sesame seeds.

The meditation on Pūrṇā: [I meditate upon] Vāṇī, whose face is radiant like the full moon, who possesses the luster of a mass of camphor, whose head is marked by the crescent moon, and who respectfully holds [various objects] with her own hands.

I worship her who is mounted upon a white bull, whose string of beads is a lute, who is rich in her own nature yet free from impurity, whose breasts are the four Vedas, whose body is adorned with divine ornaments,
and who is endowed with four arms— holding in one hand a crystal rosary, in another a white lotus,
in another a wine-cup, and in the other a book.
May that Goddess of Speech, who shines with a luster resembling jasmine, the moon, a conch shell, and crystal, dwell forever, ever-gracious, within my mouth.
The full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is performed with the root mantra followed by "vauṣaṭ"; this is the libation (tarpaṇa).

By this mantra-homa, the evils of misfortune, disease, untimely death, lack of intelligence, low birth, poverty, and so forth shall not touch [the practitioner] for seven future births; Sarasvatī becomes present, and may Sarasvatī, together with her retinue and all her limbs, be pleased—may she be pleased!
Now, Bhavānī.

I salute Sadāśiva, the Lord of Consciousness, who is radiant like ten million moons, a conch, a lotus, a mass of snow, and a string of pearls; who holds in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a bow, an arrow, and a trident; who sits in the lotus posture, is adorned with a digit of the moon, and whose body is embraced by Śivā.
Of this glorious Sadāśiva mantra: Īśvara is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda).
The deity is Śrī Sadāśiva; *hauṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *oṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). This is the application (*viniyoga*) in the fire-oblation (*homa*).

An offering of flowers in the fire; the invocation and the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth; the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with *hrīṃ* and so on: *oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ sadāśivāya namaḥ*. (108)
Cessation is established upon the surface of the earth, the mother of all beings, and in water; it is established in knowledge, in fire, and in the mind as stainless tranquility.

The past, the limit of the peak, and the five digits in the sky [are] well-known as the Kilas; above even those, one should contemplate Paraśiva. At the end of the root-mantra, "vauṣaṭ" is the full oblation (pūrṇā). This is the libation (tarpaṇa) and the respectful offering for the obstruction (nirodhārgha). Now, [the ritual] for Bhavānī:

One should always meditate upon the consort of Śiva, whose head is adorned with a crescent moon, who is stainless and worshipped by the immortals, holding a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a blood-filled skull-cup in her hands; she is red with body-unguents, girdle, and ornaments, possesses three eyes, and has limbs ever-tremulous with passion.
She has a face like the rising moon, four arms, red eyes, holds a lotus, and possesses a pure smile.

I worship Bhavānī in my heart, who stands upon a corpse and is marked by a sword, a spear, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness. Regarding this Śrī Bhavānī mantra: Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); Śrī Bhavānī is the deity (devatā); Śrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Hūṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
Offering of flowers into the fire; invocation and the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth;

the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with *śrāṃ hrāṃ* and other syllables; the oblation of pure sesame seeds with the hand. [The Gāyatrī]: "We know Durgā, we meditate upon Kārttāyanī; may that Bhavānī inspire us. (3)

Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ bhavāni hūṃ phaṭ svāhā || 108 || Oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ śrīṃ Caṇḍayogīśvarī, O Bhavānī who grants the boons of all desires, O bestower of all good fortune, hrīṃ namaḥ svāhā || 108 ||
Then follows the Pūrṇā: [one should meditate on the Goddess] who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, four arms, and three eyes.
I worship Śivā, who holds a noose, a goad, an arrow, and a bow.
With the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ," is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*). By means of this mantra-homa, there is the *nirodhārgha* (the offering for cessation).
Now, Kubjikā.

May the venerable Kubjikā protect us—she who, rising from the peak of the five-hooded, three-cornered mountain within my heart-cave, emerges with speed through the five spaces and the ten lords, possessing the color of the low-born, the eternal Mistress of Speech (Vāgīśvarī), the Leader of the Kula, and Vidalinī; she who is adorned by the five *praṇavas* and encompasses the entire Kula. [Offer] a flower into the fire.
Invocation, water for the feet, and so forth; self-assignment (nyāsa); the Gāyatrī.
Aiṃ! We know the Lord Mitra; we meditate upon Śrīkaṇṭha; may that perfection impel us. || 3 ||
An oblation of sesame seeds combined with the three sweets.
By offering oblations of sesame seeds mixed with flower buds and anointed with the three sweets, even a man who is devoid of beauty attains a state of personal fortune.

[This is] ghee with the three sweets, milk, and sugar. Thus it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Milk, honey, and ghee—these together are known as the 'three sweets' (*trimadhura*). Alternatively, the 'three sweets' [consist of] ghee, honey, and sugar. Then follows the root mantra.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ | Khphreṃ Hsyūṃ Bhagavati Ambe Hskhphreṃ Shkhphreṃ Śrīkubjike Hsrāṃ Hsrīṃ Hsrūṃ Ṅa Ña Ṇa Name Aghoramukhe Chāṃ Chīṃ Kiṇi Kiṇi Vicche Hsvlūṃ Khchreṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Aiṃ | 32 Svāhā ||
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Khchreṃ Hmvūṃ, obeisance to the Heart, Svāhā, O Blessed Mother! Hskhphreṃ Śrīṃ Kubjike, [obeisance] to the Head.
Hsrāṃ Hsrīṃ Hsrūṃ Ṅa Ña Ṇa Name, Vauṣaṭ Svāhā, [obeisance] to the Tuft. Aghoramukhe, Hūṃ Svāhā, [obeisance] to the Armor.
Chāṃ chīṃ, vaṣaṭ svāhā to the eyes; kiṇi kiṇi vicce, phaṭ svāhā to the weapon (astra).
Now follows the meditation on Pūrṇā.

Holding an arrow, a bow, a book, a rosary, the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a conch, and an utpala lotus; and bearing a khaṭvāṅga staff and a skull from her center—she is Kubjikāmbo, who sustains the world.
The libation.
Aiṃ! I salute that Kuleśvara-tattva, which is the supreme light, augmented by the three coils of bliss, and which is the great expansion consisting of six aspects.
Pervaded by five and nine, radiant with the imperishable supreme bliss, that which transcends the born and is the support of the Kula—I bow to that circle of gurus.
That supreme-non-supreme knowledge, which is auspicious and consists of the nature of formlessness—I am that very power of Rudra, who is composed of twenty-two syllables.
She is the Supreme, she is the Subtle, she is Raudrī who illuminates; by the mere remembrance of her, the cage of the body trembles.
There is no science equal to his, nor is there a family equal to his; there is no illusion equal to his, nor is there a lineage equal to his.
Just as clarified butter is the essence of curd, as the moon is among the stars, as Takṣaka is among the serpents, so is that lord among those who move through the sky.
The mantra is said to consist of five syllables, while the vidyā consists of twenty-two syllables; the deity has seven or nine clusters of syllables, and is called the Guru.
I bow to that abode of Śrīdhara, which is of the nature of an unbroken circle, wherein reside the gods, Manu, and the sciences; it has been illuminated by my gurus.
By this mantra-homa, may the goddess Śrī Kubjikā of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), together with her limbs, her retinue, and her faces, be pleased; may she be well-pleased.
Now, the fourfold Pratyāṅgirā: first among them is Siddhalakṣmī.

I bow to the Goddess, white as pure crystal, five-faced and three-eyed, endowed with ten arms and adorned all around with jeweled necklaces; she who carries in her right hands the *kādyam*, the sword, the goad, the *sṛṇam*, the trident of most brilliant luster, the essence of essences, the supreme and unsurpassed [arrow], the *utkhaṭvāṅga*, the hard and formidable *ṭaṅka*, the vigorous *ūrja*, the *aṭaṅka*, and the noose.
And a book consisting of the essence of the nectar of knowledge, as well as the gesture of fearlessness.
I bow to Siddhalakṣmī, who bears the desirable [objects] with her beautiful, auspicious hands, who is worshipped like a bimba fruit, and who has placed her feet upon a lotus and a corpse.
Of this mantra of Śrī Siddhalakṣmī: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (cchanda); Śrī Siddhalakṣmī is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja);
Hūṃ is the power (śakti); Krīṃ is the pin (kīlaka).
The application for the domestic ritual: flowers in the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one’s own body and limbs. Then, the *Gāyatrī*. An oblation (*homa*) of clarified butter and *guggulu* resin with the sacrificial ladle (*śruva*). Twenty-one times, seven times, or three times. Oṃ, salutation to all the *Siddhi-yoginīs*, salutation! Salutation to all the Mothers of Accomplishment (*Siddhimātṛs*), to her who is gladdened by eternally arisen bliss, to the sovereign lady of the entire circle and lineage (*Kulanāyikā*), to the Blessed One Caṇḍakāpālinī. It is as follows: Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hāṃ pheṃ kṣoṃ kroṃ, salutation! Oṃ, O Supreme Swan (*Paramahaṃsinī*), O Nirvāṇa...

O Goddess, who bestows the path, who pacifies calamities and obstacles, who shatters all enemies, misfortunes, and afflictions, who is the boat for crossing the ocean of all disasters, and who crushes all foes—come, come! Laugh, laugh! Play, play! O devourer of human blood, entrails, and fat, subdue my enemies! Eat them, eat them! Pierce them with your trident!
Cut them, cut them! Strike them with your sword! Rend them, rend them! Until you have accomplished all my desires, O most compassionate Blessed One!

O you who assume the form of Mahābhairava, who are saluted by the best of the thirty gods, O Mother of all mantras, O Goddess who is compassionate toward those who bow before you, O Mahākālī, destroyer of Time (Kāla), *huṃ* 3!
Be gracious; make [her] afflicted with passion, O daughter of the gods and asuras, *hrīṃ śrīṃ hāṃ hūṃ phaṭ* 3 *svāhā* 1!

Ā 20, O Supreme Haṃsinī, *namaḥ svāhā* to the heart; to the giver of the path to Nirvāṇa, *namaḥ* to the head; to the pacifier of calamities and misfortunes, *namaḥ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); to the destroyer of all evils, portents, and afflictions, *namaḥ* to the armor (*kavaca*); to the boat for crossing the ocean of all disasters, *namaḥ* to the two eyes; to the crusher of all enemies, *phaṭ svāhā* to the weapon (*astra*). || 290 ||
Now, the Mantramātṛkā.
Resembling the equal luster and appearance of the black cuckoo, the Indian cuckoo, and other such birds; she has four arms, one face, and is radiant with three eyes.
She is mounted upon a white *preta*, holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a bell; she holds a noose and a mallet in her hands, and is greedy for fat and blood.

I bow to the Mother of Mantras, who is most exalted, most formidable, possessing ninety waves, and slender-waisted; she who shatters all mechanical devices. Ā 3. [Offer] a flower into the fire for the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth. Now, the root mantra:

Oṃ hrīṃ jjāṃ huṃ hreṃ! O you who consist of great illusion, eater of blood, entrails, and flesh, mounted upon a great *preta*, with a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), skull-cup, noose, and mallet in hand: shatter, shatter all magical devices; crush, crush them; pulverize, pulverize them; rend, rend them!
For the destruction of him who hates us and whom we hate—*phaṭ* three times, *svāhā*. This is the root mantra.
Now, the Mantra-Ḍāmarikā; the third [chapter].
An elephant hide, a gourd, and a lute; a trident, an axe, and the banner of a vulture; a human skull, a heart upon the lotus of the chest, a dagger, a sword, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
With two pairs of hands she held a garland of cuckoos and swarms of bees; then, with another two hands placed upon her breasts, she took the forms of a donkey and a boar.
She holds a mantra-destroying noose and sits upon a great corpse that is dark yet white; she possesses eighteen creeper-like arms, a slender form, and fierce, distorted fangs.
I bow to the blazing Mantraḍāmarikā of those adorned with serpents.
The flower offering into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.

Oṃ phaḥ phaḥ hā hā kha 2 kha 2 khā hi 2, devour (grasa) all mantras! Destroy (nāśaya) the rites of others—sorcery, exorcism, subjugation, attraction, hatred, killing, expulsion, and so forth! Hrīṃ phreṃ phreṃ phuḥ phuḥ phuḥ phaṭ phuḥ phaṭ namaḥ svāhā! Ā! Now follows the Saptakoṭīśvarī.
(61) Her meditation is unmanifest. He says that it is seen somewhere [in the scriptures].

Seated upon a throne of seven severed heads intent on devouring, marked by the single-bell mudrā, she flashes forth from the blazing wheel of the foundation (ādhāracakra) as seven tongues of the fire of cosmic dissolution; she who does not abide within the ultimate interior, the sound that is the end of all, the Mistress of Speech in the great void— that goddess Ghoracaṇḍā, the sovereign of seventy million mantras, may she destroy our misfortune.
An offering of flowers into the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth; then the Gāyatrī mantra.
Oṃ, may we know her who is formless; may we meditate upon her who transcends power; may that Goddess inspire us. (Recite three times)
Now, the root [text].
Oṃ kaḥ saḥ caṇḍini saḥ kaḥ saptakoṭīśvarī ambāpādukābhyo namaḥ svāhā. (Recite) seven times. Offer oblations according to one's capacity.
Now, the visualization for the full oblation (pūrṇā).

For that man on earth who meditates upon her—who has a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and other implements, whose lotus-hands hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a trident, an axe, a noose, a goad, a sword, a boon-granting gesture, and a book; who has five faces and ten arms, and is seated upon Śiva—fear does not exist for him. Now, the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Oṃ! O Maheśvara, whose crest is adorned with the digit of the self-born Parameśa; O blue-throated one, mounted upon the bull, bearer of the Gaṅgā!
Speak of the goddess Pratyaṅgirā, the destroyer of fear in the three worlds, who effortlessly neutralizes mechanical devices, mantras, and malevolent incantations.
She brings about peace and prosperity, is pure, and devours the calamities caused by the planets; she pacifies spirits and *vetālas*, and destroys *kṛtyās* and *kharkhodas*.
It is common to all, formidable, the destroyer of all calamities; it is the most excellent bestower of all prosperity and the granter of all success.
When this [knowledge] is merely understood, sovereign power proceeds; within the belly of the world, there exists no other knowledge more terrible than this.
O Mahādeva, O Leader of the Universe, it is indeed through your grace that I have this name.
The Lord said:
The supreme Vidyā, which bestows happiness, good fortune, and liberation, has been extracted with two hundred and ninety syllables.
This knowledge is a great lore (mahāvidyā) known by the name Trailokyamohinī; she is renowned as Lakṣmīśvarī, the bringer of an abundance of many enjoyments.
Mahālakṣmī is remembered as the great beloved who bestows all prosperity; O Goddess of gods, in this stream there is no other equal to her.

She should be known as the pacifier of misfortune and the crusher of wicked poverty; she is the pacifier of the evils of the Kali age and bad dreams, and the destroyer of calamities arising from one's birth.
It pacifies the calamities of kings and destroys wicked bandits; it is always effective in the terrible fear of the forest and in the peril of lions and tigers.
Gaurī is always to be remembered in times of uneven terrain, dense forests, fire, fear born of spirits or epilepsy, and the danger of malevolent magic or crossing over a bridge.
When remembered even once, she burns away a flood of sins like a heap of straw; having destroyed this entire world, it is now filled with those who know Brahman.

A killer of a guru, a killer of a father, O Goddess, a killer of a mother, and likewise a killer of an embryo—such a person is liberated from sins such as the uprooting of eyes and others, even from a single transgression.
It is traditionally taught that this [mantra] liberates one instantly from sins, great sins (mahāpātaka), minor sins (upapātaka), and even the kings of sins (pātakarāja).
O Goddess, by once summoning the Mistress of Knowledge, who is the most excellent of all, one shall become possessed of fortune, illustrious, and always intoxicated like a lord of kings.

O Goddess of the Suras, by circumambulating it three times, one performs a pilgrimage bath at all sacred sites extending to the seven oceans, including those born of the divine earth and the intermediate space.
O Goddess, one becomes as if bathed at all sacred fords; there is no need for deliberation on this point. O Sovereign of the Gods, after seven recitations, one is initiated into all mandalas.
O fortunate one, by ten recitations, the thread always becomes auspicious; by twenty-seven recitations, it is born within the circle of the Mothers.
The practitioner, the lord of the kings of heroes, just like Bhairava the leader, shall himself become like Bhairava by means of one hundred and eight recitations.

That which does not exist, one cannot strive for; that which exists, one can surely accomplish through effort. [Such a person] can always effortlessly destroy even the thunderbolt-like leaves of the *nibhāḍa* tree.
O Goddess, by performing this at the three junctions of the day for seven days, there is no doubt that a living being will be liberated from bondage, even if it has been spoken of by Time (Kāla).
When there is an intermediate space between wealth, grain, and land for the practitioner, he remains forever like the divine Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Lakṣmī.
Likewise, by the mere recollection of this king of practitioners, and by this mantra-homa, may Siddhalakṣmī be forever pleased.
Now follows the libation (tarpaṇa) with the Mantra-mātṛkā.
O Great Goddess, seventy-seven crores of mantras are born from her body; therefore, she is the Mother of Mantras (Mantramātṛkā).
By this mantra-homa, may the Mantramātṛkā be pleased. Other mantras, such as those beginning with 'ka' for exorcism (uccāṭana) and so forth, have also been performed.
Then, merely by being remembered, Mantra-Ḍāmarikā slays [the obstacles]. By this mantra-homa, may Mantra-Ḍāmarikā be pleased.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim [the rite] that destroys deceivers; by the mere worship of which one is liberated from all suffering.
By worshipping her, a person goes to a solitary celestial abode; for that is the dwelling place of the lords of the gods, the locus of all enjoyments.
Whatever one desires, one obtains that without a doubt; one will not be hated in the world, but will be beloved even by women.
Neither floods, nor famines and the like, nor enemies can overcome him who always remembers the supreme Goddess, the Mistress of seventy million [mantras].
She is the seven-syllabled one, most terrible Caṇḍakālī of great power, who delights in a seat of seven severed heads and traverses a path through as many worlds.
Through the mere worship of the Goddess, one attains poetic skill, the knowledge of astrology, and mastery of the great grammars; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess of the Gods, whatever object exists in the world that is worthy of being honored—if one desires it, one obtains it directly; there is no doubt in this.
By this mantra-homa, may the Mistress of the seventy million be pleased; may she be pleased.
Thus may Pratyangirā, together with her retinue, her attendants, her faces, and her Śivās, be pleased; may they be satisfied.
Now, Caṇḍikā.
Adorned with a trident, skull-cup, sword, dagger, khaṭvāṅga, and severed head in her left and right hands,

resplendent with nine colors, possessing a single face with a brilliance like the fire at the end of an aeon, the Goddess stands upon a corpse, surrounded by her female messengers; may the Blessed Lady establish her presence within my own abode.
