[Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the invocation and other rites. We know the one whose essence is Yamāntaka; we meditate upon Kālarātri; may Caṇḍī inspire us. (3)
Oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍī kāpālinyai svāhā || 108 || Mahālakṣmī ambā pādukābhyo namaḥ svāhā || 108 ||
Hrīṃ hṛdayāya; Caṇḍi śirase; Kāpālinyai śikhāyai; Mālini kavacāya; Svā netratrayāya; Hā astrāya. [Perform] the oblation of grapes and clarified butter.
Now follows the mantra-worship of Mālinī in Pūrvāṣāḍhā.

O Lord of the Yugas, O Lord of Men, O Son, I bow to that certain supreme Śakti who has issued from the abode of the trident within the lunar light of the Self, and who is the lotus-like, triple-city Śakti within the innate abode of consciousness. [Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the invocation and other rites. Then, the root mantra.
Oṃ hrīṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ.
Laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Mātṛkā.
Oṃ na ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ tha ca dhaṃ raṃ ṇa u ū ba ka kha ga gha ṅa i ava bhaya du ḍha ṭha jha ña ja ra ṭa pa kala āsa āḥ haṣa kṣama śa aṃ u e ai o au da pha hrīṃ, homage to Mālinī, svāhā!
Thus ends the root mantra of Mālinī.
Now, [the mantra] of Lakṣmī:
Her lotus-feet are resplendent, beautified by tinkling anklets, and she is adorned with the luster of a girdle-station studded with clusters of the nine gems.
Its waistband was set with pearls, rubies, and lapis lazuli.
She was radiant in her center, adorned with three folds of skin, and graced with a navel as beautiful as the whirlpools of the river Ganges.
Her breasts were adorned with sandalwood paste, camphor, and saffron; she was more magnificent than a pearl necklace released from a rain cloud.
She wore an exquisite upper garment made of fine silk, and was adorned with armlets of lapis lazuli set in refined gold.
Her lotus-like hands are enriched with ruby-studded, shimmering golden bracelets; she is adorned with finger-rings set with fragments of rubies.
Adorned with necklaces and armlets fashioned from refined gold, her neck was as white as a conch shell, decorated with various and diverse ornaments.
Adorned with jeweled earrings shaped like the rising sun, and graced by shimmering golden ear-ornaments inlaid with gems.
Her lovely sprout-like lips possess the beauty of a *japā* flower and a *vidruma* coral; she is adorned with a row of teeth resembling the seeds of a pomegranate fruit.
Her face resembled the moon freed from the blackness of a spot; her creeper-like eyebrows possessed the graceful movement of the god of love’s bow held in his hand.
Her nose was like the splendor of a blooming lotus flower, shining with victory; the radiance of her forehead surpassed the beauty of the moon.
Her lotus-face was adorned with a tilaka of musk endowed with the fragrance of a *sārṣapa* flower, and her abundant locks of hair were graced by the play of swarms of intoxicated bees.
She bore the beauty of *pārijāta* flowers bound in her loosened hair-knots; her head was marked by a crown fashioned from priceless gems.
The abode of all loveliness, the dwelling place of the splendor of grace, the birthplace of all radiances, the adorned Mahālakṣmī who captivates the mind.
Thus, eating sacrificial food and having conquered his senses, he should meditate upon the Goddess— resembling the rising sun, with a smiling face, clad in red garments,
and anointed with unguents.
Holding with her hands a water-pot, a vessel for distribution, a goad, and a sacrificial ladle.
Seated upon a lotus, with firm breasts like two lotuses, this ocean of beauty, the bestower of the fruits of all desires at every moment—
she is this Śrī Jyeṣṭhalakṣmī.
Of this mantra of Śrī Mahālakṣmī, Śyavana is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Śrī Mahālakṣmī is the deity (devatā). *Śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja);

*hrīṃ* is the power (śakti); *oṃ* is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa), with flowers in the fire, and for the invocation (āvāhana), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Lakṣmī Mahālakṣmī, bestower of all desires, giver of all good fortune, grant what is desired! O you who are all-pervading, formless, and the dispeller of all suffering and delusion! Hrīṃ saḥ svāhā! || 108 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Lakṣmi Mahālakṣmi, obeisance to the heart, svāhā! Oṃ, O bestower of all desires, O giver of all auspiciousness, obeisance to the head, svāhā!

Oṃ, grant what is desired, twice; to the crest, vauṣaṭ svāhā! Oṃ, all-pervading, formless one, to the armor, hūṃ svāhā! Oṃ, dispeller of all suffering and delusion, to the two eyes, vaṣaṭ svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ svāhā; to the weapon, phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ.
Śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ, O Mahālakṣmī, be gracious, be gracious! Śrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā. || 108 ||
Śrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ, O Mahālakṣmī, be gracious, be gracious! Śrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā. || 108 ||
Now, the Fortune of Wealth.

I perpetually bow with supreme devotion to the Goddess Lakṣmī, whose face is red, who holds a royal skull-cup in her hand, who possesses three eyes, who is intent on her divine play, who moves upon the king of elephants, who is saluted by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, and who is served by gods and Siddhas.
Oṃ hūṃ! Give me wealth from the hands of all; hūṃ! Obeisance to Vittalakṣmī! || 108 ||
Then Lakṣmī.

[He beheld] Lakṣmī, whose hips rest upon a lotus seat, whose three eyes are like the sun and moon, whose radiance is like the rays of the rising sun, and who holds a conch, a lotus, and a sword in her hands.
I bow with devotion to her whose limbs are adorned with various pearls and gems, who has two arms, and who eternally bestows the fruits of the three worlds.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Śrī, the dweller in the lotus. || 108 ||
Now, the royal fortune.
Seated upon the pericarp of a lotus, her eyes as broad as lotus petals, with a face like a blossoming lotus and eyes like the sun and moon.
Her two breasts were resplendent with garlands of priceless jewels; she was adorned with the beauty of various ornaments and possessed eight graceful, vine-like arms.
She holds the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, and spear as her excellent weapons, her creeper-like body adorned with the syllables of the root mantra.
Lakṣmī, seated upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa, who deludes the three worlds, who is endowed with all auspiciousness, and who bestows the state of sovereignty.

One should meditate upon the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the Royal Fortune (Rājyalakṣmī), who is the family deity (Kuladevatā). Regarding this mantra of Śrī Rājyalakṣmī: Śiva is the seer (Ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (Chandas), Śrī Rājyalakṣmī is the deity (Devatā), *Śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (Bīja), *Sauḥ* is the power (Śakti), and *Aiṃ* is the pin (Kīlaka). Its application (Viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (*Homa*). [The ritual involves] offering flowers into the fire, the invocation, the water for the feet (*Pādya*), and so forth; and the ritual placement (*Nyāsa*) beginning with *Hrāṃ Śrāṃ*, etc.
Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, O Rājyalakṣmī, grant what is desired; svāhā! || 108 ||
Then, for all [the goddesses], it is full.

I bow to Lakṣmī, who in one place holds a full water-pot with her two hands, in another has her pure elephant, and elsewhere holds the conch, discus, and lotus in her palms; who in one place has her hands busy with chowries over the body of her beloved, and in another bears the goad and the noose. At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" is for the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa) with this mantra and the fire-oblation (homā). This is the water-offering (argha) for the removal of obstacles.
Now follows the Bhāgyādhirohiṇī [meter].

Holding a noose and a goad in her heart, bearing a skull and three eyes, possessing four arms, and providing protection; seated upon a lotus with her two feet placed [therein], may the Great Goddess—who is called the "Ascension of Fortune"—protect us. [Offer] a flower into the fire. [Perform] the invocation and other rites.
Śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śobhāvati bhāgyabhūte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (Verse 14). The full oblation with the root mantra; the libation.
O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of her, even a man who has committed every evil deed, though born into the family of a slave, will undoubtedly be granted a kingdom.
By this mantra-homa, the offering for cessation (*nirodhārgha*). Now, [the rite of] Bhagamālinī.

May the divine Bhagamālinī bestow prosperity upon me—she who holds in her hands the noose, the goad, the rosary, the string, and the book; she who, possessing wondrous power, bestows [boons] day and night; she who has three eyes, whose left corner is graced by the light of the moon, and who is the Goddess Śrī herself. [Offering] a flower in the southeast (Agni). Invocation, water for the feet, and so forth:
*hsrl hrīṃ*, obeisance to the sandals of Ambā Bhagamālinī in the cave of Pūrṇagiri, *svāhā*. *hsrl hrīṃ hya*, [obeisance] to the head in the cave of Pūrṇagiri.

Bhagamālinī is the *śikhā* (crown), Ambā is the *kavaca* (armor), Pādu is the *netra* (eyes), and *kebhyas svāhā* is the *astra* (weapon). With the root mantra, perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the water-offering for withdrawal (*nirodhārgha*). Now, Tārā.
I worship Śiva, who has just been born, who possesses three eyes and a moon upon his crown, whose radiance is like that of the rising sun, and who holds a sword and a blue lotus.

Of this Śrīsadyojāta mantra: Maheśvara is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); the venerable Tāreśvara Sadyojāta is the deity (devatā); hsau is the seed-syllable (bīja); hrīṃ is the power (śakti); oṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) begins with *hsau*, and so forth.
Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, svāhā. || 108 ||
The full oblation and so forth are performed with the root mantra.

I worship Tārā, the three-eyed goddess, who is the sole protector of the three worlds, eternally intent on their preservation; she is adorned with serpents, possesses the cool luster of the moon, shines with the radiance of a conch, has her neck encircled by a collar of pearls and gems, wears red garments, and holds a trident, lotus, sword, and mace, while being honored by hosts of gods led by Vaikuṇṭha. Of this mantra of the Blessed Goddess Śrī Tārā, Akṣobhya is the seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is Bṛhatī. The deity is Śrīmadekajaṭā. Hūṃ is the seed-syllable. Phaṭ is the power. Strī is the pin. This is the application in the fire sacrifice (homa).
Oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ krīṃ hūṃ ugratāre sauḥ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ svāhā || 108 ||

Pūrṇā: She stands upon the chest of a supine corpse, possessing four arms and three eyes; her face is resonant with a terrible *aṭṭahāsa* laugh, and her lotus-like mouth is fierce with the sound of *huṃ*.
She holds a sword, a blue lotus, a spear, and a skull-cup. She is short in stature, with a dark face, and her single tuft of hair is tawny.
I bow to Ugratārā, who is surrounded by fierce nāgas. At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" is for the full oblation (pūrṇā).
With this mantra-homa and so forth, [one performs] the libation (tarpaṇa). This is the offering for cessation (nirodhārgha). Now, [the worship of] Bhuvaneśvarī.

I worship here in the heart-lotus the three-eyed Bhuvaneśvarī, whose face resembles a thousand rising suns, who has full breasts, who rests upon a lotus, and who respectfully holds with her arms the goad, the noose, the book, and the *jaya* [mudrā]; she who is eternally praised with salutations and hymns by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Indra, and the sages; and who is the source of all prayers and chants. Of this mantra of the illustrious Bhuvaneśvarī: Śakti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*).

The deity is Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī. Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja). Śrīṃ is the power (śakti). Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). The application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa). [Offer] a flower into the fire;
perform the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites.
Oṃ hrīṃ bhuvaneśvaryai namaḥ svāhā || 108 || Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ bhuvaneśvaryai namaḥ svāhā || 108 ||

*Hrāṃ hyaḥ*. Then the *pūrṇā*: "I meditate upon the Mistress of the World (*Bhuvaneśī*), who possesses the luster of the rising sun, wears a crown of moons, has lofty breasts, and is endowed with three eyes; she has a smiling face and holds in her hands the gestures of granting boons (*varada*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the noose (*pāśa*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhīti*). At the end of the root mantra, recite *vauṣaṭ*; this is the *pūrṇā*. With this, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the *nirodhārghya* [are performed].
(p. 66) Now, [the mantra of] Mātaṅgī.

I worship Mātaṅgī, who wears ornaments of rubies, whose face is smiling, who has the luster of a blue lotus, whose lotus-feet are beautified with lovely red lac, and who shines with three eyes; she is intent on playing the lute, praised by the gods, dark as the plumage of a peacock, crowned with the moon, and her mouth is filled with betel.

Her crest is marked by the crescent moon; she has three eyes and the radiance of ten million moons and suns; her girdle is bound with thousands of various jewels; and she is seated upon a corpse throne.
I shall always meditate in my heart upon the blessed Mātaṅginī, the captivating one, who eternally bears a conch, a tomara-spear, a paṭṭisa-club, and a pair of lotuses in her hands.

Of this mantra of Śrī Ucchiṣṭamātaṅgī: Mataṅga is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); the deity is the auspicious Ucchiṣṭamātaṅgī Sumukhī; Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering of] a flower in the fire, the invocation (āvāhana), and so forth.
Aiṃ klīṃ, O Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī, O fair-faced Goddess, O Great Piśācinī, hrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā. || 108 ||
Oṃ krīṃ śrīṃ prīṃ prīṃ cchriṃ ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālini mātaṅgi devi krīṃ ṭhaḥ hrīṃ ṭhaḥ aiṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā. || 108 ||

The goddess, sixteen years of age, lying upon a corpse, reeling from the intoxicating essence of honey, with a dark-limbed body like a red lotus, possessing full breasts and adorned with a garland of *guñjā* berries.
One should meditate upon the Blessed One Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī within the lotus of the mind, holding a skull-bowl filled with impurities and a sharp knife in her two hands.
At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" constitutes the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). With this, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed. This is the *nirodhārgha*. Now, the *bhīḍā*.
She resembles the mass of radiance from the rising moon's rays; seated upon a full-blown lotus, she is to be praised for her four noble arms, which hold a lute, a conch, a goad, and an axe.
I bow to Bhīḍā-Bhavānī, who wears a pearl necklace and a crest-jewel upon her chest, who carries a vessel of liquor, whose face is smiling,
and who bestows the desired fruits upon her practitioners.

I worship in my mind the fierce goddess with disheveled hair, who has a face like the orb of the full moon, three eyes, white garments, and a crescent moon as her crest-ornament; she sits upon the seat of Śiva and holds a sword and a skull-cup in her hands.
*Bhīṃ Bhāṃ* (mantra).

Of this mantra of the illustrious Bhīḍābhagavatī: Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (cchanda), the illustrious Bhīḍābhagavatī is the deity (devatā), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Śrīṃ is the power (śakti), Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] a flower into the fire; [perform] the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsraiṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, O Bhīḍābhagavatī, you who have the form of a swan (haṃsa), svāhā! (Recite 108 times.)

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *hrāṃ* and so forth. For this [mantra], Bhairava is the deity, the *triṣṭubh* is the meter, and the venerable Bhīḍā is the goddess. *Aiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *sauḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *klīṃ* is the key (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*). [One offers] a flower in the fire; [then follows] the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ bhaiṃ bhīḍā bhagavatyai namaḥ svāhā. || 108 ||
Sauḥ bhīḍā bhagavati haṃsarūpiṇi svāhā. || 108 ||
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *hsrāṃ* and so forth. The *pūrṇā* [offering]. With this, the libation (*tarpaṇa*). The *nirodhārgha* [offering].
Now, [the worship] of Dakṣiṇakālikā and others.

I bow to him whose crown is adorned with the illustrious crescent moon, whose face is encircled by flames, who holds a conch, a lotus, a sword, and a mace, who is three-eyed, and who is praised by Brahmā and the other gods.

One should meditate upon Lord Bhairava, who resembles fire, as he contemplates the Goddess—the dark-hued Bhagavatī—situated on the fourth petal; one should likewise meditate upon the Goddess Mahākālī.
The Lord, whose face is like the moon and whose splendor is like ten million rising suns, is adorned with a crown and necklaces.
In my heart, I remember that Bhairavanāyaka, the beloved Kāla, the sole friend of his devotees.
Dark-complexioned, large-bodied, Mahākāla with three eyes, blue-throated, possessed of great splendor, and adorned with three eyes.
The deity holds a sword and a shield, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he holds a trident in his hand and carries a khaṭvāṅga staff, the leader of mantras.
One should always remember the Lord of Gods, the all-pervading Bhairava, who holds a Pināka bow in his hand, carries a tomara-weapon, and wields a spear and a sharp-edged blade.
With such meditation, one should contemplate the All-pervading Lord with the mind: Mahārudra, the Great Time, dwelling in the cremation ground, naked as the directions.

In his left hands he holds a skull-cup and a hand-drum, and in his right hands a trident and a khaṭvāṅga; though his limbs are adorned with serpents, he is further embellished with ashes, bones, and jewels.
Standing in the midst of a blazing fire and resting upon a bed of ashes, one should place the Kālikā mantra, reversed, upon the heart.
Having prepared for one another food to be drunk, chewed, and sucked, O Goddess, one should thus worship with devotion; then all perfections arise.
Of this mantra of the glorious Mahākālabhairava.
Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi). Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ). Śrī Mahākāla is the deity (devatā). Hūṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja). Hrīṃ is the power (śakti). Svāhā is the pin (kīlaka).
The application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering of] flowers in the fire, the invocation (āvāhana), and so forth.
HŪṂ HŪṂ MAHĀKĀLA PRASĪDA 2 HRĪṂ HRĪṂ SVĀHĀ || 108 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ juṃ saḥ, obeisance to Mahākālabhairava. || 108 ||

Oṃ; thus the six-limbed [mantra]. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ vaiśvānaryai svāhā. Oṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ yamaghaṇṭāyai svāhā. At the end of the root mantra, vauṣaṭ; thus is the full oblation (pūrṇā). With this, the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed.
Now follows the Nityākālī [mantra].
She holds a noose and a goad, is fierce in appearance, and has her hands raised with a bow and arrow.
She holds in her hands these five arrows: delusion, withering, liquefaction, moistening, and likewise killing.

I bow to the Goddess, who resides in the center of the triangle and is as red as lac. [Offer] a flower in the southeast (Agni), followed by the invocation (āvāhana), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ śrūḥ svāhā || 108 ||
*Vapa*. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). The libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having meditated in this way and performed worship, one becomes equal to Kāmadeva. By his very sight, the practitioner shall agitate the entire universe.
"By this" refers to the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now follows Bhadrakālī.
Her lotus-face was serene, her playful eyes were like smoke, she was clad in blue garments, and she wore pearl ornaments, tinkling bells, and small bells.
Her lips were like bimba fruit, reddish as young sprouts; she was adorned with a white bodice, endowed with priceless jewels, and wore a divine crescent moon.
Adorned with the flowers of the veins of various primordial lights, she possesses hips girt by a girdle that has the luster of a row of autumn clouds.
The practitioner, having meditated upon the goddess Bhadrakālī—who possesses pearl-like teeth and dark pupils, and who resembles the rising sun—should [proceed].

Emaciated by hunger, with sunken eyes, her face soiled with soot, and her hair disheveled— neither an elephant nor a woman, yet insatiable— I shall make this entire world my single morsel. Holding in both hands a fierce noose resembling a blazing flame of fire, may Bhadrakālī, with teeth like jambūnada gold, consume me and strike fear into me.
I am never satiated by her who holds the shaven head of the Creator of the universe upon the palm of her lotus-hand, who laughs, and who is always devouring all people.
I meditate upon Bhadrakālī, who is dark-complexioned like Viṣṇu and Īśa, the destroyer of the host of enemies, who holds a blazing trident in her praiseworthy arms, who is as white as fresh water,
and who is seated in the midst of corpses.

Of this mantra of the venerable Bhadrakālī: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi); Cyavana is the seer; Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); the venerable Bhadrakālī is the deity (devatā); *bhaiṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *hūṃ* is the power (śakti); *svāhā* is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering of] flowers in the fire, the invocation (āvāhana), and so forth.
KṚĪM KṚĪM KṚĪM HŪM HŪM HRĪM HRĪM BHAIṂ, let us know Bhadrakālī; KṚĪM HŪM HRĪM BHAIṂ, let us meditate upon the consort of Bhadrakāla; BHAIṂ HRĪM 2 HŪM 2 KṚĪM 2 SVĀHĀ—may that Bhadrakālī inspire us. 3.
KṚĪṂ 3 HŪṂ 2 HRĪṂ 2 BHAIRṂ BHADRAKĀLI BHAIRṂ HRĪṂ 3 HŪṂ 2 KṚĪṂ 3 SVĀHĀ || 108 ||
KṚĪM 3 HṚ (Heart); HĪM 2 HŪM 2 ŚIRA (Head); BHAIṂ Bhadrakālī Śikhā (Crest).
Hrīṃ hrīṃ bhaiṃ ka | Hūṃ hūṃ to the eyes | Krīṃ 3 to the weapon. Now, the full oblation (pūrṇā).

I worship the Goddess Bhadrakālī, who is dark-complexioned with a dark face, possessing a tremulous body and eyes like deep hollows; she who manifests in twenty-one forms, intoxicated by the wine of honey, clad in red garments; holding Brahmā, a skull, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and a girdle in her hands; radiant with the god of love, stationed upon a corpse within the lotus of my heart—Bhaiṃ! I worship you.
With the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ"—thus is the full oblation (pūrṇā). With this [mantra] is the libation (tarpaṇa). This is the offering for the restraint (nirodhārghaḥ).
Now follows Dakṣiṇakālī.

In her upper left hand she holds a sword, and below it in the palm of that same hand a severed head; in her right hands, she displays the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting—she who removes the sins of the three worlds is Kālikā.
Having recited the syllables of his name and meditated upon his power and majesty, O Mother, these eight perfections of the Three-Eyed Lord become manifest in their hands as they look upon your face.
And she who resembles crushed collyrium, lying upon the corpse of Prameta, her lotus-like face smiling with streams of flowing blood.
She possessed a pair of full and elevated breasts and full, elevated hips.
To the south [is she] whose limbs have loose hair, who delights in being naked, who is seated upon the corpse of Mahākāla, and who stands above the bliss of Smara.
She was graced by yoginīs whose faces were radiant with natural, thick smiles, who were intoxicated with joy and reeling with passion, and whose eyes were slightly reddened and wide open.
She has two corpses as head-ornaments, is radiant with a forehead-mark of sindūra and coral, and is beautified by jeweled earrings fashioned from five skulls.
She was enriched with various excellent jewels and adorned with diverse ornaments; her right side was decorated with a conch and armlets fashioned from the bones of Śiva.
In one place she was mounted upon the chest of Śiva, licking him; in another, she was laughing repeatedly with a loud laugh while devouring morsels of the flesh of a corpse.

Holding a sword and a severed head in her left hands, and bestowing fearlessness and the boon-granting gesture in her right; she is jagged-toothed, exceedingly fierce, and terrifying with her violent roar.
She was surrounded by auspicious yet terrible-looking [attendants], the destroyer of fear, uttering "Do not fear! Do not fear! to her devoted worshippers with her formidable voices.

"What do you say? What do you say? 'I shall bestow [it]'—thus she speaks. Of this mantra of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Uṣṇik is the meter (chanda); Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā is the deity (devatā).

*Hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Hūṃ* is the power (*śakti*). *Klīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire sacrifice (*homa*). [The offering of] flowers into the fire begins with the invocation (*āvāhana*). We know Kālikā; we meditate upon her who dwells in the cremation ground; may that Ghorī inspire us. || 3 ||
KṚĪṂ 3 HŪṂ 2 HRĪṂ 2 DAKṢIṆE KĀLIKE KṚĪṂ 3 HŪṂ 2 HRĪṂ 2 SVĀHĀ || 108 ||
O Goddess of terrible form and great roar, who brings about the destruction of all enemies; O Goddess, bestower of boons upon your devotees, protect me, who have come to you for refuge!
O Goddess worshipped by the Suras and Asuras, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas, O Goddess who removes the sin of dullness! (p. 69) 2.
To her who is endowed with a mass of matted locks and who resembles a flickering tongue.
The goddess who brings about swift intelligence. || 3 ||
Obeisance to you who possess a gentle form, a wrathful form, and a fierce form; obeisance to you whose form is creation—protect us! 4.
O Goddess who is affectionate toward your devotees, you destroy the dullness of the dull-witted; O Protectress, take away my delusion! 5.
O Goddess consisting of the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ*, beloved of offerings and fire-sacrifices, homage to you! O Ugratārā, homage to you always; protect us! 6.
Grant me intelligence, grant me fame, and always grant me the power of poetic composition. O Goddess, remove my delusion; protect me! 7.
O Tārā, composed of compassion, saluted by the hosts of gods beginning with Indra, whose face is like the lord of stars (the moon), protect me! 8.

The man who recites this on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth day attains perfection within six months; there is no need for deliberation on this point. One seeking liberation obtains liberation, one seeking wealth obtains wealth, and one seeking knowledge obtains knowledge such as logic and grammar. The man who constantly recites this hymn finds that his enemies perish and he becomes possessed of great wisdom.
Whether in times of affliction, in battle, during a great portent, or in the face of great fear, for one who recites this hymn, happiness is certain.
With the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*). With "by this," and so forth, is the obstructive water offering (*nirodhārgha*).
Now follows Śyāmā.

I meditate upon that dark-complexioned Kṛṣṇā, whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by the three worlds, who bears a form resembling her consort, and possesses three eyes; she carries a trident, a sword, and a great Śārṅga bow in her own arms, and sits upon a corpse as her seat. [Offer] a flower into the fire.
Śrīṃ hrīṃ krāṃ krīṃ kraṃ kraiṃ krauṃ kraḥ, O Śyāmā, essence of nectar! Release me from the curse of Kṛṣṇa; cause the nectar to flow forth, flow forth!
At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). The libation (*tarpaṇa*).
(p. 69) Now, the fourth [state].
I worship the Goddess Turiyā, who bears matted locks upon her head bound with crescents of various jewels; who holds a noose and a lotus; who is white as the moon;

who is two-armed yet possesses two hands [in her embrace]; who is auspicious; whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire; whose face is smiling; who is seated upon a corpse; and who is saluted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Flowers and other offerings [are placed] in the fire.
Oṃ drūṃ trāṃ troṃ, salutation to Mahāturyā. || 108 ||

*Trāṃ hya*, at the end of the root mantra *vauṣaṭ*; this is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). [Perform] the libations and so forth. Now, Chinnamastā: I meditate upon the Blessed Goddess Chinnamastikā, who grants the desires of her devotees; she who holds a trident, a goad, a noose, a flute, a mace, a lotus, and a skull-cup; who is mounted upon a deer, whose hair is beautifully bound, who possesses the brilliance of ten million rising suns, who is adorned with a mass of highly precious jewels set in flames, and who is radiant with the pride of the God of Love.
Always in the heart-lotus.

Of this mantra of the illustrious Chinnamastā: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Samrāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ); the illustrious Chinnamastā is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa). [One offers] flowers and other substances into the fire:
"We know her who is radiant; we meditate upon Chinnamastā; may that Goddess impel us. 3.
Oṃ, salutation to the Severed-Headed One. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ cchrīṃ cchinnamasti calacchrīṃ phaṭ svāhā.

In her left hand she holds a severed neck, and in her other right hand a large knife; she stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, with garments reaching to the ends of the quarters and her mass of hair tied up.
She drinks the stream of blood gushing from her own severed head, and she shines with three eyes that gleam like the rising sun.
At the end of the root mantra, with "vauṣaṭ," there is the full oblation, the libation, and so forth. Now, [the ritual for] Kālarātrī.
She has four arms, holding a trident, a lotus, a noose, and a goad; she is smoke-colored, possesses three eyes, and holds a trident and a lotus.
I meditate upon the Great Goddess, seated upon a lion-throne, clad in yellow garments, and bearing the form of Kālarātri.

Of this mantra of the illustrious Kālarātrī: Dakṣa is the seer (ṛṣi), Jagatī is the meter (cchandaḥ), Māyārājñī dwelling in the city of Alarka is the deity (devatā), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Namaḥ is the power (śakti), Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ drūṃ! O Kāmeśvarī, captivator of the minds of all people, paralyzer of all mouths, subjugator of all kings, destroyer of all the wicked, attractor of all women and men: break the fetters! Devour all enemies! Destroy those who hate us! Paralyze everyone! With the weapon of delusion, drive away those who bear us ill-will! Bring everything under control! Svāhā! Grant everything! Grant everything!
Salutation to Kālarātrikāminī, the Sovereign of the Gaṇas. || 108 ||
At the end of the root mantra, with "vauṣaṭ," perform the full oblation, libation, and so forth. Then [worship] Bagalāmukhī.

In the center, upon a jeweled pavilion and altar within the ocean of nectar, I meditate on the Goddess seated upon a lion throne, of a deep yellow hue. Her limbs are adorned with yellow garments and various ornaments; she holds the tongue of her enemy with a mallet. With her left hand, the Goddess seizes the tip of the tongue while crushing the enemy; with her right hand, she strikes with a mace. Adorned with yellow robes, I meditate on the two-armed Goddess.
Of this mantra of the illustrious Bagalāmukhī.

Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi). The Uṣṇik metre (chandaḥ). The venerable Bagalāmukhī is the deity (devatā). Hlīṃ is the seed-syllable (bījaṃ). Svāhā is the power (śaktiḥ). Oṃ is the pin (kīlakam). This is the application (viniyoga) in the fire sacrifice (homa). [Offer] flowers and other substances into the fire.
Oṃ hlīṃ, O Bagalāmukhī, paralyze the speech and the mouths of all the wicked; nail down their tongues; destroy their intellect! Hlīṃ oṃ svāhā. || 108 ||
Narada is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra]. Paṅkti is the meter (chanda). Śrī Bagalāmukhī is the deity (devatā). Klīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja). Svāhā is the power (śakti).
The application is for the rite of homa to paralyze the faces of all enemies. [Offer] flowers and other substances into the fire.
Oṃ hlīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Bagalāmukhi, paralyze speech and the mouth, pin down the tongue, destroy the intellect! Klīṃ oṃ svāhā!

Oṃ hlīṃ hrīṃ hya | Śrī Bagalāmukhī, paralyze the head; paralyze speech, [paralyze] the face, [paralyze] the tuft of hair (śikhā); nail down the tongue, [protect] the armor (kavaca); destroy the intellect, [protect] the eyes; klīṃ oṃ svāhā, for the weapon (astra). [This is] the full oblation (pūrṇā).

I bow to Śivā, who is seated upon a lion-throne, wearing a girdle of variously bound jewels and yellow garments, the bestower of fortune, radiant with heat, and possessing eyes like the rays of the sun and moon.

O son of Gaṅgā, I worship in my heart the Goddess Bagalāmukhī, who resembles the Ganges, whose limbs are illuminated by precious jewels, who always grants all desires and bestows devotion. At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ," [perform] the full oblation, libations, and so forth. Now, Vajrayoginī.
I worship the auspicious Vajrayoginī, who has the moon, fire, and sun as her eyes, who holds a noose and a goad, who possesses two arms, and who stands amidst a lion.
Flowers and other offerings are placed in the fire.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Vajrayoginī! || 108 ||
Śrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ aiṃ vajravairocanīye huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā || 108 ||
At the end of the root mantra, with "vauṣaṭ," there is the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the satiation (tarpaṇa), and so forth. Now follows the food-oblation (annapūrṇā).

I worship the Blessed Lady, the remover of the suffering of worldly existence— she who is red in hue, clad in variegated garments, adorned with a crescent moon upon her crest, ever intent on bestowing food, bowed by the weight of her breasts, dancing, wearing ornaments of the crescent moon, and joyful at the sight [of her devotee].
She shines with the radiance of the morning sun, adorned with jeweled armlets and necklaces; her beautiful feet and heels are radiant, and she holds a bowl and a ladle in her lotus-like hands.
I bow to her who wears a garland expanded by the rays of the jewels in her crown, who has three eyes, who drinks sweet honey, and who is filled with food.

I meditate in my heart upon that Annapūrṇā, who has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, two arms, and three eyes; she carries a trident and a rosary in her two hands, sits upon a deer, and has a serpent as her sacred thread.

Of this mantra of the illustrious Annapūrṇā: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi); Virāṭ is the meter (chanda); the blessed goddess Śrī Annapūrṇā is the deity (devatā). Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Svāhā is the power (śakti); Namaḥ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa) for the purpose of bringing food into presence. "May we know food itself; may we meditate upon it as that which is eaten by itself; may the Ordainer himself impel us toward it. (3)

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Great Goddess Annapūrṇā, svāhā! (108) Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Great Goddess Annapūrṇā, svāhā! (108) Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Great Goddess Annapūrṇā, svāhā! (108) Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Great Goddess Annapūrṇā; grant me my desired food, grant it, svāhā! (108) Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, to the Great Goddess who is preeminent in granting food, svāhā! (108)

The syllable *Tāraṃ* (Om), followed by *hṛt* (Namaḥ), then the word *Bhagavati*, then the word *Māheśvari*, then *Annapūrṇe*, and finally the pair of *Ṭha*s (Svāhā); this is the seventeen-syllable mantra. Then follows the *pūrṇā*.

In the midst of Mandāraka, Haricandana, and Pārijāta trees, and in the center of a pavilion and altar made of moonstones—O Girijā, whose crest is the crescent moon, whose forehead is beautiful, and who has six eyes on her three faces, grant alms to me who am hungry! At the end of the root mantra, say *vauṣaṭ*. Then follows the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the final respectful offering (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, the jackal.

I bow to the Goddess who dwells in Śiva—she who is praised by jackals, ruddy in hue, three-eyed, single-faced, and possessing eight arms; who holds the moon, a trident, a bell, a goad, a skull-cup, a small bell, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a book in her hands. [Offer flowers and other items] into the fire.
We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Him who has the form of Śiva. May that Goddess inspire us. 3.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Goddess Śivā, svāhā! || 108 ||
With the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, one performs the full oblation (*pūrṇā*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the offering of the vessel of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
And then there is Cāmuṇḍā.
Holding a sword, discus, mace, spear, bow, iron club, trident, *bhuśuṇḍī*, a severed head, and a conch in her hands, she has three eyes and is adorned with ornaments on every limb.
I worship Mahākālī, who has the luster of a sapphire and ten faces, she whom the lotus-born Brahmā praised when Hari was asleep, so that he might slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

One should worship Mahālakṣmī, who stands upon a lotus, possesses the luster of coral, tramples an elephant, and holds in her hands a rosary, axe, goad, thunderbolt, lotus, bow, sickle, staff, spear, sword, shield, lotus, bell, wine-vessel, trident, noose, and mirror. She also holds a bell, trident, plough, conch, mace, discus, bow, and arrow in her lotus-like hands.
Possessing a luster equal to a thick, fresh, and shining mass of lightning.
I worship here Sarasvatī, who emerged from the body of Gaurī, who is the foundational support of the three worlds, the Great One (Mahā), and the destroyer of demons such as Śumbha.
Of this glorious Navārṇava mantra: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (ṛṣis); Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh are the meters (chandāṃsi);
Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī are the deities (devatās); Nandā, Śākaṃbarī, and Bhīmā are the powers (śaktis).
*Raktadantikā*, *Durgā*, and *Bhrāmī* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Fire, Wind, and Sun are the principles (*tattva*).
The application at home: [offering] a flower in the fire; the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, [salutation] to Cāmuṇḍā, Vicce! || 108 ||
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce. Thus are the limbs (of the mantra). At the end of the root mantra, [pronounce] vauṣaṭ. This is the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa).

The offering for cessation (*nirodha*). Then, all sixty-four Yoginīs are fond of blood, meat, milk, and wine; they are fond of quarrels, clamor, song, and dance. They are small, young, mature, and old; they are black as bees, fire-colored, and moon-colored; they have distorted eyes, distorted teeth, loose hair, and terrifying tongues; they utter extremely subtle, sweet, and deep *ghurghura* sounds; they are steady and fickle, peaceful and fierce.

The twenty-seven *yogas* beginning with Viṣkambha, the twenty-eight *nakṣatras* beginning with Aśvinī, the twelve *rāśis* beginning with Aries, the nine planets beginning with the Sun, Nārasiṃha, Vīra, Kṣetrapāla, Maṇibhadra, Sāhilya, and others— [all] four-armed, capable of destroying [enemies] through peaceful, fierce, deceptive, or forceful means, adorned with divine garments and ornaments, and equipped with weapons such as the goad, skull-cup, sword, hook, trident, conch, discus, mace, spear, bow, and thunderbolt.
One should meditate on [the deity] surrounded by yakṣas. [The offering of] flowers into the fire, the invocation, and so forth.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hsauḥ namaḥ svāhā. || 108 ||

To Brahmāṇī || 1 || To Kaumārī 2, to Vārāhī 3, to Śāṅkarī 4, to Indrāṇī 5, to Kaṅkālī 6, to Karālī 7, to Kālī 8, to Mahākālī 9, to Cāmuṇḍā 10, to Jvālāmukhī 11, to Kāmākhyā 12, to Kapālinī 13, to Bhadrakālī 14, to Durgā 15. (p. 72b)

To Ambikā 16, to Lalitā 17, to Gaurī 18, to Sumaṅgalā 19, to Rauhiṇī 20, to Kapilā 21, to Śūlakarā 22, to Kuṇḍalinī 23, to Tripurā 24, to Kurukulyā 25, to Bhairavī 26, to Bhadrā 27, to Candrāvalī 28, to Nārasiṃhī 29, to Nirañjanā 30,
to Hemakānti 31, to Pretāsanā 32, to Aiśānī 33, to Vaiśvānarī 34, to Vaiṣṇavī 35, to Vināyakī 36, and to Yamaghaṇṭā 37.
To Harisiddhi (38), Sarasvatī (39), Tottalā (40), Vandī (41), Śaṅkhinī (42), Padminī (43),

Citriṇī (44), Vāruṇī (45), Nārāyaṇī (46), Vanadevī (47), Yamabhaginī (48), Sūryaputrī (49), Śītalā (50), Kṛṣṇā (51), Vārāhī (52), Raktākṣī (53), Kālārātrī (54), Ākāśī (55), Śreṣṭhinī (56), Jayā (57), Vijayā (58), and Dhūmrāvatī (59).
To Vāgīśvarī (60), to Kātyāyanī (61), to Agnihotrī (62), to Vajreśvarī (63), to Mahāvidyā (64), and to Raiśvarī (65).
At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ"—thus is the full oblation (pūrṇā). Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa).
The sixty-four yoginīs known as the Kāmarūpikas, when worshipped, worship in return and shall always bestow the power of the earth.
"By this mantra-homa," thus [said] Bhairavī. Then Bhairavī:

Uttering this mantra known as Vāgbhava— which consists of the syllables *ka*, *a*, *na*, *ta*, *da*, *bha*, *u*, *ta*, followed by the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and joined with the stable letter (*sthiravarṇa*) preceded by the first ocean (*jaladhi*)— the best of men, while reciting it on earth, attains perfection in speech that is naturally sweet and eloquent.

The mantra called Kāma is said to consist of the letter *kā* (the end of *kānta*), joined with the fifth letter of the preceding *kula* (*pa*), followed by the letter *na* (the end of *netra*), and combined with the staff (*daṇḍa*) at its end; reciting this mantra directly causes the agitation of the world.
p.

73) When joined with *dantī*, it is *daṇḍi*; the entire family known as Saṅkṣobhana is accomplished for him. Through constant recitation, the eight qualities and the power of moving through the sky (*khacaratā*) are attained. [The ritual] in the fire [involves] flowers, invocation, and so forth.
Hsaiṃ Hsklīṃ Hsauḥ, salutation to Mahābhairavī. || 108 ||

At the end of the root [mantra], "vauṣaṭ" constitutes the full oblation (pūrṇā). If the tradition of Bhairava, which begins with Akula, were to be preceded by Kula according to the teachers, [then it would be as follows].
"That very [Vidyā], which bestows swift fruit upon the earth and is exceedingly precious among the common folk, is called Vidyā. Thus ends the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, the Nine Durgās.

I meditate upon that Daughter of the Mountain, who possesses a luster like the sun joined with the moon, who wears a crescent moon as her crown, has four arms, is clad in red garments, and whose eyes are the fire, the sun, and the moon; she is the bestower of boons. Of this Śrī Śailaputrī mantra: Mahākālabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); Śrī Śailaputrī is the deity (devatā); *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *sauḥ* is the power (śakti); *namas* is the binding of the directions (digbandha).
Oṃ miti; the pin (kīlaka) is applied in the fire-sacrifice (homa). [Offering] a flower into the fire. Invocation and so forth: "We know Kāmadhātrī, we meditate upon Śailaputrī;
may Śailā inspire us. (3)

Oṃ hrīṃ sauḥ śailaputri śrīṃ svāhā || 108 || Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ sauḥ sauḥ eṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śailaputryai namaḥ svāhā || 108 || Oṃ hrīṃ—thus is the *nyāsa*. At the end of the root mantra, with "vauṣaṭ," is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). By means of this mantra-oblation, there is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the *nirodhārghya* offering. Now, [the mantra for] Brahmacāriṇī:

Worship in your heart that maiden who observes the vow of celibacy—she who holds the lotus, the sword, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she whose face is like the moon, who bears the moon upon her crest, who is auspicious, who is ruddy with ornaments, and who possesses three eyes.

Of this mantra of the venerable Brahmacāriṇī: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); the venerable Brahmacāriṇī is the deity (devatā); Śrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] a flower into the fire; perform the invocation and other rites:
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ saḥ brahmacāriṇī aiṃ phaṭ svāhā. [Recite] one hundred and eight times.
At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). With this [mantra], the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed. This is the *nirodhārgha* (the offering for cessation).
Now, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā.

I worship in my heart Śrī Caṇḍaghaṇṭā— the youthful one with a full face like the moon joined with its crescent, three-eyed, smiling and serene, holding in her hands a conch, a lotus, a bow, and a jar of nectar.

Of this mantra of Śrī Caṇḍaghaṇṭā: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); Śrī Caṇḍaghaṇṭā is the deity (devatā); Klīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Sauḥ is the power (śakti); Śrīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [The offering of] flowers in the fire; the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth.
Oṃ klīṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ sauḥ, obeisance to Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, svāhā! || 108 ||

The placement [of mantras] begins with *klām* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* is used for the full oblation; by means of this, there is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Then follows Kuṣmāṇḍī.
For this [mantra], there is no separate meditation (*dhyāna*). For this mantra of Śrī Kuṣmāṇḍī: Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*); Śrī Kuṣmāṇḍī is the deity (*devatā*);

*krīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *oṃ* is the pinning-syllable (*kīlaka*); and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*). [The offering of] flowers in the fire, the invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth [are performed].
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ krīṃ, obeisance to Kūṣmāṇḍī, svāhā! || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *krāṃ* and so forth. With the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, the full oblation (*pūrṇā*) is performed. With this [mantra], the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for the restraint (*nirodhārgha*) are made. Now follows Skandamātā.

I worship Bhavānī, whose face possesses the splendor of ten million moons, who has three eyes, is clad in saffron-colored garments, sits upon a lion-throne, is joined by the faces of serpents and other beings,
and is endowed with the *hṛcchanda* [mudrā] in her heart.

Of this mantra of Śrī Skandamātā: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Triṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Śrī Skandamātā is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hauḥ is the power (śakti); Haḥ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa), with flowers in the fire, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hauḥ, to Skandamātṛ, haḥ haḥ phaṭ svāhā. || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *hrāṃ* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* constitutes the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). With this [mantra], the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed. This is the *nrodha*-arghya. Now follows Kātyāyanī.
I bow to the auspicious Kātyāyanī, whose limbs blaze with the light of a thousand suns, who has three eyes, who is radiant in red garments, who possesses four arms, and who is united with Śiva.

Of this mantra of Śrī Kātyāyanī: Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Śrī Kātyāyanī is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Oṃ Śakti Svāhā is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa), beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) of flowers into the fire.

Oṃ hrīṃ kātyāyanyai namaḥ svāhā || 108 || The placement [of mantras] (nyāsa) begins with hrāṃ and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" is used for the full oblation (pūrṇā). With this, there is the libation (tarpaṇa) and the offering of the vessel of restraint (nirodhārgha). Now, [the mantra of] Kālarātrī:

I meditate in my mind upon the illustrious Kālarātri, who possesses the luster of a fresh cloud, the moon, and fire for her eyes; who holds a mace and a lotus in her hands and smiles; who is clad in yellow garments, and whose limbs are radiant with loosened locks of hair.

Of this mantra of Śrī Kālarātrī: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); Śrī Kālarātrī is the deity (devatā); Śrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ kālarātri klīṃ aiṃ saḥ phaṭ svāhā || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *srāṃ hrāṃ* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* is used for the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). With this [mantra], one performs the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the respectful offering for the restraint (*nirodhārgha*). Now, Mahāgaurī: I worship Mahāgaurī, who is auspicious, possessing four arms and three eyes, whose radiance is equal to the rising sun, and who wears a crown of moonbeams.

Of this mantra of Śrī Mahāgaurī: Karālabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Śrī Mahāgaurī is the deity (devatā); Oṃ Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Oṃ Sauḥ is the power (śakti); Oṃ Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa) with flowers and other offerings in the fire.
Śrīṃ Oṃ Sauḥ Gīṃ Gūṃ, obeisance to Mahāgaurī, svāhā. || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with "gām" and so forth. With the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, the full oblation (*pūrṇā*) is performed. With this [mantra], the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is offered. This is the *argha* for the restraint (*nirodhārgha*). Now follows Devadūtī.

I bow to the illustrious Devadūtī, who possesses the luster of the moon’s orb, whose eyes are like blue lotuses, and whose slender body is of refined gold; she is clad in white garments, has three eyes, and though two-armed, she has entered into the state of a *preta*.

Of this mantra of the illustrious Devadūtī: Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); the illustrious Devadūtī is the deity (devatā). Klīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Sauḥ is the power (śakti), and Śrīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa) with flowers and other offerings. [One should offer] flowers and so forth into the fire.
Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ devadūti śrīṃ phaṭ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā || 108 ||
With the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, the full oblation (*pūrṇā*) is offered; with this [mantra], the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for cessation (*nirodhārgha*) are performed.
By this mantra-homa, may the Blessed Navadurgā—along with her weapons, her vehicle, her retinue, and her attendants—be pleased; may they be gratified.
(p. 75) Now, Gaṅgā.
Holding a lotus with its stalk in one hand and bearing a lotus in both hands, she has hands in the gesture of granting boons, is white in color, has moving limbs, and is borne by a sea-monster.
Of this Śrī Gaṅgā mantra, Maheśvara is the seer (ṛṣi) and Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas).
The venerable Goddess Gaṅgā is the deity; this is the application in the fire-oblation (homa).
Oṃ, salutation to Śivā, to Nārāyaṇī, to Daśahārā; svāhā! || 108 ||
At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" is for the full oblation (pūrṇā); with this, the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed.
Now, the Vitastā.
I take refuge in the Vitastā, who holds a rosary, a lotus, a mirror, and a water-pot in her hands, and who sits upon a seat of fish and a lotus.
Flowers and so forth [are offered] into the fire.
Sāṃ Sīṃ Saḥ, obeisance and svāhā to the blessed Goddess Vitastā. || 108 ||
With the root mantra, [uttering] "vauṣaṭ," there is the full oblation, the satiation, and the offering for the seal of restraint.
Now follows the fire-oblation for the ten world-protectors.

Therein, first, that of Indra: [I salute] the unborn Lord, who resembles the splendor of ten thousand rising suns, who is radiant with the rays from the jewels of his crown, who holds a lotus and a thunderbolt in his hands, and who is beautiful with a thousand eyes.
One should meditate upon that god Indra, the guardian of the eastern quarter, whose chest is covered with necklaces of priceless, shimmering, great jewels, and whose feet are bowed to.

Regarding this Śrī-Indra-mantra: Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Jagatī is the meter (chanda); Śrī-Indra is the deity (devatā); Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Śrīṃ is the power (śakti); Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa).

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ—thus is the binding of the directions. [Offer] flowers and other items in the southeast: "We know the King of the Gods; we meditate upon him who holds the thunderbolt in his hand; may that Śakra inspire us. (3)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ, obeisance to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand; svāhā. || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consists of *hrāṃ*, *śrāṃ*, *klāṃ*, and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, with *vauṣaṭ*, one performs the full libation (*pūrṇā-tarpaṇa*), which is the *argha* for the cessation [of the breath].
Now, regarding the fire.

I meditate upon Agni, who possesses the luster of a hibiscus flower, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, and endowed with three eyes; he holds his desired power and the gesture of granting boons aloft with his long arms, wears matted locks bound upon his head, and is crowned with a diadem.

Of this Śrī Vaiśvānara mantra: Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Jagatī is the meter (chandas); Śrī Vaiśvānara is the deity (devatā); *raṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *troṃ* is the power (śakti); *hrīṃ* is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] flowers and other materials into the fire.
We know the one who holds the hand of Rudra; we meditate upon the one who holds the spear in his hand; may that Fire inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ troṃ rāṃ, grant me the siddhi of blazing with the mass of matted locks of Vaiśvānara, twice; svāhā! || 108 ||
*Drāṃ drīṃ*, etc.; with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, there is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, regarding Dharmarāja.

I worship in my heart the god Dharmarāja, who sits upon a lotus throne, blazing with the brilliance of the fire of the sun at the end of an aeon, and holding in his four arms the staff, the gesture of fearlessness, the lotus, and the boon-granting mudrā.

Of this mantra of Śrīdhara-rāja: the seer (ṛṣi) is Śrī Kālāgnibhairava; the meter (chandaḥ) is Triṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is Dharmarāja; *aiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *jūṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *hrāṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*). We know Vaivasvata; we meditate upon the one who holds a staff in his hand; may that Yama inspire us. (3)
Oṃ hrāṃ jūṃ aiṃ saḥ, obeisance to Dharmarāja, who holds a staff in his hand; svāhā! || 108 ||

The placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *hrāṃ* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* is used for the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). [Then follows] the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering of the vessel of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, [the ritual] for Nairṛta.

I meditate daily upon Nirṛti within the lotus of my heart— the supreme hero, who holds a spear, a mace, a goad, and a lotus in his arms; who resembles an autumnal cloud, wears crimson garments, and has blood-red eyes.

Of this Śrī Nirṛti mantra: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi); Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ); Śrī Nirṛti is the deity (devatā); Hrāṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hraiṃ is the power (śakti); Hraḥ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa) with flowers and other offerings.
We know the night-walker (niśācara); we meditate upon him who holds a sword in his hand; may that Nirṛti inspire us. (Recite three times.)
Oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ, homage to Nirṛti, who holds a sword in his hand. || 108 ||

The placement [of mantras] begins with *hrāṃ* and so forth. With the root mantra and *vauṣaṭ*, there is the full libation (*pūrṇā-tarpaṇa*) and the offering of the vessel of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now follows [the ritual] for Varuṇa.

I worship Varuṇa, who moves with the speed of the winds of universal destruction, who blazes like a thousand suns, who holds in his own arms the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā; who has three eyes, who is the fierce crocodile-bannered one (Kāma), who is praised by the fish and aquatic creatures, and who is the sole primordial sound worthy of praise.

Of this Śrī Varuṇa mantra: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); Śrī Varuṇa is the deity (devatā); Śrūṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Śraiṃ is the power (śakti); Śraḥ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa) with flowers and other offerings. [The offering] is in the fire, beginning with flowers.
We know the one with pure hands; we meditate upon the one with noose in hand; may that Varuṇa inspire us. || 3 ||
Śrīṃ śrūṃ juṃ saḥ, obeisance to the one with noose in hand, svāhā. || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with "Śrām" and so forth. With the root mantra, one performs the final offering (*pūrṇā*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the oblation for the seal of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, concerning Vāyu.

I worship the primordial Vāyu, the Lord of all gods, who possesses a stainless body with the brilliance of the rising sun, whose matted locks shine like gold, who holds a golden pitcher in his hand and is marked by the weapons of the twin lotuses; he is the life-breath of all worlds, adorned with white garments and other ornaments, whom I revere within my heart.

Of this venerable Vāyu-mantra: the blessed Pulastya is the seer (ṛṣi); Triṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); the venerable Vāyu is the deity (devatā); *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *hūṃ* is the power (śakti); *svāhā* is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire.
We know the one who is all life; we meditate upon the one whose hand is creation; may Vāyu inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ yaṃ klīṃ hūṃ, salutation to Vāyu, who holds a water-pot in his hand. || 108 ||

The ritual placement (nyāsa) begins with *klām* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* is used for the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). This is followed by the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering of the vessel of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, for Kubera.

I meditate upon the god Kubera in my heart— he who has the luster of a red lotus, whose form is like ten million suns, whose lotus-hands are marked with a spear and a rosary, who sits upon a majestic throne, whose face is smiling, and who possesses three eyes.

Of this Śrī Kubera mantra, Mahārudra is the seer (ṛṣi); Paṅkti is the meter (chandas); the illustrious Lord of Yakṣas, Kubera, is the deity (devatā); *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *mlūṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *hsauḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Let us know the Lord of Yakṣas; let us meditate upon him who holds a mace in his hand; may Kubera inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ mlūṃ hsauḥ, salutation to Kubera, who holds power in his hand. || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *klām* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full libation (*pūrṇā tarpaṇa*), which is the offering for the seal of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, regarding Īśāna.

I meditate upon Śiva, the Lord of Cows and Master of the Bull, who holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, possesses three eyes, whose limbs are radiant with ashes, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, who bears the Gaṅgā, and whose matted locks are bound together.

Of this Śrī Īśāna mantra: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Śrī Mahārudra is the deity (devatā), Rāṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hara is the power (śakti), Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire.
Let us know the Lord of All; let us meditate upon Him who holds a trident in His hand; may that Rudra inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ gāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, svāhā. || 108 ||

The ritual placement (nyāsa) begins with "gām" and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, saying "vauṣaṭ," one performs the full libation (pūrṇā-tarpaṇa), which is the offering for the seal of restraint (nirodhārgha).
Now, regarding Brahmā.
Brahmā is said to have four faces and be adorned with four arms; he wears a black antelope skin as his fourth [attribute] and is seated upon a lotus throne.
Having meditated upon him holding a water-pot and a staff, with a rosary and a lotus in his hands, one should place him upon the petals; this destroys all sins.

Of this Śrī Brahmā mantra: Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Śrī Brahmā is the deity (devatā); Hrāṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hūṃ is the power (śakti); Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire sacrifice (homa). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire.
We know him who is born from the lotus; we meditate upon him whose face is the Veda; may that Brahmā inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ hrāṃ hsauḥ, O Four-faced One, grant success, grant success, svāhā! || 108 ||

The ritual placement (nyāsa) begins with *hrāṃ* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, with *vauṣaṭ*, one performs the full libation (*pūrṇā tarpaṇa*) and the offering of the vessel for restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, [the ritual] for Nārāyaṇa.

From the feet to the knees it is like excellent gold; from the region of the navel downwards it has the luster of pearls; from the region of the throat it is like the rising sun; and from the head it is dark blue.

I bow to the primordial Varāha, who holds in his hands the earth, the discus, the sword, the shield, the mace, the spear, the gift-gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and whose tusks gleam brilliantly.

Of this Śrī Nārāyaṇa mantra: Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi); Triṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Śrī Nārāyaṇa is the deity (devatā); Śrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire.
We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! || 108 ||

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *śrāṃ hrāṃ* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* is used for the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). This is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering of the vessel of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).

By this mantra-homa, may the ten guardians of the directions be pleased; may they be satisfied. Then follow the mantras of the nine planets, which were previously written within the section on the homa of barley and sesame seeds.
Then follows the fire-oblation (homa) of the eight Bhairavas.
He is sky-clad, the Lord Bhairava, four-armed and three-eyed, holding a skull, a sword, an axe, and a spear in his hands.
One should meditate upon the Lord Bhairavanāyaka, whose limbs are adorned with serpents, who is embellished with ashes, bones, and snake-jewels, and who is seated upon a corpse.
Of this glorious mantra of the Eight Bhairavas: the seer (ṛṣi) is Śrī Sadāśiva; the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Aṣṭabhairava.

*Hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *oṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *krīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*); this is the application (*viniyoga*) in the fire-oblation (*homa*). *Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ devadatta hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*.
Hrāṃ, and so forth. Oṃ kṣmryūṃ, obeisance to Kapāleśa Bhairava. (108)

Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Śikhivāhana Bhairava. || 108 || Oṃ kṣūṃ, obeisance to Krodharāja Bhairava. || 108 || Oṃ jhrūṃ, obeisance to Vikarāla Bhairava. || 108 || Oṃ hvū-āṃ, obeisance to Manmatha Bhairava. || 108 || Oṃ hryūṃ, obeisance to Meghanāda Bhairava. || 108 || Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Somarāja Bhairava. || 108 || Oṃ hrkṣmlvyūṃ, obeisance to Vidyārāja Bhairava. || 108 ||
At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" constitutes the full oblation (pūrṇā). This is the libation (tarpaṇa) and the offering of the vessel of restraint (nirodhārgha).
Now, O Mahāgaṇapati!
His lotus-like hands hold a citron, a mace, a bow, a trident, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, his own tusk, a jewel-filled jar, and a water-pot.

He is to be meditated upon as embraced by his beloved, the ornament of the world, whose lotus-hands rest upon him; he who effects the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the universe, the remover of obstacles, and the bestower of supreme goals. [Offer] flowers and other substances into the fire.
Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon the one with the elephant’s face and trunk; may that Dantī inspire us. || 3 ||
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of excellent boons, bring all people under my control; svāhā! || 108 ||
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, O beloved of Gaṇapati, bestower of the most excellent boons, bring the hearts of all people under my control, bring them under my control!
"Gām," and so forth; with the root mantra followed by "vauṣaṭ," there is the full oblation (pūrṇā), the libation (tarpaṇa), and the offering for restraint (nirodhārgha).
Now, [the ritual] for Nandeśvara.

I bow to that Bhairava, who is of beautiful form, established in the beautiful *māla*, self-known, possessing his own splendor, consisting of his own bliss, and well-established in his excellent power.
The god possesses the radiance of ten billion suns and the coolness of ten billion moons; he has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes.
Seated in the midst of an ocean of nectar, established upon the Brahma-lotus, mounted on a bull, blue-throated, and adorned with all ornaments.
Resembling a heap of vermilion, with a luster like a ruby; resembling the color of jasmine and cinnabar, and possessing the radiance of a pomegranate flower.
The God holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga, resounds with the ringing of a bell and a ḍamaru drum, and wields a noose and a goad, with a mace and a club in his hands.
The god holds a sword and a shield in his hands, with a lily and a trident in his other hands; he bears a red spear and is adorned with a severed head and a skull-topped staff.
[He visualizes] Mahādeva, mounted upon Rudra, adorned with all ornaments, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and the destroyer of all diseases.
The meditation on the God of gods is proclaimed as the "Red" meditation; in union with him is the Goddess Surā, whose radiance is equal to ten million moons.
White as snow, jasmine, and the moon, she has five faces and three eyes; she is endowed with eighteen arms, with all her weapons raised in her hands.
The large-eyed goddess, laughing, stood face-to-face with the God of gods; or rather, [she stood before] the Lord of the lords of gods, the omnipresent Ardhanārīśvara.
One should meditate upon Ānandabhairava—the red-limbed one, accompanied by his Goddess, saluted by Brahmā and Acyuta, and the sole cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Of this mantra of Śrī Ānandeśvara Bhairava, Kālāgnirudra Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); Samrāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ); Ānandeśvara Bhairava is the deity (devatā); Śrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka).
The application for the domestic rite (*viniyoga*). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire:

*oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ ānandeśvarabhairavāya vauṣaṭ svāhā* (108 times). *oṃ juṃ saḥ hsrkṣmlvyūṃ*, with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*; thus is the full libation (*pratipūrṇā tarpaṇa*) and the obstructing offering (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, [the ritual] of Vaṭubhairava.

Victorious is Vaṭukanātha, the bestower of accomplishments upon practitioners; he holds a skull in his hand, wears earrings, carries a staff, possesses the hue of thick darkness, and has a serpent as his sacred thread—the cause for severing obstacles during the performance of sacrificial rites.

Of this mantra of Śrī Vaṭukabhairava: the seer (ṛṣi) is Vṛhadāraṇyaka; the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Vaṭukabhairava; *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *vaṭukāya* is the power (*śakti*); *oṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Flowers and other offerings in the fire.
Oṃ hrīṃ! To Vaṭuka, for the removal of calamities, perform [this] twice! To Vaṭuka, hrīṃ svāhā! || 108 ||
Hrāṃ vāṃ, and so forth.

One should meditate upon and worship Vaṭuka, who is white, has one face, and three eyes; he wears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, possesses a right-facing countenance, dances, and carries a noose, a goad, a hand-drum, and other implements; he is established upon the northern seat.
At the end of the root mantra, "vauṣaṭ" constitutes the full oblation (pūrṇā). The libation (tarpaṇa) is the offering for the seal (nirodhārgha).
Now, the [mantra] of Vetālabhairava.
He has flaming hair, three eyes, and is as terrifying as the lord of serpents; he wears a garland of severed heads and holds a flaying knife, a skull-cup, a hand-drum, and a great dark-blue trident.
I bow to the Vetāla, who is as radiant as the rising sun, skilled in playing the lute held against his chest with both arms, and who laughs while absorbed in the performance of dance.

Of this Śrīvetāla mantra: Rudra is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrīvetālabhairava is the deity (devatā), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Śrīṃ is the power (śakti), Oṃ is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa). [Offer] flowers and other items into the fire.
We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon the one of terrible form; may that Vetāla inspire us. || 3 ||

Hrāṃ, and so forth.
With hair like flames, adorned with serpents, of fierce form, three-eyed, the remover of fear, and the bestower of fear upon enemies.

Six oblations with the root mantra into the fire constitute the *pūrṇāhuti*; thereafter, the libation (*tarpaṇa*). [This is] the *argha* for the restraint.

KṢAṂ, svāhā to the face of Īśāna! YAṂ, svāhā to the face of Tatpuruṣa! RAṂ, svāhā to the face of Aghora! VAṂ, svāhā to the face of Vāmadeva! LAṂ, svāhā to the face of Sadyojāta!

To Abhaya; to Muṇḍa; to Khaṭvāṅga; to Vīṇā; to Ḍamaru; to Ghaṇṭā; to Triśūla; to Vajra.

Now follows the fire-oblation for the seven enclosures.

The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), the lords of the Gaṇas and others, the world-protectors (Lokapālas), the Mothers (Mātṛs), the Planets (Grahas), the Nāgas, and those beginning with Avaraṇa and Vajra—these are said to constitute the seven enclosures (Avaraṇas).
Therein, first are the Vidyeshvaras.

Oṃ hrīṃ anantāya svāhā | Oṃ jhrūṃ sukṣmāya svāhā || Oṃ mūṃ śivottamāya svāhā || Oṃ hrūṃ ekanetrāya svāhā || Oṃ kṣyāṃ ekarudrāya svāhā || Oṃ blūṃ trimūrtaye svāhā || Oṃ hjūṃ śrīkaṇṭhāya svāhā || Oṃ śrīṃ śikhaṇḍine svāhā ||
